item.dc:creator: 投资TALK君
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、市场"预设仓位"理论的隐藏悖论：越是被完美预测的事件，越不会按预测走

小涛这期最精彩的核心并非"仓位比事件重要"这句话本身，而是他不经意间揭示了一个反身性陷阱：当7月市场对"美联储鹰派+利率上行"形成一致预期后，所有本应下跌的资产（黄金、比特币、软件、大科技）反而集体上涨了。这不是宏观框架失效，而是共识本身消耗了做空的燃料——当每个人都为某个剧本清空仓位时，剧本就再也无法上演。

这里有一个反直觉的观察：一个分析师"预测极准"的时刻，恰恰是市场共识最脆弱的时刻。小涛7月的展望之所以"打了满分"，不是因为他看对了宏观，而是因为他站在了共识的反面——他做的是"仓位分析"而非"宏观分析"。这两件事经常被混为一谈，但本质完全不同：宏观分析问"世界会怎样"，仓位分析问"人们已经为怎样的世界下注了"。

二、跨领域连接：可口可乐的估值区间与心理学的"锚定漂移"

小涛画可口可乐20-26倍PE区间时，我看到的其实是行为经济学中的"参考点稳定性"——一家公司16年只在6倍PE的窄带内波动，说明市场对它的定价机制已经"仪式化"了。这和神经科学里的习惯回路（habit loop）惊人相似：当刺激-反应-奖励足够重复，大脑会跳过前额叶评估，直接进入自动化。市场对可口可乐就是这种"自动化定价"。

这带来一个跨领域洞察：真正的价值股护城河不在产品，而在"估值区间的心理仪式感"。可口可乐的护城河，一半是可乐配方，另一半是"华尔街分析师用什么框架看它"——后者数十年没变。反观科技股，估值锚每两三年就要被彻底重置一次，这才是"成长股波动大"的深层原因，而不是业绩本身。

三、被忽略的信号：小涛的"击球区间"术语背后，藏着一个被资管业刻意回避的真相

小涛用"击球区间"（借自巴菲特-泰德·威廉姆斯）来形容Costco和沃尔玛的当下估值，但他悄悄透露了一个更颠覆的观点："美股不要看指数，要看估值和参与度"。这句话如果推到极致，等于宣告了ETF时代的一个尴尬——大部分被动投资者其实在做一件"数据上不成立"的事：他们盯着的价格指数，是最不能反映"贵还是便宜"的指标。

更让人意外的连接是：小涛提到的"参与度20日均线才19%" 这个指标，本质上是市场的"生态多样性指数"，和生态学里的香农多样性指数（Shannon Index）结构完全一致。当参与度过低（少数股票扛指数）时，系统的抗扰动能力反而增强——因为多样性崩塌到了极限，任何一个信息冲击都难以让系统更差。这解释了为什么"最悲观的时刻"往往是最安全的时刻：不是估值便宜带来安全，而是"参与者结构的单一化"耗尽了继续恶化的可能性。

一个可以带走的思维工具：以后看市场，不要问"利好还是利空"，要问三件事——谁还没在场？谁已经全仓了？谁已经绝望离场了？ 前者是子弹，后两者是限制。事件只是扣动扳机的手，而是否有子弹在膛，才决定枪响之后发生什么。

📝 转录文本

精准预测的背后：仓位（SETUP）大于一切

开场：为什么"仓位"比事件本身更重要

在以前的视频里面，我经常和大家分享，每当我们要进入数据或者事件之前，我说数据和事件不是最重要的，重要的是进入这个数据和事件之前市场的一个仓位、市场的一个 setup 是什么，它影响了事件之后市场的一个走势。

今天我们针对这个观点，我们把时间线拉长一些，那拉长到一个季度、拉长到两个季度，那这样的一个概念或者这样的一个理论怎么去应用到更长的一个时间维度。

然后第二部分，本周 Costco 将会发布财报，正好前段时间有人让我聊一下 Costco，那今天我们就去聊必需品消费板块里边的一些权重股，比如说 Costco、沃尔玛、宝洁，还有可口可乐。我们从估值这个角度去出发，从基本面这个角度去出发，和大家分享一下怎么去看待这些标的的一个思路。

欢迎大家来到一个不单只聊新闻的专业美股频道，我是市场分析师小涛。在开始之前，大家记得留言、点赞加转发，让更多的人可以看到我们这期内容。

一、过去一周及7月以来市场走势回顾

1. 利率与美债

我们先一起回顾一下过去一周市场的一个走势，包括7月份以来市场的一个走势，然后我们展开去聊一下为什么整个市场的一个 setup 和仓位比起事件本身的一个结果会来得更加的重要。

过去一周资产价格的走势：美债收益率两年期上涨了12个基点，十年期只上涨了3个基点，TLT 上涨了0.5%，说明整条利率曲线在变得更加的平稳。

那随着接下去加息的这个预期，长端这一块我的一个期待是短期之内是会往下降的，包括贝森特在中期选举之前的这个布局，短期之内长债这块的利率有下降的这个动力在那边。

把时间线拉长，从一个长期角度去看的话，不论是美国国债这一块的一个增发也好，整个市场长期的一个方向，美国国债的利率应该是往上的。那么但是加息本身或者一个激进的美联储本身，无论是对于长端这一块的通胀也好，还是未来 GDP 的这个增速也好，都是一个抑制的作用，抑制的作用就会使得长端短期之内这个利率会往下降。

2. 股市：波动看似巨大，结果却很平静

那股市这边，上周其实发生了很多事情。那么从上周末开始就有 AI 这一块的放缓，然后美联储会议，然后日本央行的加息，然后又到周五的一个三巫日。最终我们会发现整个市场的波动其实非常的小：标普500仅仅下跌了0.1%，纳指还反弹了0.7%，道指下跌了1.7%。

所以在这样的一个市场里面，如果站在一周之前，你可能很难想象那一周之后我们好像什么事情都没有发生。你只要仓位持有在那边的话，其实就还好。

但是每一天，如果你真的把这个精力全放在每一天的走势，试图去合理化的话，你会发现很难去解释。对吗？周三美联储会议那天，美联储出来之后，美联储变鹰，市场下跌；然后周四马上出现了反弹，周五也出现了小幅的反弹，但是延续了周四这个反弹。你没办法理解为什么美联储鹰派然后股市却出现反弹。

所以很多时候，但我如果我们退后一步去看的话，你会发现其实还好。从另外其他的一些维度——从估值、从市场参与度，你就不会对于这一次美联储的一个加息感到非常的恐慌。

3. 板块表现：银行下跌，科技相对强势

过去一周 IGV 软件板块上涨了2.8%，比特币还上涨了4.9%，黄金上涨了0.7%。从板块这个角度去看，银行板块下跌了将近5%。

我这边画了一个箭头，为什么？市场的一个交易一个逻辑线就是：如果当美联储开始进入加息这个周期，无论是加息两次还是三次也好，对于银行板块来说应该是一个利空。因为银行板块是靠利差，那你短端这一块——短端就是银行板块借钱的这个成本——当你短端这一块的利率出现上升的时候，对于银行的盈利模式来说是一个利空。所以银行板块下跌了5%。

然后上一周反弹的板块呢，之所以标普100几乎没有任何的下跌，是因为前期大科技股相对来说非常的强势，上涨了1.1%。等权指数是下跌了1.2%的，所以整个指数整个美股其实是出现下跌的，很多多数的板块都出现下跌。标普没出现下跌是因为前期它科技股的强势和芯片板块的相对强势。

二、7月以来的"反直觉"表现：宏观解释不了的走势

那上涨了1.1%。然后我们换一个视角看一下 QQQ 七月份以来的这个走势。我这边有红色这个框框和黄色这个框框。红色这个框框，我们看一下这个背景，看完背景之后，你很难想象会出现黄色框框里的这种结果。

背景（宏观逆风）： - 七月份以来两个半月左右的一个时间 - 美债收益率两年期上涨了57个基点 - 十年期上涨了53个基点 - TLT 下跌6% - 油价还上涨了44%

结果（风险资产反而大涨）： - 黄金上涨9% - IGV 软件板块上涨15% - 比特币上涨38% - 医疗板块上涨6.1% - 芯片下跌了17% - 前七大科技股上涨9.4%

在我们传统的一个定义里边，如果美债收益率出现上升，大科技应该上涨还是下跌？那这就是我说的，在进入这些事件之前，整个市场的一个 setup 和仓位的一个问题。

三、复盘：7月初的下半年展望为何"精准"

我们回顾一下，我在七月初的时候，我对今年下半年做了一个展望。当时我这个展望里面，你现在站在当下你去看我当时这个展望，现在回过头来看，我自己也觉得非常的厉害。为什么会非常厉害？你会发现我聊的很多的板块，几乎所有的板块全部——就我认为会上涨的板块全部上涨，然后我认为会出现下跌的板块也出现下跌了。

在7月初做下半年展望的时候，里边我有聊到几点：

第一点： 我说纳指可能会出现7%~10%的调整，而这个调整是由硬件板块所带领。半导体板块7月份到现在为止下跌了17%。

第二点： 然后我说去平衡一些仓位，比如说医疗板块是可以去加的，大科技是可以去加的。医疗板块上涨6.1%，大科技上涨9.4%。

第三点： 我说软件板块都是便宜的。软件板块今年上半年情绪面是非常非常低的，那么7月份以来，软件板块上涨了15.2%。

当然，你也可以理解为市场是在硬件和软件之间的这个调整，硬件的下跌使得软件出现反弹。到最近这段时间，我仍然看到了一部分软件和硬件板块之间日内的这一个背离——就完全就是一个负相关，只要软件上涨，然后硬件就要下跌，然后反过来也是一样。

那所以也可以理解为硬件板块的一个调整带来了软件板块的这个反弹。但是我认为软件板块的反弹还是可以持续的，甚至于我认为今年的下半年我们可能会看到软件和硬件同时出现上涨。所以我认为软件板块这一波的反弹并没有结束，因为接下去还会真正发现 AI 的这个落地在软件板块这些标的身上的这个体现。

关于英特尔： 英特尔我当时说现在也不是——因为英特尔的时候我在5月份6月份就已经进行减仓了。减仓完之后我认为7月份以后进下半年也不用再去减仓，但是英特尔还是进行了一波从七月份开始然后到八月份的时候，最多下跌了34%、35%，然后最近这段时间出现了一个反弹。所以英特尔也算是走了一波过山车吧。

关于宏观和黄金： 然后我说宏观这块可能会有些噪音。那最后是黄金这一块，我认为长期可以布局的。黄金7月份到现在上涨9.2%，比特币进入加仓区域，上涨了38%。

关键洞察：所有跑赢的资产，都是上半年被"唾弃"的

你回过头去看，无论是黄金也好、比特币也好，包括软件、包括大科技——今年的大科技今年上半年是下跌了2% YTD，下跌了2%。标普是上涨了多少？我觉得8%、9%吧，但标普的一个上涨主要是来自于硬件，主要是来自于半导体。

所以我这边聊的，或者我们今年下半年所看到的走得好的一些标的，全部是今年上半年市场所唾弃的这些标的——黄金也好、比特币也好、软件也好，包括大科技也好。

所以你再回过头你把下半年利率的这个上涨，然后和这些标的的上涨结合在一起，你会发现宏观是没有办法去解释的。那唯一的一个解释是什么？就是真的是非常超卖，在这些标的身上已经没有仓位了。那只要这些标的有这个基本面，在没有仓位的情况下，你出现其他任何的一些消息，都可以把这些标的给带回来。

四、往未来看：硬件、AI Agent 与市场 Setup

那在当下这种情况下呢，很多人问我如果我们往未来去看应该怎么去看？我认为硬件板块这一波的调整可能已经接近于底部，甚至于从比较短期这个角度去看，我认为市场最悲观的这个时间点可能就是上周一——上周一就是上周末说 AI 要放缓的这一波恐慌带来周一的这个下跌，非常有可能就是短期之内一个低点。

然后这边我还想有第四点，我想要的是 AI Agent 这一块的落地比想象的是要慢很多。那我在7月份当时做出的一个判断，其实在整个九月份我们看到了 Meta 推出了一个 AI Agent 之后，我认为接下去 AI Agent 起码在今年的下半年，包括在27年的上半年，我们将会看到有更多和 AI Agent 相关的这个故事线所产生，无论是在 GPU 身上，还是在这些模型公司身上。

所以在最近这段时间，因为整个 AI——你想一下，如果是 Meta 的 Muse 是一个落地点的话，上一次一个落地什么时候？是年初的时候，年初的一个 DeepSeek。DeepSeek 到 Muse 中间有七八个月的一个真空时间，那整个 AI 一直是没有任何的一些消息。那直到 Muse 落地之后，我的期待是接下去在 AI Agent 这一块可能也会看到慢慢的一个加速。

硬件板块的 Setup：估值与参与度双低

那硬件板块的一个 setup，就是你去看一下半导体的估值，半导体估值现在就是在一个相当低的这个位置。其实从三大指数去看吧，无论是标普也好、纳指也好、半导体也好，其实现在都是在一个相对比较低的位置。

那估值本身就是一个 setup。估值是一个模糊正确，是一个相对比较长这个概念，起码是三个月对吧，两到三个月左右。因为半导体估值最高的时候是在六月底的时候，六月底七月初的时候，当时在28倍29倍左右，当时是在一个高点。然后就经过一个多月的一个回调之后，现在来到18倍左右吧。这是一个 setup——估值在低点是一个 setup。

另外一个 setup 是什么？市场的一个参与度。 你看一下标普百，上周五市场的一个参与度：20日均线才19%，连20%都不到；50日均线也是停在28%。

所以从参与度这个角度去看，我一直和大家说参与度是一个模糊正确，但是从参与度这个模糊正确的一个指标也告诉我们，当下的情绪面就是在一个低点。

不要只看指数，要看估值和参与度

我个人认为我们在看美股的时候，尽量去避开这个指数——尽量去避开指数从最高点下跌了多少，然后认为可能指数还会有15%、10%这种下跌幅度。我不认为这是一个比较好的角度。

特别是如果大家是从币圈转移过来的话，因为币圈你没有基本面，无论任何一个标的都没有基本面。但是美股是有基本面的，美股的基本面是 EPS 这个增速，之所以有了 EPS 才会有 PE 才会有估值这个概念在里边。

所以看美股的话，我个人认为到底是贵还是便宜、是高还是低，比起指数、比起这个价格本身，更加应该去看的是一个估值，或者是从参与度这个角度也可以去理解。一个是相对比较短期的（参与度），估值的话可能会相对长期一些。

那所以把这些东西全部结合在一起，包括我在上周和大家分享另外一个指标——AAII 投资情绪面指标，你会发现从很多的一些指标可以看到，一个模糊正确的一个角度可以看到当下的市场情绪面就是低的，估值也是在一个便宜的阶段。

这就是一个 setup。在这种 setup 情况下，你说我还会去花非常多的精力去担心宏观这一块有没有些风险吗？我不会。

所以 setup 仓位本身、市场的这个仓位、情绪面本身是非常的重要，比起这个事件、数据来说会显得更加的重要。

把概念再放大一点：长期做多，短期加减仓

然后我再把这个概念稍微聊得笼统一点。因为我们在聊美股的时候，美股是有基本面的，个股也是有基本面，然后指数本身也是有基本面。很简单，就是个股或者指数本身，它的基本面没有变糟糕或者在持续变好的情况下，短期之内无非就是涨多了就跌、跌多了就涨，但是从长期这个角度去看就是一个向上的趋势。

所以我们从一个市场参与者这个角度去看，长期就是应该去做多，然后短期根据不同的一些指标去判断，进行在标的身上的加仓和减仓，但并不是 all in 或者清仓。

五、必需品消费板块：估值与基本面剖析

好，然后我们切换一个话题来聊一些防守属性比较强的这一个板块里边的一些标的——必需品消费。

1. Costco：进入合理估值区间

首先是 Costco。Costco 的话正好是上周有人问我。我们看下 Costco 的一个估值，截止到上周五的收盘 39.29 倍。那在5月初的时候，在2025年初的时候，55倍的这个估值。从 EPS 增速年化10%这个角度去出发，这类的标的55倍的估值明显是非常非常贵的，对吗？

那从2025年年初的一个55倍现在来到了39倍，39倍是什么概念？

估值对比方法的重要提醒： 我强调，我没办法拿 Costco 的这个估值和它的一个增速去和比如科技公司去做对比——你没办法对比的。市场愿意给 Costco 这一类的公司一个相对来说的一个溢价。你也没有办法拿一个 PEG ratio 去衡量 Costco，这也是一个非常错误的一个视角。你说"哎，Costco 的 PEG ratio 是3倍，所以 Costco 的这个估值比如说你和 AMD 去做对比的话，就比 AMD 的估值要贵"——不可以这么去做纵向的这个对比。在同一个板块里边你可以拿 PE 过去就去做对比，在不同的板块里面不能这样去做一个对比。

所以 Costco 是一个比较好的可以和它估值本身可以和历史上的一个估值去做一个横向的一个对比。

两个阶段的估值区间： - 第一阶段（2019-2023）： Costco 的估值就是在 30-39 倍这个区间里边波动。短期之内，可能在21年底、22年初的时候，可能会去到45倍左右，但是你会发现在22年、23年还是回来了。所以第一个阶段 Costco 的估值就是在30至39倍里边，四年左右的时间在这个估值区间里边横动。 - 第二阶段（2024至今）： 然后2024年开始估值不断地上升，2025年年初的时候见顶，然后25年26年其实都是在修复估值这个过程之中。

那现在这个估值在39倍，去到了第一个阶段的一个上区间，我认为已经进入了一个合理的区间。如果再往下的话，一个更加合理或者更加低估的一个估值是在35倍。我并不认为 Costco 的估值可以跌到30倍。

所以从这个角度去看，当然这是个比较主观的看法——Costco 现在这个价格本身已经进入了一个击球区间。

2. 沃尔玛：与 Costco 对比

然后把沃尔玛的估值加进来，你会发现：

第一个观察： 蓝白色这条线（Costco）一直是高于蓝色这条线（沃尔玛）——市场一直是愿意给 Costco 更高的这个估值。

第二个观察： 沃尔玛的估值上周五的收盘34.4倍。你会发现从四五月份以来，白色和蓝色这条线都出现了下降——其实市场是在杀跌整个必需品消费板块。

然后沃尔玛本身，你会发现在2025年的3月份，当时是一个相对估值的一个低点，是在30倍。所以沃尔玛和 Costco 本身，我认为这两个价格、这两个标的或这两家公司，都进入了一个击球区间。从这个位置开始都进入击球区间，再下面那个估值就是从现在这个点位下去10%左右。

3. Costco 技术面

然后是 Costco 的技术面。我这边看的是日 K 线，日 K 线然后结合下面的那个 RSI。

我看到2025年、2026年，我下面有一二三四五五个箭头。这五个箭头你会发现，从日 K 线 RSI 这个角度去看，Costco 其实很少会去碰到 RSI 30 以下，它不会去到很低，它不会去到20或者十几。基本上就是在30——正好碰到30，在31或者说28、26左右，RSI 就会进入一个阶段性的底部。

那所以截止到上周五的收盘，差不多是在35、36，应该30、35至40之间嘛。所以你说下跌还有没有空间？也许还有一些空间，但是已经进入了一个技术区间了。

六、可口可乐：估值已在上区间

然后我们来看下一个标的——可口可乐。可口可乐也非常的有意思，它是必需品消费里面的第三大权重股。可口可乐的估值就明显比前两家公司强很多。

你可以看一下，我从2014年到现在，过去十几年——将近要16年左右的一个 PE。在从2014年到现在为止，我画了一个上区间和下区间：上区间是在26倍，下区间是在20倍，非常的明显对吧。估值就是在这一个区间里边去进行波动。

当然了，短期之内因为一些事件，比如说2020年，估值一度跌到了17倍。那这种事件它不是一个——我们不应该期待疫情这种事件会经常发生，所以不能够把17倍的估值就当做是一个可口可乐一个低区间。你不能这么去做。所以一个合理的低区间就是在20倍左右，在没有非常重大的事件出来的情况下。上区间也非常的明显，曾经有三次碰到过，就是在26倍。

那现在的估值在多少？现在的估值在 25.5 倍。 所以现在可口可乐的估值明显是在一个上区间。所以在这种时候，可口可乐你应不应该去追？绝对不应该去追的。 你可以继续持有，甚至于你在这个位置如果仓位比较大的话，其实可口可乐应该去做一些减仓的。

基本面是否支持突破区间？

当然很多时候我们看到一个标的或者一家公司，它的估值去到了历史比较高的这个位置，我们必须要去关注它的基本面有没有变好、有没有改变。如果基本面真的有变好、有改变的话，那是值得市场去给它一个比以前还要高的这个估值，或者说可以突破前面的26倍。

那我们来看一下市场的这个预期：

营收增速： - 第一个圈里边是营收的这个增速，2026年是4%，27年、28年市场预期是1%和5% - 和前三年的6%、2%、2%，其实没有太大的一些差别

EPS 增速： - 这一块稍微会好一些，26年的话10%，27、28年市场的预期7%、7% - 差不多就是23至25年的一个平均数

所以简单地扫一下，对比营收也好、EPS 的增速也好，其实并没有比过去这段时间走出了一个更高的一个区间。

更深入的基本面指标：Organic Revenue Growth

那如果我们有关注这一个标的，简单的知道一下这家公司的一个基本面，其实有一些比较好的去衡量这家公司基本面的一些指标，比如说 Organic Revenue Growth。

22年到25年的同比增速：16%、12%、12% 和 15%。而在过去，特别是23年、22年至24年这段时间，它的营收增速非常的高。为什么？来自于哪里？主要是来自于涨价（Price and Mix）。那三年涨价分别是11%、10%和11%，三年的涨价幅度非常的高。

但是未来四年你可以看一下市场的预期，每年的涨价就是在2%~3%左右。因为在没有通胀的情况下，每年的涨价幅度自然就不会很高，但是每年都会涨价。

最终营收的这个增速来自于哪？来自于涨价和他们这个 unit case——你卖出了多少个单量。从单量这个角度去看： - 22年至24年每一年 5%、2%、1%，其实就是一个低增速 - 然后未来的四年是 3%、2%，都基本上在2%至3%之间

你把单量的这个增速加上它的一个 Price/Mix，再加上它通胀的这个涨幅加在一起，差不多就是在5%。所以在未来四年，你可以看一下 Organic Revenue Growth 平均每年就是在5%。那5%就是过去这段时间的一个常态。

所以像可口可乐这一类基本面非常稳的这一类的公司，你想它那个营收增速——organic revenue growth 就是5%，加上它一部分的运营效率——那它每一年 EPS 这个增速就会停在9%至10%左右。那么这已经是最好状态了；差一点的话就是7%至8%，营收增速5%然后你的 EPS 增速就是在7%至8%。

所以看现在，根据现在市场的预期去看的话，其实市场也并不预期可口可乐走出了以前的这种营收或者盈利增速的一个常态，就还是和以前一样。所以它基本面并没有出现非常大的一个变好或者变糟糕。

那在这种情况下，你再回到前面那个估值这种状态下，当下在25.5倍，最高区间是26倍，那现在就是在一个相对偏高的一个估值区间里边。那有了这样的一个模糊正确，然后再匹配自己的这个仓位，就应该知道自己的仓位应该怎么去做了。

就像我前面说，如果仓位非常大的话，像可口可乐现在在比较高的一个估值区间，就是应该去进行减仓；但是你仓位比较小的时候，你就可以继续持有，或者说去做一些移动止盈。

移动止盈的技巧：价值股 vs 成长股

那讲到移动止盈，因为这些是价值股，价值股的波动本身就小。那么所以价值股你在做移动止盈的时候，和一些成长股和半导体你在做移动止盈的时候，这个波动和范围一定是不一样的。半导体的话，比如说你去做10%的这个移动止盈；这些价值股身上，你最多只能做4%至5%。你要这些价值股你去做10%的移动止盈，可能就会把你以前非常大的这一波涨幅全部擦掉了，因为价值股的波动本身就小。

七、宝洁：估值在相对低位

好，最后是宝洁。那宝洁其实也是类似的。宝洁的话当下收盘估值是在 20.74 倍。那这个估值其实离最高点26倍其实是有一段距离的。然后下区间我这边画了两条线，分别是在20倍和18倍。那我认为20倍是便宜的，如果去到18倍的话就是非常便宜。

宝洁的这个估值现在也是在一个相对比较低的这个位置。

估值低位买入的安全边际逻辑

估值本身它是一个模糊正确，我一直是聊它没办法告诉我们、帮我们去判断短期之内的一个低点或者高点。但是当估值在一个相对比较低位的时候，我们去买入这些标的，我们下面的一个安全边际就会比较的大。

并且如果我们买在估值的一个低位，我们要知道，因为这些公司它的 EPS 增速是都是正的，那未来我们可以获得的这个价格上的一个回报可以来自于第一点——估值上的这个回归。

举例说明： 宝洁，我不是建议大家去买宝洁，我自己也没有，比如说宝洁的估值如果从现在20.7倍反弹到了原来的23倍，那就是你估值就带给你10%的价格上的一个反弹。在这个基础上，我们假设它花一年的这个时间，那么从20.7倍到23倍，在这个基础上它的 EPS 的这个增速如果还能够有5%~10%，那全部加在一起，你价格上的这个回报就是在15%~20%。

那么对于一个价值股来说，一年能给出这样的一个回报已经是非常好的这种结果了。

好吧，那希望这一类估值的分享对大家有帮助。

八、公告与活动

温哥华线下活动

然后今天再和大家分享活动 CFA 之前，有一个东西我想聊一下——公告。我在上一次一期视频里面我有聊过，10月3日早上9点至12点，那天是周六，我会在温哥华做一个线下，场地我已经找好了，这个场地还不小，那现在还有一些位置。

大家如果感兴趣的话，可以通过置顶留言里面的这个链接去进行报名。还是非常期待和大家线下的这个交流的，没有任何的门槛，如果你报名只要能够过来的话——我不会抽啊，你提前报名的话我就提前预约你了。然后我会在活动开始的可能四五天之前把地点分享给大家，这个地点我已经找好。置顶的这个留言里面可以进行报名。

Seeking Alpha 量化选股策略

然后就是我们今天的活动——Seeking Alpha。那 Seeking Alpha 首先是他们那个量化选股策略，现在这个量化选股策略也可以免费试用了，并且第一年可以立即节省50美金。

在两三个月之前，他们推出了另外一个量化选股策略，那这个量化选股策略是针对一些防守属性非常强的这些标的，那所以他们叫做 Quant Growth and Income，包括他很多选的一些标的都是有 Dividend、都是派股息的。那这一个策略本身现在第一年也会有50美金的这个优惠。

所以我会把 Seeking Alpha 这两个量化选股的这个策略的订阅连接放在置顶的留言里边。

那今天这期内容就到这边，我们下期见，拜拜。

item.description:
## 一、市场"预设仓位"理论的隐藏悖论：越是被完美预测的事件，越不会按预测走
小涛这期最精彩的核心并非"仓位比事件重要"这句话本身，而是他不经意间揭示了一个**反身性陷阱**：当7月市场对"美联储鹰派+利率上行"形成一致预期后，所有本应下跌的资产（黄金、比特币、软件、大科技）反而集体上涨了。这不是宏观框架失效，而是**共识本身消耗了做空的燃料**——当每个人都为某个剧本清空仓位时，剧本就再也无法上演。
这里有一个反直觉的观察：**一个分析师"预测极准"的时刻，恰恰是市场共识最脆弱的时刻**。小涛7月的展望之所以"打了满分"，不是因为他看对了宏观，而是因为他站在了共识的反面——他做的是"仓位分析"而非"宏观分析"。这两件事经常被混为一谈，但本质完全不同：宏观分析问"世界会怎样"，仓位分析问"人们已经为怎样的世界下注了"。
## 二、跨领域连接：可口可乐的估值区间与心理学的"锚定漂移"
小涛画可口可乐20-26倍PE区间时，我看到的其实是**行为经济学中的"参考点稳定性"**——一家公司16年只在6倍PE的窄带内波动，说明市场对它的定价机制已经"仪式化"了。这和神经科学里的**习

item.title: [Lex Clips] Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) vs Psychoanalysis | Andrew Scull and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被战争偶然塑造的心理范式

最让人意外的一点是：CBT 之所以能成为今天的主流治疗范式，很大程度上不是因为它临床上更"真"，而是因为它的行政基因更适合美国的资助生态。当访谈中一句轻描淡写的话浮现——"临床心理学家花两年学科学方法和研究，于是他们知道怎么申请联邦经费，而精神分析师完全不懂"——这句话其实是整个心理治疗史的暗门钥匙。

也就是说，CBT 的胜利首先是赠款申请书写作水平的胜利，其次才是疗效的胜利。二战时因人力短缺被临时征召的心理学家，无意中获得了一份"能被科学化包装"的方法论嫁妆；他们回国后，恰好碰上 NIMH 和退伍军人管理局的资金洪流。这不是达尔文式的"最强者生存"，而是一种更冷酷的"最可拨款者生存"——一种疗法能否存活，取决于它能否被写进一份15页的 R01 申请书里。

与软件开发的隐秘同构

这里有一个很少被指出的跨领域连接：CBT 与敏捷开发（Agile / MVP）几乎是同一种认识论，而精神分析则是"瀑布模型"。

  • 精神分析说：先做完整需求分析（童年、无意识、移情），再重构整个系统架构（人格），历时数年，无法中途验证；
  • CBT 说：识别一个具体症状（bug），写一个可复现的处理流程（sprint），跑一个 6–12 周的迭代，用量表当作单元测试。

"症状是打地鼠"——这句精神分析的经典批评，其实就是软件工程师对"只修表象不重构架构"的抱怨。而 CBT 的回答也非常"硅谷"：先让产品能用，架构问题以后再说。更妙的是，二者都因同一个原因被批评——"你只是在压制症状/技术债"；也都因同一个原因流行——它们能被打包、被测量、被规模化交付。这不是巧合。二战后的美国心理学，是在福特主义生产线成熟之后进入"心灵工厂"阶段的：它必须可复制、可测量、可培训、可计费。CBT 是心理治疗的 SaaS 化。

Aaron Beck 的"双面间谍"式颠覆

Beck 这个人物值得单独一段。他不是从外部推翻精神分析的——他是内部叛徒，而且他造成的连锁反应远超他本人的意图。

他做了两件事：一是从内部指出精神分析师之间诊断根本不一致，这个批判直接催生了 DSM-III；二是发明了 CBT。但这里有一个几乎从未被指出的历史反讽——DSM-III 建立的"清单式诊断"，恰恰是制药工业需要的东西（你必须先定义"重性抑郁障碍"这个可勾选的实体，才能设计针对它的临床试验和药物营销）。于是一个 CBT 的开山鼻祖，实际上为百忧解时代扫清了知识论障碍。他想让心理学更科学，却顺手把心理治疗市场的很大一部分让渡给了药物。

一个隐藏的系统性真相

如果把访谈中的所有线索连起来，你会看到一个反直觉的图景：

美国没有全民医保 → 心理治疗必须能被个人自费购买 → 疗程必须短、可预测、可比较 → CBT 而非精神分析成为默认 → 但对更严重的疾病（如精神分裂症）CBT 证据薄弱 → 这部分被丢给了药物 → 于是"轻症靠 CBT、重症靠药物"的分工体系诞生。

换句话说，你今天走进任何一家心理诊所，看到的治疗菜单，其实是1945年美军人力短缺 + 1965年国会拒绝全民医保这两个宏观事件的下游产物。而不是任何深思熟虑的临床科学选择。这也解释了 Cochrane 综述那句让人尴尬的评价——"低到中等证据强度"。当一种疗法的合法性主要来自它的可测量性，而不是它的疗效，被测量的东西自然会显得越来越薄。

📝 转录文本

战时的转折点：Menninger 与陆军精神病学

The head of the US military — the first one died; the second one — was a man named William Menninger, from the Menninger Clinic in Kansas, where he and his brother ran a psychoanalytic treatment facility. So Bill Menninger became the head of the Army psychiatry.

He concluded that the best treatment for these soldiers breaking down was psychotherapeutic in nature. Their — the origin of their condition — was trauma. And so, in a watered-down way, Freud's ideas — those were the ones that the people that were recruited quickly and retrained as psychiatrists absorbed.

So they formed, after the war, a fairly coherent group of people, separate from the psychiatrists in the state hospitals, who were still very biologically oriented.

心理学家的意外崛起

Another group emerged during the war precisely because you couldn't produce enough psychotherapists who were MDs quickly enough. Psychologists were drafted in and asked to treat. So what the psychologists discovered was: "Hey, we could do this stuff too, and we really like it. It's interesting. It's challenging. We should do that."

So after the war, similar kind of problem. Mental illness is a massive problem. The returning soldiers is a big problem, but it's also a problem in the community. These guys — the psychiatrists — don't go and work in the mental hospital. They start outpatient treatment. And by 1958, about 80% of psychiatrists are working in outpatient rather than in the hospitals.

So the psychologists organize themselves, and federal money — again, "we need you, we need you, we need more of you." So the VA, the Veterans Administration, and then once the National Institute of Mental Health is established, they start providing a lot of money for training. And they train not just psychiatrists — they train psychologists.

一个"聪明"的训练模式

So the question is: how are the psychologists going to set up clinical training?

What the psychologists come up with — the clinically oriented ones — is a training program where would-be clinical psychologists spend two years learning basic scientific psychology and research methods, and then they have two or three years of clinical work and experience.

And that's very clever, because it means when they start looking for grants, they know how to do that. And the psychoanalysts don't have a clue how to apply for federal grant money, and they don't get any, almost.

治症状 vs 治根源：范式之争

Beyond that, these people begin to work on treating symptoms.

The psychoanalysts think to treat a symptom is to play whack-a-mole. If you don't deal with the underlying problems of the personality — the interaction between your id, ego, and superego — you suppress that symptom, and another one will pop up over here.

The clinical psychologists go: "We're going to treat the symptoms of what are troubling people. We're going to treat the symptoms, and we're going to develop techniques that allow people to cope with those symptoms and eliminate them."

And how are we going to do that? We're going to do it primarily through what initially is cognitive behavioral therapy, and later interpersonal therapy, and some other variants emerge. But basically, what they try to do with those techniques is develop things that work relatively quickly, work specifically on one set of problems or a small subset of problems, and try to get those under control.

And how does it work? You've developed really bad habits — the way you react to being socially snubbed or being ignored, the way you deal with your coworkers, and the trouble you're having with your disruptive child. It will help you see the patterns that you've fallen into, and will give you exercises that will work to give you a better way of coping with those things that don't produce these symptoms. I'm oversimplifying, obviously, but basically that's the fundamental thrust of this.

可打包、可复现、可测量

And one of the other contrasting things about CBT — cognitive behavioral therapy — is that it doesn't have necessarily that heavy requirement of five hours a week.

— Exactly.

So these therapies could be packaged. They could be reproduced. They could be tested to see whether they worked. So they had an evidentiary foundation. The psychoanalyst would say, "It's going to take us years, and it's hard to measure." These guys were: "Well, we'll measure what happens when we treat people this way."

— Psychologists.

— Yeah. The symptoms are what matter, not the underlying, you know, the underlying more complex thing that psychoanalysts claimed to be treating. And so it's shorter. It's reproducible. Whereas psychoanalytic, you know, every patient is a new patient with a new set of complicated things going on. Here we are — we're going to do this.

关键人物：Bandura、Ellis 与 Aaron Beck

— And the key figures here are Albert Bandura, Albert Ellis, Aaron Beck.

— Yes. Bandura and some other psychologists launching this movement. And then later on Aaron Beck, who went by Tim Beck, who just recently died at — I think he was 99. Extraordinary.

— Crossed 100.

— Maybe 100, yeah. Maybe 100.

— There are videos of him talking at that age, and he's still killing it. So wise.

Beck 的双重贡献

Aaron Beck is a remarkable figure, because he was also one of the first, in the 1960s, to look at psychiatric diagnosis and show how unreliable it was — how difficult it was to get psychiatrists to agree on what was wrong.

— So he was a psychoanalyst, right?

— He had been trained as a psychoanalyst, became disillusioned with it. And so there were two important strands that stemmed from his work.

First, he was one of the ones within the community itself who said to his fellow psychiatrists, "You know, we're not very good at this diagnosis business — maybe we need to work on that." And that was very important for the movement towards DSM-III.

The other side of the coin was: he broke with the idea that treating symptoms was a waste of time, and joined with the psychologists who had already embarked on that journey — to say, "How can we develop techniques to overcome these self-destructive ways in which people are responding? How can we help with their ability to interact?" So interpersonal therapy is much more with the way in which, if your relations with other people break down, that damages your emotional stability. If you repair those relationships, that helps your emotional stability come back.

美国例外论与自费医疗

So all of this develops, and Americans are unusual. Most of the rest of the world has what we call socialized medicine. America doesn't have that, so we're used to paying for medical care.

And so Americans were more willing, I think, to pay for clinical psychologists. And they attacked some of the problems of everyday living — the more, I was going to say minor, but these often quite distressing things. Those were what they were most successful at doing.

证据基础的实情

If I look at the literature on CBT, for example, and its uses in cases of schizophrenia, the evidence is pretty poor that it works. And even the evidence for the milder conditions is a bit more ambiguous than they like to pretend.

The Cochrane reviews, which are a systematic attempt to assess how strong the evidence for particular approaches to diseases of all sorts is, say that, at best, the evidence for CBT is of low or medium confidence.

But I think, again, there are patients for whom this helps. And indeed, for the milder forms of depression, I think CBT works better than the drugs — without some of the side effects that the drugs have. And indeed, NICE, which is the British organization that passes on what treatments the National Health Service will support, and which ones are sufficiently evidence-based, has come to that same conclusion.

直觉层面的合理性与其局限

— So, I think one thing to just say about cognitive behavioral therapy: it has some elements of kind of surface-level, intuitive kind of things — like being aware of and adjusting your thought patterns, being aware of triggers that get you down a negative spiral, and then basic behavior changes, habit changes that lead to a healthier life. So I think any of this kind of "getting your life together" process is intuitive — that that would have a positive effect on some percent of the population. But as you get more and more serious into the land of mental disorders, it starts to be a little bit less conclusive.

— Yes, I think that's an accurate statement of the way I read the literature. And it's not a cure-all, but for some patients, this really does seem to improve things quite a lot.

And it does make sense that you have developed poor ways of responding to signals from the outside world, and they've become habitual. And habits, as we know, are very hard to break. You know, there's a lot of homework, there's a lot of exercises you have to do to try to reconfigure the ways you deal with the world.

And it's not for everybody, and it doesn't work for everybody, but there's some subset of people for whom this seems to have positive effects.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一个被战争偶然塑造的心理范式
最让人意外的一点是：CBT 之所以能成为今天的主流治疗范式，**很大程度上不是因为它临床上更"真"，而是因为它的行政基因更适合美国的资助生态**。当访谈中一句轻描淡写的话浮现——"临床心理学家花两年学科学方法和研究，于是他们知道怎么申请联邦经费，而精神分析师完全不懂"——这句话其实是整个心理治疗史的暗门钥匙。
也就是说，CBT 的胜利首先是**赠款申请书写作水平的胜利**，其次才是疗效的胜利。二战时因人力短缺被临时征召的心理学家，无意中获得了一份"能被科学化包装"的方法论嫁妆；他们回国后，恰好碰上 NIMH 和退伍军人管理局的资金洪流。这不是达尔文式的"最强者生存"，而是一种更冷酷的**"最可拨款者生存"**——一种疗法能否存活，取决于它能否被写进一份15页的 R01 申请书里。
## 与软件开发的隐秘同构
这里有一个很少被指出的跨领域连接：**CBT 与敏捷开发（Agile / MVP）几乎是同一种认识论**，而精神分析则是"瀑布模型"。
- 精神分析说：先做完整需求分析（童年、无意识、移情），再重构整个系统架构（人格），历时数年，无法中

item.title: [Lex Clips] Do anti-depressant drugs work? | Andrew Scull and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被"发明"的市场：先有药，后有病

这段历史里最诡异的因果倒置在于——不是抑郁症催生了SSRI，而是SSRI的商业逻辑重新塑造了"抑郁症"的边界。1960年前后，制药公司认为抑郁症"市场太小"，因为定义局限于住院的忧郁型精神病人。真正发生的事情是：药先落地，然后诊断标准在其周围缓慢膨胀，直到市场足够大。这与"科技公司先发明产品再制造需求"(智能手机催生"随时在线"焦虑，社交媒体催生FOMO)的路径完全同构。你以为治病的药物在追赶疾病，实际上疾病的边界在追赶药物的产能。

二、"诊断膨胀"是一个跨领域的普遍现象

Scull借用Nick Haslam的"概念蔓延 (concept creep)"框架来描述精神病学，但这个机制在别处到处都是：

  • 软件工程里叫 scope creep
  • 法律里叫罪刑扩张解释
  • 金融里叫次级标签下沉 (subprime creep)
  • 医院账单里叫 diagnostic upcoding

它们共享同一个结构：一个刚性的核心 + 一层可协商的"半影带 (penumbra)"。真正的战场从不在核心，而在那圈半影里。当DSM把丧亲之痛纳入"抑郁症"，它扩张的不是医学，是可以被编码为商品的人类经验的疆界。

三、一个几乎被跳过的解剖学细节，可能颠覆你对整件事的理解

Scull顺口提了一句：血清素主要在消化系统里生产——这句话像被埋进沙里的钥匙。人体约90%的血清素分布在肠道，脑内SSRI几乎必然扰动肠脑轴 (gut-brain axis)。当整整一代人被开出以"重新平衡大脑神经递质"为叙事的药物，而这种递质的绝大部分根本不在大脑里，你就明白为什么SSRI的副作用是全身性的钝化、为什么停药反应如此惨烈：药物影响的从来不是一个器官，而是一个跨越两个"大脑"的分布式系统。市场故事讲的是脑，生物学发生的却是全身。

四、一个悖论：最孤独的痛苦，最社会化的疾病

Michael MacDonald那句 "the most solitary of afflictions for the sufferer, and the most social of maladies for those around them" 是整段访谈的哲学核心。它无意中暴露了一个经济学问题：家属组织(如NAMI)代表的是家属的利益，不是患者的利益——两者的利益经常是相反的(是否强制住院、是否长期服药、是否披露诊断)。这本质上是一个委托代理问题 (principal-agent problem)：当被代理者失去话语权，"关怀"的结构会悄悄重构疾病定义本身。你能在老年照护、儿童教育、监护制度里看到同样的机制。

五、藏在语言里的诡计："统计学显著 ≠ 临床显著"

在60分量表上改善1-2分足以让论文过审，却对你的生活毫无影响。这个话术不是精神药物专属——它同样渗透在加密项目白皮书、AI 基准测试、健康食品广告、政治民调解读里。学会条件反射地问一句"clinical or statistical?"是一种可以迁移的认知肌肉，一旦长出来，你对整个信息生态的免疫力都会变。

六、被忽视的结构性转移：处方权的"去专业化"

访谈末尾一句轻描淡写的话隐藏着最大的一个结构性变革——"antidepressants are dispensed by primary care docs, not psychiatrists"。这与法律走向LegalZoom、心理咨询走向App、投资建议走向Robo-advisor是同一场运动：专业化守门人被系统性绕过。它降低了成本，也降低了摩擦——而"摩擦"在原本的系统里恰恰是保护机制。当处方SSRI只需要一次15分钟的初诊问诊，诊断膨胀就有了执行层的加速器。

📝 转录文本

The Origin of Second-Generation Antidepressants

The SSRIs, they are also came to be Prozac, Zoloft, Paxil.

Yes, all of that. All of that.

Well, again, they're the second generation of antidepressants. So, that's a complicated story. Again, it's an accident. They're treating patients with advanced tuberculosis in the 1950s. Now, that's a very unpleasant thing that's also going to kill you. So, tuberculosis, very advanced cases, you're coughing your lungs up, you're depressed as all get out. And here we have two new drugs, iproniazid, that we can use that maybe will treat the condition. You give it to the patients and these depressed tuberculosis patients start acting happy, dancing about. Their mood changes. Bingo, we've got something that maybe we can use over here to treat depression.

However, the drug companies in circa 1960 think of depression as a small market because what they're talking about is the kind of melancholic psychotic depression that leads people into the mental hospital. And that's not an insignificant group, but it's not a huge group. So, it's really much later on that things begin to change.

Depression as "the Common Cold of Psychiatry"

Right now, it's fair to say depression is the common cold of psychiatry. It's, you know, it's abundant. The depressive diagnosis probably the most commonly given one among psychiatrists.

So, part of that is a deeper understanding of the human mind and a big part of that is probably the drug companies convincing the world.

Well, it's transforming. Yes. So, there were big disputes, for example, when DSM-5 was being contemplated about whether grief bereavement would count as a mental disorder, as count as a form of depression. If you lose a parent, if you lose even worse, a child, um it's a deep — How can I put it? Deeply upsetting?

Yeah, it's one of the most horrible things that can happen to you.

Yes, exactly. As I unfortunately know from personal experience. So, um if you're feeling emotionally pretty wrought in the aftermath of an event like that, does that mean you're mentally ill? Does it mean you need an antidepressant? Well, some psychiatrists say yes and some no.

Diagnostic Creep

But it's an example of what happens in psychiatry repeatedly, what I would call diagnostic creep, which is a term actually a an Australian named Nick Haslam came up with, but it's a phenomenon I described before that. You start with a core of unambiguous deviations from the norm that are so serious that any competent member of the culture knows that's that. But then it you begin to say, well, there's this penumbra, you see, and just outside that core, there are people who are also disturbed, not perhaps as sufficiently disturbed that you actually recognize it, but it's happening. And so, that has tended to happen over and over again.

Parents with an autistic child won't necessarily agree with what I'm about to say, but the chief editor of DSM-4, Alan Francis, is convinced the huge increase in the number of diagnoses of autism is more driven by the fact he loosened the criteria for the diagnosis than it is because there more actual cases. Autism used to be a fairly rare phenomenon and now sadly it's a very broad one. And I understand why parents react very negatively to that because the diagnosis is the key to all sorts of social supports and educational supports and all the rest, and they're dealing with the child who is extremely difficult. But there is a real difference between the most severe forms of autism where people lose the capacity to speak and very often any ability to interact with other people and so forth, and the other cases that are of a still serious but milder sort.

Diagnostic creep is not driven just by psychiatric imperialism, the desire for more territory, more patients. It is driven as well by patients and people, and they resist it being pushed back very often. So families have formed organizations like NAMI, but those aren't the mentally ill, those are the family members of the mentally ill. And there are differences in the perspectives and the interests of the family members and the patients.

Mhm.

Um and that's easy to forget.

The Social Dimension of Mental Illness

One of the things you talk about is — I mean the quote you had was — used the word "madness"...

Mhm.

...but that, um, madness or mental health maladies, if you're suffering from them, it's a deeply lonely experience. And then if you're around somebody suffering from it, it's a very social experience.

Yeah, this is actually — that's a paraphrase of — I was quoting one of my friends and fellow historians of psychiatry, Michael MacDonald: "The most solitary of afflictions for the sufferer, and the most social of maladies for those around them." And there's lots of ways in which you can see that very powerfully. And that's why I think there are a ton of people who suffer in various ways from mental disturbances of one sort or another. But the effects aren't confined to them. They extend out to everybody else around them, and that's really powerful.

First-Generation Antidepressants: MAOIs and Tricyclics

So, we had this first generation of — there were actually two different kinds of antidepressants. MAOIs as they're called in the trade, and tricyclics, which are called tricyclics cuz they had a third ring of a certain element in their molecule.

Those had, as I say, a limited market, but also there were complications associated with them. It was easy to overdose and die. And so, depressed — giving a depressed patient a bunch of pills that if they took too many of them would kill them, was tricky. Um, they also could kill you another way, because, um, for example, you couldn't — certain dietary items, cheese, cured meats, in combination with them were very very health threatening. Maybe even fatal.

The Rise of Prozac and SSRIs

Now, in the late '80s, the drug companies came across a new class of antidepressants that didn't have those side effects. As we'll see, they had other side effects, but not those. And the most famous of those was Prozac. They were a class of drugs called SSRIs — and again, forgive the acronym — but what it means is selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

Serotonin is something manufactured in our bodies — actually in our digestive system — and it performs a variety of functions in the body, but it's also one of the neurotransmitters in our brains. And the way these drugs worked was by, um, slowing the reuptake of serotonin in the brain, which was marketed by the drug companies as the solution to depression: that when you got depressed, it was because you didn't have enough serotonin in your brain, and these pills solved that problem.

It was like — well, Tipper Gore, Al Gore's ex-wife, was, like many politicians' wives, depressed for reasons I fully understand or at least partially understand. And she went to her psychiatrist, and that was one of the things she was given, and she became one of the big public advocates for SSRIs, which still are the most prescribed antidepressants.

Do They Work? Statistical vs Clinical Significance

Do they work, and what are the side effects?

Yeah. So, here's where we get into slippery territory. Every time you do a controlled study of these antidepressants, they beat placebo in a statistically significant margin, but not necessarily in a clinically significant margin. And this is when you see drug ads, be very careful. "This one significantly improves X or Y." Does that mean clinically or does it mean statistically?

Because the fact — if you, when we measure improvement with depression, we tend to use rating scales of various sorts. Um, and if you improve on one of the major scales that's used by one or two points on a 60-point scale, it may be enough to show statistical significance — this drug's a lure it a little better than placebo — but it doesn't really affect your quality of life much.

And for most patients, um, antidepressants are marginally better than placebo. But a lot of the effect is the placebo effect.

Side Effects and Withdrawal

And they come with very difficult side effects. A lot of people describe them as numbing drugs. They flatten everything out. Um, so you can't experience the highs and lows that normally we take as part of human experience. And then, um, the numbing extends elsewhere in your body. In particular, lots of patients find, um, a complete loss of libido. They can't get an erection. They can't climax if they're a woman. Their sex life just goes away. And sometimes it doesn't come back after you stop the drugs.

Next layer of problems: getting off the drugs for some people turns out to be hell on wheels. Uh, they get worse depression than they had before. They get terrible feelings. Their brain is sparking. Something's wrong. Um, and so many patients find themselves trapped on those drugs for a long time. And we don't know what the effects of that are going to be. So it's a very mixed picture.

You know, uh, that's why I think groups like NICE in England are saying use CBT as the first line, not drugs.

Three Response Groups, and the Shift Away from Psychiatry

Um, but again, it's also fair to say — I think what we find, and there was a recent Lancet study that I think was revealing on this point — it's like this with both antipsychotics and antidepressants:

  • You have a group of people who respond pretty well, and the side effects for them are bearable or even they don't experience them. That's great.
  • You have a group of people — and it's significant with depressed patients, we're talking 40 or north of 40% — who aren't responding. Okay. So, drugs aren't doing anything for them, and they're running a risk.
  • And then in the middle, you have a group of people who get some positive improvement, but they also get side effects.

And that's where, you know, this cost-benefit analysis, if we can call it that, comes into play. And it's very difficult, and the problem is: going in, you don't know which group you're going to fall in, and your doctor doesn't know which group you're going to fall in.

And, more importantly, one of the things that drugs revolution did was it moved the diagnosis and the prescribing of things away from psychiatry alone. So, many of these things, particularly antidepressants, are dispensed by primary care docs, not psychiatrists.

item.title: [All-In Podcast] Adam Foroughi, Applovin CEO: Surviving a 92% Drawdown, Ads as ML 1.0 & the $50B Game Ad Market
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：AppLovin 的"隐身"其实是护城河，而不是缺陷

大多数创始人把"没人听说过我"当成融资劣势，Adam 却把它变成了结构性优势。注意他讲述崩盘那段的时序：市值从 400 亿掉到 38 亿，他做的第一件事不是路演救火，而是主动切断与投资人的沟通——"They're not buying our stock. It's a waste of time."

这里藏着一个反直觉的资本论断：当市场对你定价错误时，沟通是负 EV 的。因为你每一次公开表达都在缩短错误定价的窗口。他把公司变成了自己股票最激进的买家，用运营现金流回购了 20-25% 的股份。等他 2023 年 9 月飞到纽约"重新出现"时，一周之内市值从 280 亿跳到 550 亿——他在等一个信息不对称达到峰值的时刻兑现。

这不是运气，这是逆向做市。他把自己活成了 Ben Graham 教科书里那个"市场先生"的对手方。

二、跨领域连接：广告是 ML 1.0，但真正被复用的不是模型，是"闭环反馈的哲学"

Adam 有一句被轻轻带过但极其重要的话："when you build a model, you're predicting a future outcome... but you can translate the value of that prediction immediately."

这句话可以从广告业跨接到三个看似无关的领域：

  • 药物研发：为什么 AI + 生物药迟迟无法出现类似广告业的爆发？因为反馈闭环要 7-10 年。
  • 教育科技：Duolingo 之所以能起来，是因为它把学习伪装成了广告业——每 30 秒一个可衡量的行为闭环。
  • 代码生成：Cursor / Copilot 的 retention 曲线远超其他 SaaS，因为它借用了广告业最古老的形态——用户在几秒内就能判断预测是否正确。

也就是说，广告业不是 ML 1.0，广告业是"快速反馈经济"的原型。凡是能把预测-反馈周期压缩到秒级的行业，都会诞生一个 AppLovin。你可以据此预测：下一个 84% EBITDA margin 的公司，一定出现在某个刚刚把反馈周期从"周"压到"秒"的传统行业里。

三、被所有人忽略的一层：他其实在做"注意力套利"，而 Meta 做不到

Adam 说自己在和 Meta 竞争 discovery advertising，但他略过了一个更深的结构差异——他的用户处于"注意力被强制暂停"的状态。手游玩家为了拿到一条命，愿意主动看完 30 秒广告。这在广告心理学里叫 captive attention，其转化率理论上限比 Meta 的 feed 广告高一个数量级，因为用户不是在"划走的边缘"看广告，而是在"渴望结束"的心理弯曲里看广告。

这里有一个被投资者严重低估的洞察：Meta 的算法在优化"如何不被划走"，而 AppLovin 的算法在优化"如何让被迫等待的 30 秒变成快乐"。这两条曲线的斜率完全不同。前者是防御性的，后者是进攻性的。

再叠加他提到的一个细节：用户会抱怨"给我推更相关的广告"——这在人类行为学里几乎是不可能的偏好，只可能出现在 captive attention 场景。这解释了为什么他 84% 的 EBITDA margin 能持续——他不是在广告市场里竞争，他其实垄断了一个隐蔽的品类：强制注意力时段的算法分发。等他把这个能力从游戏迁移到 e-commerce（他现在正在做的事），本质上是在把"captive attention 的心理学专利"卖到一个 10 倍大的市场里。

啊哈时刻：AppLovin 真正的产品，不是广告平台，是一门关于"人在等待时会花钱"的行为学专利。这门专利，Meta 拿不走，Google 也拿不走——因为他们的用户从来没有被迫等待过。

📝 转录文本

Adam Foroughi（AppLovin CEO）访谈整理

开场：被低估的"隐形巨头"

Adam is probably the best founder no one's ever heard of. There's an ad platform hiding inside 100,000 mobile games and is quietly outperforming Facebook ads for e-commerce brands. Of all those thousand plus IPOs, the number one most valuable is AppLovin.

The founder mentality has got to be: chase winning. They're going to print something like $6 billion in cash this year. In a world where things don't make sense, people think you're cheating, instead of realizing you built one of the cooler technologies the world's ever seen.

Please welcome Adam Foroughi.

一、AppLovin 是什么？一个被严重低估的市场

All right. Welcome, Adam. Hey, man. Big man. How you doing, bro? Good to see you. Likewise. Adam, thanks for being here.

主持人： Um, we thought it'd be really great to chat because a lot of people don't talk as much about — you're not in the headlines all the time with your business. You're operating your business almost like absent media. You don't do a lot of press. You don't get out there a lot talking about the company, but it's such an incredible business. Can you just tell the audience kind of what AppLovin is and maybe also frame up the market a little bit for us?

Adam： Yeah, totally. I think the fact that we were able to build a very big company without having VC funding at the early stage created this world where we just had to build quietly — and then obviously the goofy name didn't help us all that much as well.

But what we are ultimately is an advertising company that's helping mobile game developers monetize that space. Now what people don't realize is just how big the mobile gaming universe has become. You've got over a billion people a day playing mobile casual games. These are all adults, heads of households, and the scale of the opportunity is just humongous.

We disclosed last January, so nearly two years ago, that on our own platform there was $11 billion a year of ad spend. Since then, we've grown 60% year-over-year roughly. And so, if you gross that up to a nice round number today, you get $20 billion. Now, we're not the only player in this marketplace — this is a market that's monetized by a lot of other ad companies as well. So then you'd probably more than double that again and round it off and say there's probably about $50 billion of advertising being spent every single year in this mobile gaming ecosystem.

It was not very long ago that social was a $50 billion opportunity. Space is growing really quickly. A lot of audience — these people watch ads. A lot of times they watch the ads to get rewards. And so that dynamic creates this possibility to create intent.

For most of the AppLovin company's life, we've been creating that intent to drive a user to take one game's experience and go to the next game's experience. And what's really gotten investors excited about our company — and just us excited about the opportunity that we have in front of us — is that deep learning models have gotten so powerful now that you could take that same space and try to take that adult and give them a shopper behavior experience. And that allows us to tap into much larger economies, make more of an economic impact in the world. And that's why our team's just really pumped up on what we're doing.

二、广告即 ML 1.0：技术如何从广告走向 AI

主持人： The first wave of internet advertising was in many ways the spark for a lot of critical technologies that then sort of diffused out into the world. So like if you think what Google was able to do with AdWords, AdSense, Applied Semantics, all of that whole range of technology — is that true in this generation of internet advertising? Are there technologies and things that are being birthed here that are consequential and foundational now to the rest of the internet?

Adam： Yeah, I mean advertising is like ML 1.0 — but really was the first implementation of all these technologies that now are driving AI today. And the economic value of a large language model and what it's doing in our society today is much greater than advertising. But advertising is a very profitable implementation of a deep learning model.

Now, recommendation systems are structured differently than large language models, but in a lot of ways they follow the same trajectory. So a lot of the research that's being done in the large language model space can port to recommendation systems and vice versa. A lot of the researchers in the large language model space might have started early in their careers looking at advertising systems. So these two spaces are really related.

The nice thing about our business — and any advertising business — is that when you build a model, you're predicting a future outcome (an advertisement, or if you're building a social network, an engagement post, or a sequence of them), but you can translate the value of that prediction immediately.

三、2006 vs 2026：用户对广告的态度进化

主持人： Is it true that there's just a broad-based behavior around humans' reaction to ads in 2026 versus 2006? Like, has there been an evolutionary arc that's very predictive?

Adam： Yeah, it's interesting. I started my career in 2005, so I saw the ads back then — complete garbage. It was all spam and the technologies just weren't powerful enough. And your old company, Facebook, did a really good job of realizing: if you can take all the data we have in front of us and pair it with good technology, the ads can become really relevant.

If you talk to most people who shop today, most of their shopping recommendations are coming from Instagram. The ads have become very much like content. And in our domain as well, people love the ads that we show. And you would think people wouldn't like them, but we see tons of engagement on little mini games that are appearing in other games. And people are playing these previews because the technologies have gotten so good at recommending something relevant to someone.

四、AI 时代的广告：搜索广告 vs 发现广告

主持人： There's been a lot of hand-wringing about the impact AI will have on the ad networks, specifically Google's interface. And OpenAI has an ad product now. I'm sure you've been monitoring it and trying to learn from it. What is advertising going to look like when people are doing five or six queries with a chatbot? Because it's pretty obvious 95% of the world are not going to pay 20 bucks a month for this technology. They're going to expect it to be free. ChatGPT has already said they're going to make it free. Tell us what they're doing in advertising. Is it going to be less effective each time, but in aggregate people are going to use it more? Or is it going to just be even better than Google search's franchise?

Adam： Yeah, I mean there's two sides of advertising.

One part is bottom-of-funnel advertising — where a consumer sort of knows what they want to buy, but they're doing research to go complete the transaction. And that's Google search's business. If I wanted to buy a pair of dress shoes, I'd go to Google historically, do some research, and they'd direct me to where I need to go based on the ads. And today you can go to a large language model and close the loop on that same thing. So that ads model is almost going to exclusively compete with the Google search business.

What we operate in is a world where we're showing a user an ad and we don't know what their intent is. So we're trying to create something that didn't exist before. Show them a recommendation and get them to go, "Wow, that looks really cool. Let me go transact on that and do it really quickly." That's what drives Facebook's ad business too.

And so the reason that's interesting to me is that the transaction via search or LLM was going to happen anyways. If the LLM didn't exist and Google Ads had never come into existence, but Google search existed, that closed-loop transaction would have happened. So there's not actually a whole lot of economic expansion that happens from that. But when you show a consumer an ad for something that they had no idea existed, they didn't know they needed to buy —

主持人： Discovery basically.

Adam： Totally — complete discovery. And this is what makes Meta so amazing in their ad business, and what we aspire to do. You create that discovery moment. Not only is it a really fun moment for the consumer — because then they're excited about what they bought, they wait for the package, they're excited to open it up — but you create economic expansion.

五、"手机在偷听我"的都市传说

主持人： What about the arms race that develops over time where some people say, "you know, I mention something with my friends at lunch and all of a sudden I show up and there are these ads on Meta or wherever." Is that just us overreacting or is that actually happening? And is there a push not to be more intrusive but, you know, the tendency to want to sell more? That's creepy.

Adam： Yeah, it feels creepy when it does happen.

主持人： Or just to push the boundaries. What is actually happening when people say I say something at lunch and all of a sudden an ad for that same thing appears?

Adam： I mean, I think you've done other actions that are trackable — like a search, browse a website, do a product search — and you don't realize it, and then you say something related to it and you start seeing ads that are relevant. So, it's not like the mic is on or there's an app that has actually taken space.

主持人： There's a theory though that if we were all at lunch, especially with these apps, you know, our geolocation — you've kind of put us into a group. So we might be talking about this new car we're all interested in, or a watch. And then Freeberg, when he's leaving, searches for the watch to bookmark it after the conversation, but you're tracking all of our locations, and then you say, "Okay, let's give all four of them the ads for the watch." And you're mixing and matching based on — is that what's happening? That's what I'm told.

Adam： I don't think advertising companies can track location. So, we don't track location at all. It's a really heavy concept to track people's precise location to then render an ad. And then to imagine the amount of data that's transferring if you're — mic'd, to then parse the mic on content to try to translate to an ad — not realistic.

主持人： But what about us being friends and being connected together, like groups?

Adam： So, we wouldn't have that data. But if you're on a social network, of course, your relationships together might drive an ad experience. If Chamath searches for something, then you might see something relevant to it. There's nothing wrong with that.

I mean, the one thing that people lose — there's a creepy factor that scares people somewhat, but all of the data collected at this point, given the scale of advertising across all these companies, is pretty much controlled in a lot of ways. What people then forget is the economic value that's created from these ads becoming that relevant. That ad that you saw — you recognized that ad. 20 years ago, you would not have recognized the ad. And there's a big part of GDP that's now coming from this digital ad economy. The better these technologies get, the faster GDP growth.

六、IPO 之后的坠落：从 400 亿到 38 亿

主持人： Adam, let's go back to — what I find so fascinating about the business is the way you've operated it. You're based in LA. Is that right?

Adam： I'm based in LA. Company started in Silicon Valley — we're in Palo Alto.

主持人： Palo Alto. But you're here, and then you have a lot of developers in China. Is that right?

Adam： We have — our engineering offices are in Palo Alto, Beijing, and Singapore.

主持人： And then the company didn't raise a lot of venture money. You take the company public 2021. It went public like $20 billion market cap out the gate.

Adam： Yeah, we were a COVID IPO. We went out in April 2021. It was about $28 billion.

主持人： $28 billion. And then in 2023, what did the market cap collapse to?

Adam： Well, this is the funny thing about the public market. So we went out in 2021 — $600 million of EBITDA, $28 billion market cap. We got as high as $40 billion. And then in '22, the stock went down literally every day. We got to about a $3.8 billion market cap. In that year, we did a billion dollars in EBITDA.

主持人： That's incredible.

七、逆向反击：把最惨的时刻变成最大的回购机会

主持人： So hold on. So the market's in disbelief for some reason about the business. And what do you do?

Adam： Yeah. What you learn pretty quickly — and I'm a finance background so I had good education on this — is that your price in the markets is determined by the quality of your investors. And we had private market investors — both private equity and ex-founders and other team members — that were going to sell when we went public. And because there were so many companies going public during COVID, by the time we went out, blue chip investors weren't doing the research to figure out "what is this goofy-named company?" So we ended up with no demand and a lot of supply.

That construct created this world where we just tanked, and the multiple went from fairly high — I mean, I wouldn't really value companies on 50 times EBITDA — but to something that was absurdly low: sub 4x.

So being that finance-minded person, you have to remember: with that kind of a bashing, you do have an opportunity on the other side of it. And I turned internal to the team and said: I'm not going to talk to investors at all anymore. They're not buying our stock. It's a waste of time. But guess what? We generated a ton of cash. Let's start buying our own stock. Let's become our best investor.

So we kicked off a super aggressive buyback program. Since then, I think we bought roughly $6 billion of the company's stock, retired 20 to 25% of the shares outstanding. At peak, that $6 billion was worth over $50 billion. And so you can take that moment which does feel super depressing and turn it into a huge —

八、崩盘时如何管理团队与内心

主持人： How did you manage — sorry — did you feel that way from the whole time or was there this period of depression where you're like —

主持人 2： Oh my gosh, that's what I was going to ask. How do you manage the internal culture when the stock is off 92%?

Adam： It's tough. I mean, like — I'll tell you, I would get phone calls from family members, friends: "Are you suicidal?" And I'm like, look, we got stuck at a penny. The stock's still like 10 bucks. It's still up a lot.

But it's very tough then because you realize as a CEO, your team is getting those same phone calls from their family members.

主持人： Exactly. And they don't have the gravitas that you do, nor the ownership.

Adam： So we built it by just saying, "Look, it's an us-against-the-world mentality." Like, everyone's turned against us. We're going to buy back shares. And we implemented a performance stock plan — which typically goes to CEOs — but we did it across key people in the company and said: "You know, we understand it's tough right now. We understand you thought you had a house and now you don't. But if you dig in and we recover, you're going to make a ton on the upside."

九、从 ML 1.0 到 ML 2.0：重生的技术拐点

主持人： And then what — investors started showing up and saying "hey, we're paying attention again"?

Adam： It was interesting because for us, what happened was we went from ML 1.0 — like we talked about a couple minutes ago — to ML 2.0. We went from a regression model to a deep learning model. And the outcome was: we're driven by our advertising algorithm. The better it works, the better advertiser return is on our platform. And everything is performance-based. So we're selling revenue to advertisers — the more they scale.

And so the company just started growing really quickly. Now, we turned into '23 and launched that model in April. We still weren't talking to investors. So people hadn't found out. And then it was somewhere around, I think, September of '23 that I went to New York, and I said the stock's now like 80 bucks and we'd recovered quite a bit because performance was good. But I said, "I'm going to start talking to investors, because market cap's getting high enough and we can't really buy back all that aggressively anymore."

And in that week, the stock went from 80 to 150. And I think it was like $28 billion to $55 billion — from you being in New York.

主持人： From me just going out and saying, "Hey, our company still exists. We survived this."

Adam： Yeah. And then people — I'd sit in the meetings and — it's pretty easy to read the other side of the room if you do that kind of thing. Sell your company. I sit in the meetings, I'm like, these people are literally calling their friends in the room going "buy buy buy buy buy." And I was like — ah.

十、从 $9 到 $750：估值的双向极端

主持人： And then what's the opposite side of that? Once they're long, are they now asking you, "Okay Adam, how do we expand? How do we grow faster? Why just games? Why not e-commerce? Why not this? Why not that?" Absolutely. Damned if you do, damned if you don't.

Adam： So unfortunately, not a lot of people are contrarians. So you can go to the extreme down, and then on the other side of it, you can go extreme up too. We ended up going from $9 to $750 a share in a matter of 2 and 1/2 years. And so, it was like a $3.8 billion market cap — some people bought some options back then and are probably living in some massive homes — and we got to $250 billion market cap. So extreme on both ends.

We've now settled into a place where we have a lot of excitement about our growth opportunities. But I found public market investors are not all that different than private market investors. They follow trends, but a lot of times later than you'd want. The most sophisticated hit those trends early. And that's why you have really good VCs and you have average VCs. You have really good public market investors, you have average public market investors.

十一、隐私、Apple 和监管环境

主持人： Maybe you could talk a little bit about privacy. Apple, the EU, really are looking at companies like yours, and they — this is a little too aggressive in terms of the data you're collecting. Some video game developers don't like having data collected on their users, and they've tightened the screws a bit. Zuckerberg had to deal with it specifically. So what's the headwind on this business, and how do you manage privacy when Apple really is trying to — let's call it what it is — they're trying to nuke your business?

Adam： Look, in any of these spaces, you want the regulations to be clear. Once they're clear, technology can deal with them. So if you could precisely target a user 5 years ago on iOS, and today someone says "I don't want you to precisely target me," you group them in a bunch and you serve them a worse advertisement.

Now, the funny outcome of that is: we'll get a lot of complaints after that change that Apple made from users that say, "Serve me more relevant ads. You're showing me a bunch of spam."

So there is this notion that you need privacy regulation so that technology companies can do exactly what's expected of them. On the other side, consumers do want relevant ads. It helps them discover products. If you're sitting there in a game and you're watching an ad for 30 seconds to get a free life, you're getting something that has monetary value. Now, if you're doing that, do you want to sit and watch garbage for 30 seconds or do you want to watch something relevant?

And so what's happened since a lot of the privacy noise is — a lot of the rules were written, technology companies have adapted, and deep learning networks are really powerful.

十二、为什么卖掉了自有游戏工作室

主持人： Consumer — just one quick followup with this amazingly profitable business. I think you dabbled in buying some of the games — and we have Bending Spoons coming on today to talk about their aggressive acquisition of not-bad businesses, but let's call them slower growth businesses that maybe venture isn't interested in. Is that going to be a sustainable plan for you to become a game studio? And does that put you in conflict with the partners?

Adam： Yeah, we sold all those games. We bought them originally as a data play. When we built our first deep learning model, we needed to have data to train it, and game studios don't tend to want to share data to third-party companies. So we bought our own studios, we seeded the training data in our first model, we built a model that was really successful in market, we started growing really quickly. Once we started doing that, third parties were coming in and we divested that.

十三、Agentic Commerce 时代广告还有位置吗？

主持人： What's the world of advertising look like where there's agents everywhere, agents are servicing you, maybe the human interface to compute changes — so it's not necessarily a computer that you're typing on or a phone that you're browsing. Maybe it's the Meta glasses or some other device. What role does the ad play, and what happens in this agentic commerce that so many other people are trying to now push into existence?

Adam： Yeah, I mean, I think the reality is: part of the world will start using things like agents to optimize per certain shopper behavior that's consistent. For instance, I might put my supplement subscription into an agent and have it optimized every single month and delivered on time.

But these discovery platforms aren't that. And the typical shopper is not the person who's deep into agents and sitting on Twitter and adopting the latest technology. I sort of say — our audience is the New York Times audience. There's still a ton of people using Yahoo properties every single day. The typical shopper wants to find a product and wants to actually go through that shopper behavior. They want to window shop. They want to go through the transaction experience.

主持人： They want to compare, probably.

Adam： Totally. They want to track it. And if you told them after the fact, "Hey, an agent could have done this for you and saved you 20%" — I don't think that matters on a $50 transaction because the dopamine hit from going through it is what they enjoy.

So I think there is this part of the world that is technologically advanced that's going to adopt these technologies. I just think we really overindex on the Twitterverse and forget that the average shopper is not that.

十四、小公司凭什么打败 Meta 和 Google？

主持人： Let me just try and understand how you won. Because two of the smartest companies in the world with the best engineers — Meta, Alphabet/Google — make most of their revenue from advertising. They've built their own models. They've been doing it now for one to two decades. How did a small company compete in this particular domain and win? And what's the operating model that you think gives you an advantage to continue winning?

Adam： Yeah. Here's something that helped us get to this point. We never think we won. We think every day we wake up and we're probably going to get screwed right now, and we better work hard.

And so you've got a company that's lean with a lot of subject matter experts who are really focused on this thing — this mobile gaming experience and translating into transactional behavior on the other side. And so I think there's this ability to take on giants. If you're very focused, you remain lean, and you can just move faster than them.

十五、84% EBITDA 背后的商业结构

主持人： And what's the leakage in the business then? So meaning, when you look at a P&L — I did this thing with Amazon a decade ago where you look at all of these places in which they were leaking, and our big insight is: wow, they'll just absorb these things and they'll become the new businesses. And that was our long thesis for Amazon.

Adam： Yeah.

主持人： What's that version for you? Is it payment infrastructure? Is it other kinds of things? Jason asked you about apps but I guess you've divested that. So where's the leakage — or said differently, where's the opportunity for margin expansion so that people underwrite this thing?

Adam： Well, our EBITDA margins I think are number one in the market — it's 84%. So I don't know how much leakage we have.

Yeah, given the metric. But the way to think about it is: an advertiser comes into our platform and they have a transactional model. Let's say they're selling lipstick. We give them an arbitrage. They — buying from us — are buying the consumer. That consumer transacts and they cover the cost of the consumer immediately. So the consumer buys the lipstick for 20 bucks. They pay us less than the 20 bucks minus cost of goods sold. They're happy. They scale up. And that performance model is very scalable.

Now, our leakage is — we're not the full chain. We're not the advertiser in the equation, but we want to power the advertisers to meet the consumer. And we've run extremely lean and been so algorithmically focused and automation focused that we haven't had a lot of points of leakage.

十六、为什么高利润没被竞争压低？

主持人： The other side then is: when you have 85% EBITDA margins, people say "Wow, they could be over-earning." Right? That's the classic phrase. And then you have competition that says, "I can compete Adam's margins away. I'm willing to do this at 60% or 50%." But sort of maybe as a corollary to David's question — that hasn't really happened, and it's been incredibly sustained. Why do you think that is?

Adam： Because these technologies are really complex, and if you can innovate and you have differentiated data, you can build an advantage. I mean, by that token, Anthropic shouldn't be running away with the large language model space. But the power of a model that then reaches a point of scale and gets adopted by a large-scale community becomes something that is a moat that is hard for other people to overcome.

十七、中国团队与"跟聪明人一起工作"

主持人： And talk to us about the team in China and how big of an edge these folks are.

Adam： I mean, Chinese people are very humble. They're very, very hardworking. They're very sharp. And if you can work with them — whether out of China, or the United States, or any other part of the world — you're working with some of the brightest minds in the world.

And so, when I started the business, one of my goals at this company was just: work with great people and figure things out. And so, when I sit in a room with some of the people on my team, I know I'm probably the dumbest person in that room. And that gets me excited to show up.

主持人： Got him. Gets me to show up for the — feel when you hear that.

Adam： Yeah — works for me.

结束

All right, let's give it up for Adam. Adam, thank you. Thanks, bro. That was great. Thanks, man. Thanks, man. Great to see you.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：AppLovin 的"隐身"其实是护城河，而不是缺陷
大多数创始人把"没人听说过我"当成融资劣势，Adam 却把它变成了结构性优势。**注意他讲述崩盘那段的时序**：市值从 400 亿掉到 38 亿，他做的第一件事不是路演救火，而是**主动切断与投资人的沟通**——"They're not buying our stock. It's a waste of time."
这里藏着一个反直觉的资本论断：**当市场对你定价错误时，沟通是负 EV 的**。因为你每一次公开表达都在缩短错误定价的窗口。他把公司变成了自己股票最激进的买家，用运营现金流回购了 20-25% 的股份。等他 2023 年 9 月飞到纽约"重新出现"时，一周之内市值从 280 亿跳到 550 亿——**他在等一个信息不对称达到峰值的时刻兑现**。
这不是运气，这是**逆向做市**。他把自己活成了 Ben Graham 教科书里那个"市场先生"的对手方。
## 二、跨领域连接：广告是 ML 1.0，但真正被复用的不是模型，是"闭环反馈的哲学"
Adam 有一句被轻轻带过但极其重要的话："
