item.description:
## 一、最出人意料的观察：这场"末日恐慌"本身可能是一场精心设计的**寡头护城河工程**
表面上，Jacob Coxon 放弃 Anthropic IPO 前的巨额股权、Hinton 高调警告、Dario 呼吁"减速"——这看起来是良心觉醒。但如果把这些事件放在**博弈论的信号传递模型**中审视，会发现一个诡异的对称性：
**越是喊"AI 会灭绝人类"的人，越是站在算力金字塔最顶端的人。**
Dario 呼吁"让安全人员长驻公司审查训练"——这句话翻译成产业语言就是：**给前沿实验室套上一套成本极高的合规枷锁**。Anthropic、OpenAI、Google 已经跑到最前面，它们**恰好**是唯一付得起这套合规成本的玩家。这就形成了一种**"用恐惧建立监管俘获"**的经典范式——历史上，大烟草公司主动推动 FDA 监管、大银行主动拥抱巴塞尔协议，都是同一个剧本：**当你已经在山顶，最好的防御不是造更高的墙，而是让山脚下起雾**。
黄仁勋的愤怒之所以罕见地情绪化，恰恰是因为他站在**卖铲子的位置**——他需要千百家 AI 公司都活着买 GPU，而不是只剩三家。这不是善恶之争，

item.title: [Business of Sport] How Nike Lost $200BN in Value
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反常识的观察：Nike 的股价崩盘不是"跌了"，而是"神话塌了"

真正令人震撼的数字对比，视频里只是轻描淡写地提到——营收只下滑了 10%，市值蒸发了 80%。这中间的 70% 差额，本质上不是"运动鞋生意"的价值，而是"神话溢价"（narrative premium）的崩塌。市场从来不是在给 Nike 的鞋子定价，而是在给"Nike 代表未来"这个故事定价。

这解释了一个隐藏的悖论：当 Nike 决定"站队"的那一刻，它就从一个神话变成了一个观点。 神话可以让所有人投射自己（Jordan 是每个孩子的梦想，Federer 是每个白领的优雅），而观点必然排斥另一半人。视频中提到 Phil Knight 的话——"让没有运动员天赋的人感受运动员的感觉"——这是代理式超越（proxy transcendence）；而 Kaepernick 合作则是部落式认同（tribal identity）。前者的市场是全人类，后者的市场永远只有一半。

跨领域连接：Nike 的"鞋底脱胶"和"价值观漂移"其实是同一件事

视频里 Charlie 抱怨自己的 Nike 跑鞋三个月就脱胶了。这个细节被当作"顺便一提"，但它是整个故事最锋利的一刀——产品质量的滑坡和政治定位的高调，在时间上完美同步。

这不是巧合。这是组织注意力守恒定律（organizational attention conservation）：一家公司的高层带宽是一个零和游戏。当 CEO Dono 花大量时间处理 DEI 议题、DTC 转型、垂直业务重组时，那个曾经痴迷于"日本 Onitsuka Tiger 到底能不能造出更好的跑鞋"的产品偏执就消失了。华为、丰田、Zara 这类真正长青的制造企业有一个共同特征——他们的顶层永远在讨论产品的一颗螺丝钉。当 Nike 顶层开始讨论宏观叙事时，鞋底就开始脱胶了。这和罗马帝国晚期元老院辩论哲学而边境失守是同一种病。

最出人意料的洞见：Kaepernick 合作意外地"训练"了 Nike 的杀手

大家都在说 Kaepernick 让 Nike 失去了保守派客户——这个分析太浅了。真正的杀伤力是它给了竞争对手一份"品牌难民"名单。

在 Nike 站队之前，Hoka、On Running、New Balance 都只是小众技术品牌，没有一个足够大到能挑战 Nike。但当 Nike 主动把自己的顾客推出门时，这些顾客并没有停止跑步——他们只是在寻找一个"不谈论政治的运动鞋"。这批被驱赶出去的高购买力中产阶级，在四年内把 Hoka 和 On 从边缘品牌抬进了主流。Nike 用自己的营销预算，教育了一个原本不存在的替代市场。

这里有个更深的规律：帝国的衰落从来不是被击败的，而是主动放弃了阵地。 中国的"国潮"运动（安踏、李宁的崛起）也是同一个机制——Nike 主动通过 DTC 撤出零售渠道时，货架上的空位不会保持真空，本土品牌带着更便宜的碳板跑鞋和民族自豪感填了进去。

一个反直觉的战略结论

视频中一句话被低估了："如果 DTC 容易，所有人都会做。" 但真相更深——DTC 不是一种销售渠道，而是一种要求客户先信仰再购买的宗教模式。零售模式是"传教式"（在货架上和竞品并列，用产品说服你），DTC 是"教堂式"（你必须先决定进门）。Nike 犯的错是：在自己神话开始崩塌的时候，选择从传教改成了盖教堂。 一个正在失去信众的宗教，最不该做的就是关掉传教士的门。

Elliott Hill 现在做的所有"回归"动作——回到运动垂直、回到批发商、回到产品本位——本质上是同一件事：把 Nike 从"观点公司"变回"神话公司"。 能不能成功，取决于神话是否还能被相信。这是 Nike 现在真正的赌注。

📝 转录文本

Nike 如何蒸发 2000 亿美元市值

一、序章：一个几乎从未失手的品牌，如何在四年内跌去 80%

This is uh something which is very much in the sports industry mind at the moment with regards to the biggest sports merchandise brand of all — Nike.

Now Nike has had a phenomenal run of it. Absolutely phenomenal run of it. Really there have been a few ups and downs in the meantime, but over 40 to 50 years they've barely put a foot wrong during my lifetime. They are the behemoths.

Brilliant.

They're the behemoths of the sports merchandise um space, and they're a quoted company — which means they're listed on the stock market in the USA. Um, and by sort of the time just after COVID, they were one of the biggest companies in the world. They were in the S&P 100. The S&P 100 is the list of the hundred biggest um companies on the US stock market, right? And because the vast majority of the biggest companies in the world are American, it's not far off being a fair denomination of the biggest companies in the world.

That was about sort of 2021, 2022 — that type of period.

Anyway, since then Nike shares are down by 80%. 80%. Or $200 billion.

$220 billion — 160 billion pounds.

Just think about that. That's the reduction in value at that business over the last four years.

Now, you'd assume that that's because the company's losing lots of money — but it's not. It's not losing lots of money. Um, it's lost a bit of revenue. So, at its absolute peak in '23–'24, it got up to 51.5 billion in revenue, and it's now down to more like 45 billion. So it's lost 10% of its revenue during that time. And that's, by the way, really bad for an established company. And all the stock market analysts will be crawling all over that saying, "Oh, hang on a second — what does that mean in terms of your cost margins? What does that mean in terms of your EBITDA? What does that mean in terms of the dividend you're going to be able to pay?" — and therefore putting out sell notes on it.

There's no doubt that this is partially driven by revenue. But it's not just driven by revenue. It's driven by market sentiment as well — in terms of where Nike has got itself to and whether it still feels like that sort of brand that everyone can love.

二、Nike 曾意味着什么：卓越的追求

What's Nike meant to you? You've — and please this is not an age joke, right — you've been around for long, closer to the time of Nike's existence. What did it mean to you?

I think what it meant, and what it has meant, is: it is always up with and just ahead of the trend, right? So Nike sets trends and decides — it sort of, you know, it slightly makes the weather, right? So you've got the big merch companies um who chop out their merch, do it as cheaply as possible and sell it to you as expensively as possible. And sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't work. You know — Adidas and all these types of guys. And then Nike are the ones who have been able to somehow, despite becoming massive, still maintain a bit of the energy of a challenger brand.

That's been their genius. That Nike swoosh — which is just the most wonderful brand logo, that swoosh with the uptick — has always looked towards the future, has always somehow signaled a sense of "we are part of the future," and therefore by buying our brand you are buying into the future. And look — some of the decisions they've made, obviously their legendary partnership with Michael Jordan — they've just made so many good judgment calls to keep their brand in place.

三、转折点：与进步主义政治的公开结盟

And then it seems like around about the time of COVID, or just before COVID — the pandemic — and then since COVID, they took a corporate-level decision that they were going to ally themselves effectively with progressive politics. All of this package of things that left-wing political people have put at the forefront of what they've been trying to sell — preach to the rest of the world — for the last half-decade to a decade. And Nike decided, very conspicuously — it's almost hard to overstate how conspicuously — they decided to ally themselves with that.

Now the cornerstone of that was a decision to go into partnership with a um American footballer called Colin Kaepernick, who became famous in the US for refusing to stand for the US national anthem. And the amount of controversy that generated in the US was absolutely huge — um with, you know, a vast chunk of the country feeling totally affronted by it, and then also a very good chunk of the country saying, "You know, good for him — he's standing up for those who the American state has oppressed or has not been run for the benefit of," or whatever it might be. But it was a very polarizing thing.

And then for Nike to enact a partnership with that, was a moment in time when a good chunk of middle America — who is where the real spending power lies — [thought], "Well, if that's what Nike is about, that's not for me. I'm proud of the USA." And I'm proud, because up until then it had always been roughly associated with America, right?

And so, yes — completely coming back to the question I asked you — to me, it's always been about excellence. The pursuit of excellence. Being the absolute best you could be.

四、《Shoe Dog》与被遗忘的初心

Phil Knight — the founder of Nike. Have you ever read Shoe Dog?

No.

Read it. My god, it's one of the best books — anyone out there, read Shoe Dog. The fundamental reason I loved it so much was because, again, from someone that has only seen the later years — I've only ever seen Nike as this massive massive success — but the story of creating this business and how he created it is absolutely extraordinary. And 90% of the book is that. It's not about how great we are and have been over the last 30 years. It's about what it took to get there — and what it took to get there is what they've lost now.

And I just went back to the book. I was interested, as I was reading through it a few years ago, what I'd highlighted. And there were a couple of quotes from Phil that I think Nike need to remember and bring back into some of this.

One of them is: "What if there was a way, without being an athlete, to feel what an athlete feels?" In other words: through our brand, you are going to feel like the people that you look up to, and we're going to make you feel like that. Whether that's wearing Michael Jordan's shoe, whether it's dressing like Roger Federer, whether it's walking out on a golf course wearing your red Nike top like Tiger Woods — we will put you in those positions and we will leverage talent to do that with brilliant product, top-of-the-range product. So not only do you feel good, but you feel like you are the best prepared you could possibly be.

Wow. To me, that is the best sell as a consumer looking at a sports product you could give me. What do I not care about? I don't care about buying another lifestyle product that pitches itself in the middle of — as you say — a discourse around broader global politics.

Also, Charlie, I think what's really important about that — cuz I totally agree with everything you've said — is that sport is the place we go to to forget about those debates. Right? So you sit around the dining room table, you listen to the radio station, you read the newspaper, and you're in the middle constantly of these political and cultural debates.

Yeah.

And then we go to the golf course, and then we go and watch a football match. And whilst we're watching the football match or playing golf, we do not want to be part of a cultural debate, right? That's not sport. Sport is for its own. It's a recreation.

And for Nike, it's been about participation. It's been about getting involved. They've replaced participation with inclusivity. And this is not the place for me — as a wearer of Nike, as an aspiring athlete — where that is the front and center of my mind. My mind gears purely towards: how do I get the most out of my buy? How do I get the most out of resonating with a brand?

Now, if victory, if winning, if excellence is that north star of the brand — that is the one thing they should always stick to no matter what they do.

Yeah.

Right. You look at the biggest businesses — they can make lots of changes, but they always have one north star and they do not compromise from it. That again is why that book is so fascinating: because with Phil Knight's obsession — he was a runner. So it started very much with athletics, right? It was about the best running shoe you could ever create. Whether it was going to Japan in the 70s, making a flight and a trip that was far more complex than it is today with Onitsuka Tiger, trying to figure out how they created and captured the power of their running shoe and bringing that into a US market. Whether it is moving into sports and recognizing emerging talent like Michael Jordan — because that, for Nike, as everyone knows, has been an incredible partnership. Started long before Michael Jordan was Michael Jordan.

So the things again that made them great have kind of fallen a little bit by the wayside.

五、领导决策失误（一）：从"运动垂直"到"男女童分类"

Now, with that comes leadership challenges. And I've written, as we were going through this, kind of a list of a few things that we should cover off as part of this — because you have this overarching theme, I think, that you can definitely say of "go woke or go broke" linking to the demise.

But there's also things that have actually directly happened, off the back of that, that have created it. One of which — that we can directly link to that — was this move from verticals: sporting verticals, athletics division, football division, basketball division, to men's, women's, and kids.

Yeah.

So again, if we're going back to why I go to Nike over other things: I go to Nike over other things because when I want to buy my pair of football boots —

Yeah.

— they're the brand.

Yeah.

If I want to go and buy my golf clothes, I want to look like the guys. I want to win. They're the best products. I don't go because they have a good men's range. Broad, unspecified, lack of focus. That's not why I shop with Nike.

The leadership that they had — John Donahoe, who was the chief executive from what, 2020 to 2024 — made changes here that are now being unpicked. That is one of them. Nike now moving back to the sporting verticals.

六、领导决策失误（二）：从批发零售转向 DTC

Another major one — and John Donahoe elevated it and accelerated it, but it actually started under Mark Parker, who was the chief exec previously — was a move from very strong wholesale retail partnerships…

I think this is probably the biggest single factor, actually.

…to a direct-to-consumer [model]. Do you — explain?

Right. Okay. What Charlie just said there was — I think — is probably, notwithstanding what we just said about "go woke, go broke," probably the single biggest decision. Which might be put under a different banner, which is: um, Nike got too big for its boots.

Um, so in other words, the way in which most merchandise brands sell their product is by having very strong relationships with the big retailers.

Yeah.

Right. So those retailers will get some pricing power because they're buying in volume, but in return, the big merch producers exert power over how their product gets displayed, how they market it together, and all these types of things.

Nike decided they got themselves into such a powerful position in the marketplace — people like me and Charlie could just go online and just buy direct from Nike. And that came at the cost of certain B2B relationships, which started to be downgraded or degraded effectively. And the problem was — the B2C, that's the business-to-consumer direct market — had not yet sufficiently developed, and may indeed never do so, to replace what they were losing on the B2B side. And there's absolutely no doubt that that was a massive factor.

It's a huge point. Um, look — first, if DTC was easy, everyone would do it.

Yeah.

Okay. You have much higher margins. You get 100% of everything you sell. You get all of the data from it. You can leverage your consumer experience from the first time they access the brand to make a purchase, right? Brilliant.

When you are a truly global business, to own every single point of that relationship is incredibly expensive and incredibly hard to do. It is also, no matter how big you are, never going to put you in front of as many people as you could be put in front of. Hence why going wholesale retail — in your JD Sports, your Foot Lockers, your massive US stores — that is worth the 50% cut that you may take on your end sale price. Because you are firstly selling stock in bulk. So you're selling a huge amount in one go. You are also giving someone else the job of shipping, of managing um the customer experience that is maybe not the easiest part of a job.

Now, I get it. I get it from Nike. I do understand why they wanted to do it, particularly from a world where we always talk about experience, right? And customer experience — and connecting to want to own more of that makes a lot of sense. Especially when they've tried to bring a lot more innovation and creativity to, as you say, the digital studio there — the experience when you go into the Nike store. The Nike app is excellent.

Mhm.

It's a really good app. But I still have to go on to that Nike app. I don't come across that Nike app by chance. It is a decision that I make consciously.

And to make that decision, Charlie, you have had to have pre-decided: "I am definitely going to buy Nike."

Yes.

Now, this is the biggest issue, I think, in the wholesale versus the DTC thing — which is that the vast majority of people who buy Nike are not solely Nike buyers. Nike has to back itself that in a competitive marketplace, people will choose their product.

七、离题小插曲：Hamleys 还是 Lillywhites？

Right? So — I actually currently, my current trainers are tatty and I need to go and get some more today. So what I'm going to do is: I'm going to go off on my way, walking down through town. I'm going to go to Hamleys, and I'm going to go in there where I know that there will be a large selection of different brands.

Sorry — Hamleys?

Sorry, not Hamleys. Um, I mean — I'm going to go to buy some Playmobil. I'm going to — I'm going to Whitely um—

Lillywhites.

Sorry — Lillywhites.

[laughter]

Charlie.

Oh dear. When you get — he has — this is not the drunk down. Just so we can — it's not too busy.

There's a certain moment in time. Yes. I'm not going to go to Hamleys. Well, I might go to Hamleys, but not for this purpose, I hope.

So your daughter will be delighted to—

My daughter will be here. I'm going to Hamleys. I'm going to go Lillywhites. I'm going to go to Lillywhites um at Piccadilly Circus, where I know that I will find a great selection of trainers.

八、消费者主权与"多品牌货架"的战略意义

Now, because in the past I valued Nike as a product, my eye will be drawn more naturally towards the Nike products, and I am more likely to make a Nike purchasing decision.

But for me, that's a really easy marketplace, right? I don't have to go on lots of different apps. I don't have to go onto the Nike app first and then onto the Adidas app here. I can go into a shop and see all of them, and therefore make what I regard as being an informed decision in so doing.

Now, Nike have to back themselves that their brand is strong enough that once I put myself in that multi-product situation, I'm going to choose Nike, right? But effectively, by asking me to go on the app, they effectively are telling me: you need to have already made that decision before. And that slightly puts you under the headline of "mug" — because then they can start exerting pricing power on you. They can say, "Well, since you're here anyway and since you're plainly planning to buy Nike, we can start to push the price a little bit."

So I think you're right. I think betting — in stuff that you're going to actually wear, clothes, shoes, socks — putting yourself in a situation where you're expecting people to simply make that decision always to go with you, is strategically a very risky thing to do.

If they were going to do this properly, what they had to do is they had to double down on the core identity of Nike — i.e. a DTC thing — they had to bring me more into "I need to feel like an athlete" than I've ever been before, if you were going to own that relationship.

The fact that they had category changes like they did — removing verticals — and then asked me to go and make purchasing decisions on a site which I actually stopped understanding, with the clarity that I'd always had with that brand, was a horrible combination of factors that work together.

九、品质滑坡：经典款的过度开发与鞋底脱胶

And when they go into this period, they made quick careless decisions about which products they really doubled down in, to try and ensure that the revenue didn't take a hit.

What do I mean by that? They went all in on what we would call the classics. Air Force One, Jordan — those brands that they could shift, in their mind, huge amounts of inventory for very quickly because there was a demand. But the demand for those brands had often been built on one thing, and it was exclusivity. And in doing that, they stripped out a huge value of what those classics — a lot of that heritage product — had done.

They deviated from the quality of the core product to the extent where — I don't know about you — but since that has happened, I've had a few pairs of Nike running shoes. They fall apart like that.

Really? That's really—

Foam thing at the moment. And what you see in this foam thing is — a lot of them have a line through the foam sole. And that foam sole is actually clearly glued on. Right? I reckon for this pair of shoes, I probably ran in them for 3 months. Separation in the sole. They were pretty much unwearable after that.

The product — that running shoe that Phil Knight strived to build, that was better than anyone else — had suffered. Now, if you are creating a verticalized strategy with developers who know they're coming in to create the best products — because I am creating a running shoe — that doesn't happen to my product. If I've got a load of developers in there saying "we're creating men's, women's, and kids products," and then we're going to sell them in a new retail — well, sorry — a new sales strategy, that developer is not going to have that specificity, that focus, to create the best product to then sell in your new environment.

So — I honestly, the reason I wanted to drill into that piece was because I think that's a really important part.

十、Elliott Hill 的回归与批发渠道的重建

But what is notable to say just at the end of it is that Elliott Hill, the new CEO who they had to bring out of retirement — he'd been at Nike for 32 years, um, and has now been pulled out of a four-year retirement to come and un-fuck this, basically. He is now trying to rebuild these relationships.

And it is worth saying that 2026 wholesale is up 6% to 27.5 billion. It is moving back in the right direction. It will not change quickly enough — anywhere near quickly enough — to move that share price to the extent that they will get them back into a kind of top business conversation in the next few months. But if they can do it properly, can they recover from this? Absolutely. Can they get people back buying to it? Yes.

But I do think they need — they have to get that north star, that core piece.

十一、其他难题（一）：中国市场的失守与"国潮"崛起

There are other problems. There are other problems. There are other problems as well.

Tap China straight away. Mentioned that.

The trading relationship between the US and China over the last 3 years has been significantly impacted by the imposition and then removal and imposition of various tariffs. Um, and that is having an impact on lots of different brands and lots of different situations. Because even if the tariffs get put on and then removed, in the meantime you're removing B2B certainty. So that's obviously caused significant problems.

Have you got the numbers there in terms of what's actually happened, Charles?

So you mentioned uh financial year 2021 as being a major year for the value of the company.

High watermark.

The revenue in China was 8.29 billion in 2021. The revenue in 2026 was 5.85 billion.

So that's minus 30% of their Chinese revenue gone in 5 years — in a market where sportswear spending has actually grown by about half in the same time period.

Why? What it has seen is the rise of Chinese domestic challenger brands capturing a huge amount of this market. Anta and Li-Ning being two in particular — domestic brands that are slightly more affordable. I mean, Anta alone now holds 21.8% of China's sportswear market, where Nike previously would have captured far more of that.

And if you lose your quality differentiation in the meantime, and then a local challenger brand comes along — what's the normal charge that you would make against a local challenger brand? You say, "Well, probably the quality is not going to be up to all that much." But if you yourself have not kept up your own quality level, and a local challenger brand comes along, then you lose that bit as well.

Guochao — you know what Guochao is? I think I pronounced it right. Some state-encouraged consumer pride movement, basically. It's this um—

"Buy Chinese"?

Buy Chinese, yeah. Buy Chinese products, support the industry, invest more, and we'll be able to do more.

Uh — why have I — I don't know — Anta and Li-Ning, well Li-Ning in particular, been very good? Well, they've created the foam type running shoe that I was talking about previously — that Nike would have marketed as what made them different and the best in their markets. And they've said, "Hey look, we can do this, and we can do it for 80 quid rather than 180 quid," which I think is — if you look at those top running shoes — what Nike will charge for them.

So product innovation, through national pride in the brands that they want to start promoting, has basically given a Chinese public a different opportunity, a different alternative.

Yeah. So if you're looking at the diminution of revenue from peak to now — to being about 5 billion a year — you know, about half of that's from China.

Do you know what's interesting? Nike is also terminating its online distribution deals with thousands of Chinese retail partners from the 1st of January 2027. They're consolidating their own site, their own app. What they're stripping back in all the other regions, they're actually rolling out in China. In China, they want to basically be DTC.

But it does talk about the challenger element to it — the rise of other brands.

It does — because it's very hard to keep on being the challenger when you're 50 years into your evolution.

十二、其他难题（二）：美国联邦反歧视调查

And there's one final bit I just wanted to bring up — which is that they are actually currently under investigation by the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. Um, and this is investigating whether Nike has discriminated against white employees and applicants for employment.

So in other words: in their manic drive to be DEI and all this type of stuff, there have been a sufficient body of complaints — evidence — to support a fairly significant investigation into whether they've actually practiced systematic discrimination.

You don't want to be investigated by the US federal government. It's just a horrible, horrible place to be. Those cases can go on for a long time, can cost a vast amount of money, and the fines that tend to get levied by the federal government in the US are vast — they're absolutely huge. So it wouldn't surprise me if part of the current share price problems that they're facing is: when you've got a company that's under investigation by the feds, you're not in a good place, right?

So — I think loads of different things.

十三、结语：Nike 会不会真的完了？

It is. But in the meantime also, you have a very strong market that doesn't have one company that has grown up and been competitive. It's got a number of companies that have been competitive. And while you've left retail — right — that leaves a lot of shelf space, and that's been filled by the likes of Hoka, On Running, more of Adidas. New Balance doesn't publish its figures but is significantly up.

There's been a huge elevation in alternatives to people. So it's far harder for Nike to go, "I identify one challenger — we're going to grab that market share back," when a whole number of businesses have come to grab that from them.

And you know, just finally — I think, because there's really a question here as we ended up: are they terminally screwed, or is this recoverable? You know — those companies I've just named, everyone looks at and says, "Oh, haven't they grown in the same time?" They've also, and are also, having significant challenges. On's shares fell as much as 22% by August '26 on a revenue miss. Right? Public company.

Yeah.

Hoka's growth decelerates into single digits. So we're not saying the market is booming. There are real challenges out there for everyone. And if the running boom is entering kind of a normalization phase, then in a flat market Nike are going to have a far better opportunity, I think, of grabbing some of that market share back than they do in an accelerating one.

They just really need to sort out who they are and remember what the business was.

Read — every single person making a decision at that company should just go back and read the book that their founder wrote, as to what it means to wear Nike.

item.description:
## 一个反常识的观察：Nike 的股价崩盘不是"跌了"，而是"神话塌了"
真正令人震撼的数字对比，视频里只是轻描淡写地提到——**营收只下滑了 10%，市值蒸发了 80%**。这中间的 70% 差额，本质上不是"运动鞋生意"的价值，而是**"神话溢价"**（narrative premium）的崩塌。市场从来不是在给 Nike 的鞋子定价，而是在给"Nike 代表未来"这个故事定价。
这解释了一个隐藏的悖论：**当 Nike 决定"站队"的那一刻，它就从一个神话变成了一个观点。** 神话可以让所有人投射自己（Jordan 是每个孩子的梦想，Federer 是每个白领的优雅），而观点必然排斥另一半人。视频中提到 Phil Knight 的话——"让没有运动员天赋的人感受运动员的感觉"——这是**代理式超越**（proxy transcendence）；而 Kaepernick 合作则是**部落式认同**（tribal identity）。前者的市场是全人类，后者的市场永远只有一半。
## 跨领域连接：Nike 的"鞋底脱胶"和"价值观漂移"其实是同一件事
视频里 Charlie

item.title: [Lex Clips] John Nash's schizophrenia (A Beautiful Mind) - failed horrific treatments | Andrew Scull
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"80%治愈率"作为一种人类学化石

Scull不经意间抛出了一个惊人的模式："80%这个数字在这些疗法中反复出现"。这不是巧合，而是一个未被言说的社会心理学常数。为什么不是95%？不是100%？因为80%正好落在"奇迹阈值"与"合理性阈值"的交界带——高到足以震撼、传播、吸引投资，低到足以为失败案例留出解释空间（"那20%本来就无药可救"）。

这个数字与庞氏骗局承诺的年化回报率、邪教宣称的"觉醒率"、创业孵化器吹嘘的"成功率"惊人吻合。80%不是医学数据，是一种叙事货币——它是骗子、狂热者、真诚的错误者共同发现的"最优说服比例"。萨克尔从德国戒毒所走到纽约诊所、从治疗诈骗中挣到200万美元（1960年代币值，约合今天2000万美元）的整个轨迹，本质上是这个数字的社会学套利。

二、萨克尔的"精神分裂脑细胞"辩护：一个思维病理学标本

当被告知胰岛素休克疗法杀死脑细胞时，萨克尔答："是的，它们在杀死精神分裂的脑细胞。"

这句话值得被写进认知科学教科书。它展示了一个完整的自我封闭系统（closed epistemic loop）是如何工作的：任何反驳证据都被重新分类为支持证据。这与柯顿"局部感染理论"、拉马克主义抵抗基因证据、乃至今天某些AGI乐观论者对齐问题的辩护结构完全同构——它们不是被证据说服，而是被证据强化。

一个跨领域的连接令我震撼：萨克尔的辩护逻辑与加密货币社群面对市场崩盘时的"淘汰弱手"叙事、与硅谷"快速失败"文化对失败项目的美化，共享同一种深层语法——"破坏本身即是筛选，筛选即是进步"。当破坏成为疗效的证据，我们就进入了一个再无证伪可能的宇宙。

三、纳什悖论：那个"美丽心灵"或许是治疗塑造的

这里有一个几乎没人提及但令人战栗的可能性：约翰·纳什的博弈论直觉（尤其是他后期思想的某些奇异跃迁）可能与胰岛素休克造成的脑损伤存在无法切分的关系。

传统叙事是："纳什尽管接受了这些恐怖治疗，仍然成为数学天才。" 但如果我们诚实面对神经科学：60次胰岛素昏迷+可能的脑细胞损伤，绝不可能"绕过"他的大脑。那个我们通过电影浪漫化的"战胜精神分裂的美丽心灵"，实际上是一具被20世纪精神病学重塑过的神经系统的产物。他没有战胜疾病，他被迫在受伤的地形上重新绘制心智地图。

四、真正令人意外的观察：这个疗法链条的"设计模式"

把萨克尔（胰岛素昏迷）→ 梅杜纳（樟脑/卡地阿唑抽搐）→ 电休克，看作一条演化链，你会发现一个惊人的"降本增效"轨迹： - 胰岛素昏迷：需要几十小时护理，风险极高，但戏剧性强 - Metrazol：注射即抽搐，但患者体验"濒死感"，且骨折率高 - 电休克：秒级、可控、可重复

这不是医学进步的曲线，是"疗法商品化"的曲线——从手工业到工业化，从匠人到流水线。每一代新疗法解决的不是前代的疗效缺陷，而是前代的规模化缺陷。

这个模式的跨领域投射极其锋利：它是"制造流水线"、"内容工厂"、"SaaS化一切"的原型故事。当我们今天目睹AI心理咨询、AI医生、AI教师的快速迭代时，那个1930年代维也纳诊所的幽灵仍在场——规模化的冲动会伪装成对痛苦的关怀，直到某天，我们发现"电击"版本的AI疗法已经无声地取代了所有更慢、更贵、更人性的替代品。

📝 转录文本

一次真正的20世纪医学胜利：胰岛素的发现

We talk about triumphs of medicine, so let me talk of one of the real triumphs of 20th century medicine, which is interesting to refer to because it wasn't a cure — just like psychiatric drugs aren't a cure for mental illness. It was a symptomatic treatment, but it transformed lives, and that was the discovery of insulin in the 1920s.

Previously, particularly what we now call type 1 or juvenile diabetes was a death sentence. You got it, and whatever you did — you tried various quack remedies, you tried diet, you tried all sorts of things — the inevitable thing was it killed you. And then came insulin. Now, insulin doesn't mean you're cured of your diabetes, but what it means is you can live a relatively normal life, and your lifespan is greatly expanded. So, by any measure, you have to say that's dramatic progress.

But insulin is something our bodies produce, we hope, unless we're really seriously diabetic. Those of us with type 2 diabetes, our bodies resist insulin, and we have to resort to other ways of trying to cope. But if you get too much insulin, it makes you unconscious.

从戒毒所到精神病院：萨克尔的胰岛素昏迷疗法

And that's how another one of these desperate remedies came along. A man named Sakel, working in a German clinic for drug addicts — they were using putting people under mild comas to help them through the withdrawal symptoms as they got over their addiction. So he was familiar with that. And when he moved to Austria, he decided he'd try this as a treatment for schizophrenia.

And so he put people into comas, sometimes comas that would last hours, days. They would be revived by giving them glucose, usually intravenously, sometimes not. During the time they were in comas, they often seized, had seizures. He saw that as a therapeutic sign. And he claimed that this insulin coma treatment cured 80% of his — 80% tends to come up again and again in these treatments as the sort of percentage that you cure.

And he was invited to New York and demonstrated this at the Halloran Valley Mental Hospital.

It spread. This is in the '30s.

This was starting in 1933. The visit to America was, I believe, 1936. And Sakel ended up settling here. He had a very lucrative private practice in New York. And when he died, he left his partner, I think, in an estate of about $2 million, which in the early '60s was a very substantial amount of money that he'd earned from practice.

疗法的代价与"精神分裂脑细胞"的辩护

So insulin coma therapy was widely adopted. What kept it from being a large-scale thing was it required an enormous amount of nursing and medical attention, because people were literally hovering on the brink of life and death. They could go into a permanent coma, they could just die. So their vital signs had to be monitored, they had to be brought around very quickly if need be.

And there's some evidence that the treatment killed brain cells. And when Sakel was told that, he said, "Yes, that's probably true. They're killing the schizophrenic brain cells." That's just nonsense. That's just nonsense, but that's rational.

Insulin comas weren't subjected to a randomized controlled trial until the 1950s. And when they were subjected to a controlled trial, they failed it. And so it died out. That's, I guess, scientific progress again in a way, but took a long time.

约翰·纳什与"美丽心灵"

One of the people who received insulin coma therapy — have you seen the film A Beautiful Mind?

Mhm.

He did receive insulin coma therapy, ironically at Trenton State Hospital where Cotton had been.

So John Nash received —

Got insulin comas, and they were going to lobotomize him. And they didn't. But he was at risk of that.

We should say that this treatment — patients would thrash, moan, and convulse before falling into a coma. The treatment required a course of up to 60 comas. It turned out to have a mortality rate of 1 to 5% and caused significant brain damage and obesity.

Yeah.

Yet was hailed as a miracle cure for schizophrenia.

And yes, that's right.

Performed on John Nash, one of the great minds of the 20th century.

Yes. And Nash clearly did become delusional. But that was one of the treatments he was subjected to. And well represented actually in the film of A Beautiful Mind.

人工癫痫：从樟脑到 Metrazol

So I mentioned seizures. Also in the Austro-Hungarian in this period, another psychiatrist decided that you couldn't be both schizophrenic and epileptic.

Mhm.

That there was somehow an antagonism between the two. So if you had epilepsy, you didn't have schizophrenia. And if you had schizophrenia, you couldn't have epilepsy. I should say at the outset that's not true. But that's what he believed.

So then the logical next step was: well, if we could create an artificial epileptic seizure, maybe we would drive out the schizophrenia. So what to do?

He first tries injecting camphor, a natural substance. Natural substances are necessarily benign substances. That caused abscesses, and it wasn't very effective. He sought an alternative, and he settled on something that was called Cardiazol, or Metrazol, depending which side of the Atlantic you were on.

And injecting that into a patient usually caused a seizure — a big seizure, like a grand mal seizure, where your body arcs back, your legs contract dramatically.

You can fracture spines, and hips, and bones.

And you ended up, yes, with fractures of the vertebrae, fractures of the hip socket, because when the muscles in the thigh contract that badly, what happens? The thigh bone is driven into the socket —

Mhm.

— at such a rate that it fractures. So these were among the complications that Metrazol produced.

濒死体验：一位病人的视角

More than that, he himself conceded that between the injection and the seizure, the patient felt as though he were on — or she was on — the brink of death.

Now imagine — pretend you're a mental patient. You're brought in in a straitjacket. A man in a white coat with a big hypodermic injects something into you. You feel as though you're going to die. And maybe that lingers for 2, 3, 10 minutes, and then you seize with those possible fractures following.

Violent seizures.

It's violent, and hard to witness, and is very unpredictable. So it's used, but people are not very happy — and that's how we get electroconvulsive therapy, electroshock as it's first called.

item.description:
## 一、"80%治愈率"作为一种人类学化石
Scull不经意间抛出了一个惊人的模式：**"80%这个数字在这些疗法中反复出现"**。这不是巧合，而是一个未被言说的社会心理学常数。为什么不是95%？不是100%？因为80%正好落在**"奇迹阈值"与"合理性阈值"的交界带**——高到足以震撼、传播、吸引投资，低到足以为失败案例留出解释空间（"那20%本来就无药可救"）。
这个数字与庞氏骗局承诺的年化回报率、邪教宣称的"觉醒率"、创业孵化器吹嘘的"成功率"惊人吻合。**80%不是医学数据，是一种叙事货币**——它是骗子、狂热者、真诚的错误者共同发现的"最优说服比例"。萨克尔从德国戒毒所走到纽约诊所、从治疗诈骗中挣到200万美元（1960年代币值，约合今天2000万美元）的整个轨迹，本质上是这个数字的社会学套利。
## 二、萨克尔的"精神分裂脑细胞"辩护：一个思维病理学标本
当被告知胰岛素休克疗法杀死脑细胞时，萨克尔答："**是的，它们在杀死精神分裂的脑细胞。**"
这句话值得被写进认知科学教科书。它展示了一个完整的**自我封闭系统（closed epistemic loop）**

item.title: [Alan Chen加州生活号] 加息25个基点，市场却开始挤空：AI下一轮领涨已经换人 | 美股圆桌｜
item.dc:creator: Alan Chen加州生活号
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、隐藏在租金里的"暗物质"：AI 商业周期的相位切换

这期节目最容易被听众忽略、但真正值钱的信号，其实藏在 NBIS 那个几乎被一笔带过的细节里——CPU 租金涨幅超过 GPU。

大多数人还在用"训练时代"的心智模型看这轮 AI 行情：Nvidia 是唯一的太阳，其他都是绕着转的行星。但租金曲线其实在悄悄告诉你另一个故事：AI 已经从"造模型"进入"跑模型"的相位。Alan 那个"CPU 是车间主任、GPU 是工程师"的比喻其实很惊人——推理需要的是编排、调度、事务性逻辑，不是暴力算力。这意味着 AMD、Intel、Arm、AMAT 这些被市场视为"上一代"的公司，实际上是在被下一代需求重新召回的老兵，而不是在追赶潮流。

跨领域连接：这个模式跟电力工业史惊人相似。1900 年代初期，所有资本都追捧发电机制造商（相当于今天的 GPU 厂），但真正跑赢 30 年的公司是变压器、电表、配电盘——它们对应的正是"让电真正被用起来"的基础设施。今天 CPU 租金反超 GPU，就是那个"电已经发出来了，接下来看谁把它送到千家万户"的转折点信号。

二、"预期已满"的量子态：加息利空为何变利多

节目里 Alan 说"上涨的预期已经 fully priced in"，这句话背后是一个被反复验证但很少被讲清楚的市场悖论：在信息市场里，被观察的风险会失去破坏力。

Fear & Greed 指数触及 Extreme Fear、20 日均线上方个股跌到 20%——这些不是超卖信号，这是"所有人都已经把最坏情况想到"的市场共识指纹。当 FOMC 真的加了 25bp，反而释放了一个更强的元信号：所有人担心的那件事，已经不能再吓到任何人。

这个现象跟量子力学的"退相干"是同构的：叠加态一旦被观察，就坍缩成确定态。市场也是这样——一件事只要被充分讨论、充分交易、充分定价，它就从"变量"变成了"常数"。真正需要警惕的从来不是被讨论最多的风险（关税、加息、AI 泡沫），而是当前完全没人在讨论的东西——比如今天 10 年期和 30 年期国债在股市反弹时依然阴涨，这个反相关的裂缝，才是被市场遗漏的量子态。

三、川普输中期选举 = 股市的"稳态悖论"

节目末尾那个反直觉观点很值得深挖：川普赢中期选举反而是股市的利空。听起来违反商业媒体的常识，但它其实揭示了资本市场一个更深的规律——市场爱的不是政策取向，是政策边界。

一党独大意味着单方向政策可以无阻力推行，这在数学上等同于方差扩大：能推行的政策空间变宽，市场无法用制衡逻辑收敛出预期。而"两党对峙"看似低效，却给市场提供了一个天然的贝叶斯先验：任何激进政策都会被稀释、被延迟、被谈判。

跨领域连接：生态学里有个"多样性—稳定性假说"——物种越单一的生态系统对扰动越敏感（想想爱尔兰土豆饥荒）。政治权力结构对市场的作用完全同构：制衡不是低效，是抗脆弱性的定价机制。所以 2018 年中期选举后市场那个"12 月 20% 反弹"的老故事，本质不是"川普失去众议院"这个事件本身，而是方差被重新压缩的重定价。

四、彩蛋：S-1 文件本身就是催化剂

最后一个容易被跳过的洞察——Anthropic 递交 S-1 后，供应链会先涨。这不是"利好兑现"，而是一个更微妙的机制：S-1 是公开知识的诞生。

在博弈论里，"共同知识（common knowledge）"和"每个人都知道"是两回事。私下都知道 Anthropic 增长很快，跟"所有人都知道所有人都知道 Anthropic 的 ARR"，是完全不同的两个市场状态。前者不会改变行为，后者会立刻改变所有下游厂商的采购、议价、扩产决策。IPO 招股书的价值，从来不是融资本身，而是它把"私人信念"升级为"公共协调点"。这也是为什么 SpaceX 当年临近上市传闻时，太空板块一次次爆发——共同知识的形成，本身就是最强的多因子催化剂。

📝 转录文本

开场

Hello everyone, welcome back to our Meizhou Meigu Yuan Zhuo。上周我跟 Will 聊了 AI 小作文，市场当时非常 panic。这一周有一些大的波动，大市和股市都上下颠簸。周三 FOMC 加息 25 个基点——上周我预测可能会加，Will 预测可能不加。稍后我们会回顾各自的思路。本周要聊的东西很多，今天先从 FOMC 说起。

一、FOMC 25bp：为什么市场反应还算体面

我们上周先请你（Will）复盘一下思路，包括为什么这次加 25bp 的市场反应其实是可以接受的。

  • 过去一年多以来，指数已经处在比较低的位置；
  • 20 日均线之上的个股占比只有 20% 左右；
  • 这种位置一般是需要反弹的，此时再去追空，废纸的可能性会更大。

二、点阵图 vs. 市场预期：分歧才是机会

第二点是看点阵图。我觉得可以补充一些细节：

  • 其实点阵图释放的信息并不等于市场预期；
  • 点阵图只释放了后续再加两次的信号；
  • 但市场（看 WATCH 工具）预期到明年年底其实是 3–4 次的加息（原文口误，语境为"降息"）。

所以真实情况没有预期得那么糟。在这个背景下，超卖的、擅长做多的人就跳了出来，现在的大盘就是一个超卖反弹。

不过我依然是"加 0.25"的那个观点——上周我就说了，市场已经把 25bp 打满在 WOS 里；如果他选择加，影响不会太大；但如果他不加，可能会影响到他的 credibility。所以我当时判断他会加 25bp，同时维持美联储的独立性。

三、风险偏好的信号：QQQ 未创新低、标普创了

我觉得市场表现挺好。周三我们社区 Q&A 的时候我就跟大家说过：QQQ 没有创新低，但标普创了。整体来说是一个 risk-on 的好信号。

我们也聊到了 Fear & Greed Index，已经触及 Almost Extreme Fear，包括收盘时依然处在 panic 状态。美元上涨之前，我也在 X 上贴过自己的观点：当前的恐慌情绪已经很到位，价格不会跌破 25、也不会跌破 50——预期已经 fully priced in。

其实 9 月 18 日的波动可能比 FOMC 本身更大。目前来看，这是一个 miss。

四、大牛市结构与半导体估值

我们上周聊过，无论是标普还是纳斯达克，整体都在走一个高位牛市结构，对吧？我记得那之后我们做了一波多头。当时我们就说过——

我们整个 SOXX 半导体板块，也在这样一个正面背景下：估值非常、非常有吸引力。即使已经涨了一周，当前估值仍然很强，让那些还没上车的朋友仍然可以继续考虑。这就是我们在言宝社区里的判断。

调研中还有很多可以分享的内容，包括 SMH 从技术形态上是一个比较标准的头肩底形态，这些都在兑现之中。感兴趣的会员朋友可以在 ALANTSLA.com 上看到我们中线、国内和长线所有过往交易，包括哪些股票具体输了、赢了。

五、网络安全 & AI 小作文余波

本周（包括昨天）一些个股上涨，其实和上周发生的事情关系很大：

  • 一是网络安全板块从周一开始起涨；
  • 我们周日聊过 AI 小作文，Dario 开始吓人；周一、周三 all-in summit 出来之后，情绪有所反弹；
  • 尤其是周一，NBIS（Nubi 博士）说要涨价，把整条半导体产业链的情绪都带起来了，包括"订单删除"的情绪。

六、NBIS 涨租的秘密：CPU > GPU

我们发现一个很有意思的现象。Will，你帮大家梳理一下——我说太多了。

这条信息其实非常关键：本周 NBIS 的新租约，不管是 GPU 还是 CPU，租金都在涨；而且 CPU 涨得比 GPU 还要多。

第一，大厂并没有跑路，基本上都还在——因为全场的控制逻辑是"折旧被高估"。但如果我的老芯片、老显卡还在涨，那它的会计算盘就是合情合理、有利有节的。

第二，CPU 和 GPU 的需求都在持续增长，尤其是 CPU。CPU 是做什么的？我们在报告里说过——CPU 在推理阶段的需求非常高，因为推理的占比越来越大。CPU 就像车间里的一个"主任"，需要管理软件和其他方方面面的事情，才能让推理顺利跑起来。

（此处为一段较长的转录静默段，从略。）

七、大厂建新数据中心背后的隐含预期

我们都知道，建一个 data center 的工地至少要 3–5 年。原本纯 CAPEX 是压在今年年底的，但如果他们真的认为 PIX（peak capex）就在今年年底，为什么还愿意投钱去建新的 internal 技术？

所以我们此前的假设需要改一改，还需要进一步研究。但今天，包括 AMD、Intel、Cadence 这样的半导体公司——

八、半导体的"50 军线"与内部分化

关于这个半导体板块，我可以多说几句。这大概是你在外面、如果没人告诉你，可能不太理解的：

整个半导体板块给人的感觉像是"50 军线"刚刚站上——但在这条线里面，其实有很多个明显强于其他公司的强者。

比如为什么我们刚才聊到"推理未来的需求可能高于训练"？——你就能清楚地看到，那些沾 CPU 的公司，跑得比纯 GPU 的更好。

  • AMD 为什么今天接近历史高点？可能下周就要突破？因为它主要做的就是这方面业务；
  • Intel 两周前就已经在早期启动；
  • 包括 Arm——今天也是。它开始发展这一模式，也刚发布了新产品 CBR4 Rebus，同样基于推理。

所以如果你把这些串起来：订单 → 存储 → AMAT → 其他硬件，你就能更清楚地判断谁会是这一轮的 leader、哪个版本、哪些标的。我们会在社区里跟会员详细讨论。

九、比特币反弹与 RWA

这周（包括今天）更大的一件事，是比特币又涨了：今天涨了大约 6%，看起来风险情绪回来了。

主要原因是本周 Clarity Act 失败，失败之后先大跌，休息了两天，今天似乎是通过美股链上的 RWA（Real World Assets）实现了这样的交易。所以他们的 leader、Yang Hu——市场愿意再承担一些风险。

十、前方的不确定性事件

但前方还有很多不确定事件：

  • 下周有 APEC（原文"春节"疑为口误）；上次他们在北京开会时美股大跌，会后如何仍不确定；
  • 中期选举：现在只剩不到两个月，市场已经很早地开始定价"民主党回归"；
  • 伊朗战争：德国等会尝试拿掉一些共和党席位——因为能源价格仍然偏高，尽管有企稳趋势；上周我们也提过原油。

看起来 OK，但又有一点"不太合理"。

十一、债市的"裂缝"

本周还有一些点值得注意，包括 30 年和 10 年国债：虽然走势偏稳，但今天也在涨——股市和债市同时上涨。

这说明债市对通胀是否被完全控制仍然有些担忧。因为如果没有担忧，它应该在加息之后与股市呈负相关——毕竟这次是 0.25bp。

今天如果 equity 表现这么好、债券反而下跌，我们会更放心。但目前来看，市场可能更在乎的是——川普是否在跟伊朗释放利好？油价是否会下来？——市场好像有一种"抢跑"的感觉。

十二、川普外交的"猜谜"

这个挺有意思的：他之前说选举结束之后战争才会结束。但现在的问题是——战争没有结束，选举基本已经结束了。所以我不知道他现在在打什么算盘。

刚看到几分钟前他又发消息说要和习达成很多协议。我们还需要更多信息，才能知道他在葫芦里卖什么药。你还带了一堆中国企业家。但问题是：如果你不让他们投资美国，那这些中国企业家来是占便宜的。

表面上关系看起来还可以接受，但实际上更多的是继续 decoupling。

十三、Anthropic IPO 猜想

所以还有一件即将发生的事——Anthropic（AdRabic）的招股与落地即将官宣。

我们之前也聊过：SpaceX 上市前是被选中的公司；Anthropic、OpenAI 和 SpaceX 基本上是同一量级的公司。看看这次会不会发生。

这里有个很有意思的观察：一旦它宣布要发 S-1，这件事本身就更有利可图——因为你的 S-1 会披露 ARR、营收、增长、指引。理论上下游会得到更多订单：存储、光模块、GPU、CPU，以及各种光机等等，都会受益。

那么等到它真正 IPO 的时候，可能就会出现类似 SpaceX 上市时那种少见的现象。所以短期来看，这应该会让这些 AI 相关板块再涨一轮。

个人观点：我更看好 DaFan（大范）。至少下周，我觉得还是 OK 的。过程会更痛苦，因为要走长期；但总体在这个位置，仍然是不错的一段时间。

十四、季节性与中期选举的历史类比

除了大选年，9–10 月这段一般都比较危险。除了 2018 年——那一年大盘也在中期附近，从 12 月一路涨。当时也很出人意料：结果 12 月出现了 20% 的反弹，把大家都吓出去了。

如果控制多数席位——川普会没有人能够监管他；但如果民主党回来，又可能在经济发展方面带来担忧。到底会不会……

我个人认为，川普中期选举失利，其实对股市是好事——市场不喜欢不确定性。但如果他失去这个能力……

十五、技术面展望

从技术指标看，我认为我们应该会有另一次挑战前高的机会。但能涨多少，我们不知道；能不能走到终点，我们不知道。

这里有一种"不确定性恐惧"——因为每一次中期选举，都会给人一种"要出大反馈"的感觉。市场要么会安心，要么想等等看，看测试结果如何。所以我觉得我们也可以关注这样一种可能性。但在那些恐惧真正开始之前——

item.title: [All-In Podcast] Bill Gurley: Searching for Feynman
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

关于 Bill Gurley「寻找费曼」演讲的系统性观察

一、这是一场关于「搜索算法失效」的演讲，而非关于新冠

表面上 Gurley 在讲根因分析，但更深层的结构是：他在用费曼的方法论去寻找一个费曼。这是一个递归自指的问题——当科学体制本身成为被调查对象时，谁来做调查者？他列举的五个灾难中，都有独立于当事机构的「第三方节点」（NIST、NSF、参议院、学术委员会、独立记者），构成了一个分布式验证网络。而新冠事件的独特之处在于：所有本该充当独立验证节点的机构，都与被调查对象共享同一个知识网络。

用密码学的语言说，这是典型的拜占庭容错崩溃：当超过 1/3 的验证者被同一利益污染，整个共识系统失效。Gurley 三年前讲「监管俘获」（regulatory capture），今天讲的其实是科学俘获（scientific capture）——一个更危险的升级版本，因为科学声称自己是终极仲裁者。

二、一个几乎无人提及的观察：性别的完美镜像

Gurley 展示的五位「阻拦者」（Collins、Fauci、Daszak、Farrar、Baric）全部为男性，且全部是同一代际、同一学术圈的内部人；而他致敬的五位「搜索者」（Chan、Eban、Kopp、Tufekci、Young）全部为女性，且分散在分子生物学、财经记者、非营利组织、社会学、调查记者五个完全不同的领域。

这不是巧合，而是一个系统性信号。跨领域连接：这个模式在其他历史时刻反复出现——沙利度胺灾难中的 Frances Kelsey、安然事件中的 Sherron Watkins、Theranos 事件中的 Erika Cheung、烟草诉讼中的 Jeffrey Wigand（男性但为局外人）。当核心圈层高度同质化并共享既得利益时，突破性的真相往往由「结构上的局外人」揭示——他们既没有社交资本要保护，也没有被邀请进入"共识制造"的房间。女性在科学体制中的边缘地位，反而使她们成为最可靠的搜索节点。

这里有个反直觉的推论：多样性不仅是道德议题，而是认知安全议题。同质化的专家网络在正常时期高效，在危机时期危险。

三、规模的悖论——伤害越大，调查越少

Gurley 提到一个惊人的数字：新冠的死亡人数是他列举的所有其他五个灾难总和的 3000 倍，但投入调查的人力资源大约是 1/1000。这看起来违反直觉，但如果你把它建模成一个「institutional flight response」（机构逃逸响应）函数，就完全合理了：

调查强度 ≈ (公众关注 × 记者独立性) / (被调查方规模 × 意识形态载荷)

飓风卡特里娜的调查对象是陆军工程兵团——一个可以被围剿的、政治上安全的目标。而新冠的调查对象是整个全球生物医学建制，加上一个战略竞争对手（中国），加上一个已被极化的政治议题。分母膨胀到无穷大时，分子再大也趋于零。

四、跨领域连接：这场演讲预示了 AI 时代的核心风险

最令我意外的是 Gurley 在演讲末尾看似顺带的一句话：「我的 P(second COVID) 远高于我的 P(doom)」。这句话轻描淡写，但颠覆了整个 AI 安全叙事的框架。

主流 AI 风险讨论聚焦于「模型能力失控」，但 Gurley 指出了一个更近迫、也更被忽视的风险：制造共识的机制已经被证明可以在没有 AI 帮助的情况下扭曲全球集体认知。Proximal Origins 论文一周内写成，绕过了正常的科学审议，成为维基百科的引用锚点，让整个话题变成禁忌——这已经是前 AI 时代的信息战完美案例。

推论：真正需要担心的不是 AI 会不会说谎，而是当这套「制造共识」的社会机制被 AI 加速 1000 倍时，人类的分布式验证系统是否还能运作。Gurley 演讲的真正议题，其实是「知识论的抗审查性」（epistemic censorship-resistance）——这与比特币解决的问题在深层结构上同构。

五、一个隐藏的元讽刺

Gurley 在演讲中把自己反复归入「读过顶级 1% 资料的人」——这是他给自己颁发的信誉徽章。但整场演讲的核心论点恰恰是：权威徽章不是真相的来源，独立搜索才是。他必须援引徽章来让台下的风险投资人听进去，但他真正想传达的信息是「不要相信徽章」。

这个内在张力揭示了一个更深的系统性困境：在一个低信任社会中，即便你要传播「打破权威」的信息，你也必须先建立自己的权威。这是所有改革者的双重束缚，也是为什么真正的范式转换往往需要一代人的时间——因为老一代必须先死去，新一代才能在没有旧权威负担的情况下重新开始搜索。

一个具体行动建议：如果你相信 Gurley 的框架，最有杠杆的干预点不是捐款给某个调查组织，而是降低「搜索者」的社会成本。每一次公开为 Alina Chan 或 Zeynep Tufekci 的观点辩护（即使你不完全同意），都是在给系统的搜索能力增加冗余节点。反之，每一次沉默都是在验证「围剿有效」这一策略。
