item.title: [All-In Podcast] Jared Isaacman: A New Era for NASA and American Space Exploration
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的洞察：NASA 正在从"梦想服务商"变回"承包总工"

Isaacman 讲话中最刺耳、也最少被注意到的一句话是——"我们发明了一种叫做 dream state as a service 的东西"。这句自嘲背后藏着一个惊人的组织病理学诊断：过去二十年的 NASA 并不是在造火箭，而是在向承包商"外包梦想"，再用政治叙事回购这个梦想。

这与硅谷 SaaS 的兴衰曲线惊人同构：当一家公司把核心能力全部外包给 vendor，只保留 PPT 和采购部，它就从"造物者"退化成"叙事者"。Isaacman 实际上在把 NASA 从 SaaS 模式重新拉回 vertically integrated OEM 模式——这和 Tesla 自造电池、Apple 自造芯片是同一个动作。太空竞赛的胜负，可能首先是一场"组织架构反 SaaS 化"的胜负。

二、跨领域连接：月球南极的"停车位经济学" = 曼哈顿地价 + 石油海上钻井平台

Isaacman 反复强调"月球南极只有那么几个好停车位"（only so many good parking spots）——这句话看似轻描淡写，却把一个天体力学问题瞬间翻译成了 房地产经济学 + 大宗商品期货。

  • 曼哈顿逻辑：南极面积仅相当于华盛顿特区，永久阴影区（水冰）与永久光照区（太阳能）的组合稀缺性，本质上是"稀缺土地上的双资产复合租值"。
  • 北海钻井平台逻辑：Starship 一次着陆会喷出碎片污染邻居——这和海上钻井平台的"安全间距 + 优先占用权"完全一致，中国主动去 Shackleton Ridge 的动作，可以直接类比为"抢先插旗打井"。

最出人意料的推论：真正决定第二次登月竞赛胜负的，可能不是火箭推力，而是着陆坐标的先占权——这是一场用航天器进行的"地契战争"。谁先着陆，谁就在国际习惯法层面建立事实占有。中国 2030 年的登月节点，本质上是一份"月球土地契约的交割日"。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：核能才是叙事，登月只是"融资故事"

表面上，整个演讲围绕"重返月球"展开。但如果你把它当作一份 投资备忘录 来读，就会发现真正的战略资产其实是核动力（SR-1 Freedom, SR-2, SR-3, SR-4）。

Isaacman 藏得很深的一句话是："核动力 NASA 是我们在承担那些'没有明显商业模式'的任务"。翻译成风险投资的语言：登月是有商业追随者的市场（Blue Origin、SpaceX 会跟进），所以 NASA 不该重复投；但深空核推进没有商业买家，只有政府能做，因此这是 NASA 唯一不可替代的护城河。

这个逻辑与生物医药中的 孤儿药策略 惊人相似——政府补贴那些市场不愿做的、但社会价值巨大的领域。Isaacman 实际上在把 NASA 重新定位为"深空领域的 DARPA + NIH 合体"，而不是运载火箭承包商。

四、一个几乎没人注意到的信号：Starfleet Academy 是最长期的地缘政治伏笔

演讲中一笔带过的"United States Space Academy"（他直接说"就叫它 Starfleet Academy 吧"）看似浪漫，实则是用长达 40 年的时间尺度锁定人才管道。

对比看：西点军校奠定了美国陆军百年霸权，海军学院奠定了两洋制海权。空间学院意味着华盛顿正在为 2065 年的地月经济体系提前储备"殖民地总督"级别的人才。这个动作的时间视野远远超出了任何一届总统任期——这才是最真正的"长期主义"，一种连 VC 都不敢做的时间跨度赌注。

五、意外的组织行为学观察：Isaacman 反复说"我不是来当你们的 VC 的"

在一个满是 VC 的房间里（All-In Podcast），他毫不客气地说："如果你想让我为你的梦想投资、发明新市场，请去找商务部。"

这种在需求方最集中的场合公开拒绝需求方的行为，在任何组织行为学教科书里都是极其罕见的——它是一次信号博弈中的强承诺（costly signaling）。他必须在硅谷这个"人情最厚"的场景里当众划清界限，才能对内部工程师和对外部承包商同时释放"这次是真的"的信号。这种"在最容易妥协的地方公开拒绝妥协"的姿态，历史上最像的先例是艾森豪威尔卸任演讲里点名"军工复合体"——这不是一次演讲，这是一次公开的组织契约重签。

📝 转录文本

Jared Isaacman: A New Era for NASA and American Space Exploration

开场：一个转折时刻

Ignition sequence start, all engines up.

"It's good to have an aviator and astronaut in charge." — Jared Isaacman, the new NASA administrator.

"NASA's still hot. Humankind will not be contained to planet Earth indefinitely. In the next giant leap capabilities, that's nuclear power and propulsion. That's what extends America's reach farther into the solar system. That's what guarantees the third race will never be in question."

Please welcome Jared Isaacman.

一、我们所处的历史时刻

Good morning everyone. It is an absolute honor to be here at All-In.

We are living through an extraordinary moment in history, aren't we? It took just 65 years from Orville and Wilbur's first flight to Neil and Buzz walking on the surface of the moon. Now, it's been 57 years since Apollo 11. And for a while there, pace of progress hasn't been all that inspiring, but look at what is on the horizon right now.

We got artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, robotics, additive manufacturing, the promise of fusion energy, biotech to heal the disabled, autonomous transportation, this whole abundance thing everyone's talking about — all converging in the years ahead is beyond what most people can comprehend. Our world will fundamentally change: how we live, how we work, how we fight wars, how we reach out and touch the stars.

But we are not alone on this journey. We are living through a great power competition. Other nations understand the opportunities that can elevate nations and change civilizations. And perhaps nowhere are the possibilities, the competition, and the consequences of getting it wrong more apparent than in the ultimate high ground above us.

二、NASA 过去的病灶

Now at NASA, we are doing things differently and we are regaining our swagger and putting wins on the board. But absent this president, absent this geopolitical competition and the very real possibility of losing the second space race, I suspect very little would have changed.

For too long, resources at the world's most accomplished space agency were spread everywhere, trying to make everyone happy. Much of it was through external imposition, but plenty of it was self-inflicted. We partnered for the sake of partnerships, oftentimes becoming a drag on the mission instead of accelerating it.

As a result: - We have the Orion spacecraft that we can't inject into low lunar orbit like we did during Apollo. - The prior administration cancelled the Mars sample return mission that was on track to cost more than an aircraft carrier. - We created programs that were too big to fail, too costly to truly succeed, in the hope that they would survive administrations.

The results being a rocket that was designed when China was predominantly operating coal-fired locomotives, and now becoming operational as China operates 25,000 miles of high-speed rail and is just a few years away from their own Apollo-11-like moment.

Core competencies and tens of thousands of the NASA workforce were rented, outsourced, or lost, which turned what should have been months worth of progress into years at tremendously greater cost. Eventually, too little was left to do things the right way — the way NASA showed the world how to do it in decades past.

So we invented this whole "dream state as a service" thing, forgoing the playbook of success and shifting the impossible burden onto others. The result is: - Our moon rocket is in fact less efficient than Saturn V at converting launch mass into payload headed for the moon. - More time between the Artemis 1 and Artemis 2 missions than all 12 of the Gemini missions that were flown 60 years before. - A lunar space station that whenever it may have been delivered put our astronauts in a position to look down on the most desirable lunar real estate instead of operating on the surface and occupying it. - One X-Plane that wasn't flying very much. - Billions spent on failed nuclear programs that had not left the laboratory since 1965.

Now, during the first space race, we were slow out of the gate, but NASA ultimately ran up the score. The second will be much closer than it ever needed to be.

三、一个不同的选择

Since becoming the administrator of NASA last year, we have made a different choice. We are not going to try and make everyone happy. We are not going to spread every penny across every district or partner with every nation just to try and make everyone happy, or because that's how people incorrectly believed it always was.

I am certainly not here for the money, to favor companies, for the title, the notoriety, the politics. I'm not here to be your VC — to entertain your dream or invent new markets if it detracts in the slightest way from the missions that we have been entrusted to achieve on behalf of the American people. You can take those conversations up with the Department of Commerce if you like.

I'm here to execute on President Trump's national space policy — to align and focus resources, to work alongside and unleash the best this nation has to offer, from the NASA workforce to our industry to our partners, and deliver the world-changing outcomes. The kind of outcomes that put Neil and Buzz on the moon. The kind of outcomes that inspired many of you to be in this room in the first place.

This is a very reinvigorated and energized NASA, and America is back in the business of sending our astronauts to the moon.

四、Artemis 计划：从 2 到 4

Now, Artemis 2 was just the beginning. Those four heroic astronauts, recent recipients of the Congressional Space Medal of Honor, rode 8.8 million pounds of thrust to near-Earth-escape velocities, traveled farther into space than any humans in history around the moon, and back home safely. And that was just the opening act.

We are not waiting 3 years to fly again. We are not turning every rocket into a work of art. Artemis 3 is already being assembled right now at a pace many doubted was possible just months ago. Before year end, we intend to roll out to launch complex 39B for a tanking test and send a message to our workforce, our industry, and our rivals overseas: NASA is back and we are not going to sit idly by. We are not just a procurement organization. We are going to do the extremely demanding work and achieve our objectives safely, responsibly, and urgently — because that is what meeting the moment requires.

Now, in the summer of 2027, Artemis 3 will launch on SLS into low Earth orbit and rendezvous with lander test vehicles from Blue Origin and SpaceX in what will be a remarkable display of the three most powerful rockets and spacecraft in the world. We will test interoperability and show what a future multi-launch campaign can actually look like. What we learn will inform the uncrewed test landings that follow — and then Artemis 4 in 2028, when American astronauts return to the lunar surface, and this time to stay.

五、月球基地与"生存的科学"

In parallel, we are establishing humanity's first outpost on another world — a moon base. And this time we are leveraging the NASA playbook of decades past. We are not jumping directly to the dream state. We will launch missions on a near-monthly cadence and undertake the science of survival.

That means: - autonomous and crewed mobility - surface improvement - in-situ resource utilization and manufacturing - logistics, habitability, power, communications - all the science instruments the mass budget affords

We will bring it to you live and HD on the moon-based website. And we will leave no doubters this time. We go for the scientific and the economic potential. We go to learn about the formation of our solar system, but primarily because the lunar south pole, where the water ice is, is going to be the technological proving ground for where we inevitably go next, which is Mars.

六、核动力 NASA 的到来

In 2028, NASA will leave decades and billions of dollars of failed nuclear programs behind and launch SR1 Freedom, a 100-kilowatt fission reactor that will finally get America underway on nuclear power. The mission will transit Mars and release Skyfall, which carries three Ingenuity-class helicopters and uses ground-penetrating radar to scout subsurface ice and future landing sites.

This will mark the beginning of the nuclear NASA — pivoting our workforce and facilities back to doing the near impossible. Missions with no obvious business case, what no company, no agency or nation is presently capable of accomplishing, but that extend humanity's reach farther into the outer solar system. And just like during the Apollo era, the technology that we pioneer to get there will surely benefit life back here at home.

There will be lots of nuclear missions — SR2, SR3, SR4. Alongside our industry partners, we will push the boundaries of high-temperature materials, more efficient power conversion, reduced radiator mass, and higher-performance electric propulsion as we visit some of the most interesting moons like Enceladus, Europa, and Titan — worlds with oceans, complex chemistry, and perhaps the ingredients for life. A reminder that some of the greatest discoveries in human history may be waiting for us in our own backyard. We could answer the question: are we alone? And are we alone even in our own solar system, let alone the galaxy and universe around us?

Someday, a chemically-augmented nuclear-powered transfer vehicle, part of an American Starfleet, supported by an armada of Starships and other spacecraft, will carry humans to the surface of Mars and bring them home safely to tell us about it. And not just once. We are on this great destiny of human exploration, and we are not turning back.

七、"顺便做的其他事情"

Along the way, we are going to do the other things.

Commercial satellites are being printed off at a rate that will help us affordably understand the only planet we presently inhabit, our home star and space weather, better predict weather, and perhaps respond to wildfires and natural disasters better — freeing up more resources to build the exquisite flagship science missions that only NASA can undertake.

  • Dragonfly — nuclear-powered octocopter, 2 kW MMRTG converting to just 100 W of electricity (barely better than an old light bulb), journeying to Saturn's moon Titan in 2028.
  • Europa Clipper — will arrive at Jupiter's icy moon in 2030.
  • Roman Space Telescope — nearly 300-megapixel wide-field instrument, JPL-built coronagraph. In the moments ahead, Roman will open her eyes, and in that instant she will see more of the universe than any scientific instrument we've ever put in space before. Her surveys will seek to understand the mysteries of dark energy and dark matter and reveal tens of thousands of worlds hidden behind distant stars. Roman will return images so large and in such detail there is no screen on Earth large enough to display them.
  • NEO Surveyor — will find asteroids and comets that can threaten Earth.
  • Next-generation telescopes — will seek out habitable planets orbiting other stars.

八、点燃太空经济，而不是强迫它

The last few decades have shown us that the future in space we all imagined as children will never be realized if it's perpetually funded by taxpayers. NASA will do everything within reason to support an orbital, and perhaps even lunar, economy someday — building on the proven markets of launch, observation, and communication. Whether the next frontier is:

  • orbital data centers
  • commercial space stations
  • on-orbit manufacturing
  • regolith resource extraction
  • asteroid mining
  • or industries none of us have even imagined yet

Now, it's not NASA's job to force an economy, but we will do all we can to ignite one as we pursue our missions.

九、航空的第一个 A

And in the service of the first "A" in NASA, we are rebuilding our X-Plane fleet. The X-59 is researching quiet supersonic flight — but it's just the beginning as NASA recommits to flight test and works alongside industry to push the boundaries of airframe and propulsion design. It will not be long before NASA is flying once again as high and as fast as we have from decades past — and then even more.

十、Starfleet Academy

But if this frontier is going to expand as rapidly as we believe it will, we will have to cultivate the talent to lead it. The space domain deserves an institution focused on that future — and call it what many already have and should, a Starfleet Academy.

That is why the president established the commission for the United States Space Academy, a NASA federal academy to prepare the next generation of astronauts, scientists, engineers, technicians, operators, pilots, and leaders.

Just as the need for Space Force became clear as the domain evolved, we should be equally forward-looking in preparing those who will build the moon base, operate nuclear-powered spacecraft, command missions to Mars, ensure our national security, and create industries in orbit we can barely imagine today.

十一、世界会记住谁第一个到

And there is no time to waste. I want you all to think about where you were when Artemis 2 astronauts sent back those images from the moon. Who did it touch? Your parents, your friends, your colleagues, your children.

Now, I want you to imagine astronauts climbing down the ladder. Only this time, it is not grainy black-and-white footage from July 20th, 1969. It's high-definition color streaming live to billions of people all around the world. The astronaut steps foot on the lunar surface. The camera pans up — and the flag on the spacesuit is not American.

There will be no footnote explaining that we spent more. No disclaimer that our architecture was complicated. No one will care how many studies we completed, how many meetings we held, what congressional districts benefited, who all the all-star lobbyists were for their hardware, who served on the committee, or how many times we slipped the schedule for what someone thought was a perfectly reasonable reason.

The world will just see who got there.

China intends to put their astronauts on the moon by 2030. Its robotic missions are targeting the Shackleton crater of the lunar south pole next year, and there are only so many good parking spots in that neighborhood — and they intend to occupy them. They are working with Russia on their own nuclear-powered moon base.

And to be clear, China will accomplish what the Soviets never could during the first space race. They have a very achievable two-launch architecture, the national will, and the capabilities to put their astronauts on the surface of the moon. And if America has not returned despite the decades of promises and the more than $100 billion invested, the shockwave will be felt around the world. Our allies will notice. Our adversaries will notice. Every nation deciding whose technology to buy, whose standards to adopt, whose security guarantees to trust, and whose vision of the future to follow will take notice. And perhaps most importantly, our children will notice.

十二、结语：选择去，然后我们就去了

That is why we must remain focused on the objectives that matter — why NASA was established in the first place. There is no time anymore for lobbying against America's interests or further tolerating the status quo. Only extreme ownership, competence, and action.

Those of us inspired by the pioneers and heroes of decades past know they set the bar high. But we do not honor them by living forever on what they accomplished. This is our time to pick up where they left off, return, and never give up the moon again — and then set our sights on Mars and beyond.

None of this will be accomplished by NASA alone. We have the support of President Trump. We have Congress. We have a clear mandate in the national space policy. But it will take brilliant entrepreneurs, scientists, engineers, our allies, and Americans across the country who still believe that great nations can do great things — because our children will either inherit the confidence of a nation still capable of the extraordinary, or the memory of one that used to be. That responsibility, that choice, belongs to all of us.

And I believe when history looks back on this moment, let it record that America did not hesitate any longer. We did not allow the bureaucracy, the complacency, the waste, inaction, or fear of failure to constrain what we could accomplish. We chose to go, and we went.

Thank you.

Q&A: 与 All-In 主持人的对话

关于 NASA 讲演的天然优势

"I was commenting backstage on how easy it is for NASA to come and do speeches, given the capacity to show visuals like this. Can you imagine like Housing and Urban Development trying to do a presentation?"

— "No, we have unbelievable material to work with. I'm thankful every day that I don't lead the IRS or Social Security."

Q1：月球本身是不是一门可行的经济？

We are extremely fortunate. We've been gifted a moon 3 days away to test out everything we need on this great adventure of discovery. This is where you want to go to really dial in:

  • Power
  • Spacesuits (it's taken us decades to build replacements for Apollo-era suits — let's test them on the moon)
  • Habitation modules
  • In-situ resource manufacturing
  • Robotics

EVAs are fantastic — astronauts bouncing around on the moon is going to be highly inspirational. But that's one of the last things you should do when you have a moon base: send somebody outside in that extremely dangerous environment. Let robotics do it.

To accomplish all of this you have to send an extraordinary demand signal to industry. Over the next four years, we're talking dozens of landers, dozens of rovers, lots of in-situ resource manufacturing experimentation. You're giving industry all the opportunity in the world to figure out how to unlock value from the lunar regolith.

But I can't guarantee it. And that's my point on the Department of Commerce — they have a whole space commerce office that can work through that. I am going to make sure that NASA can master the skills necessary to go to Mars for its scientific potential. We'll put radio telescopes on the far side to inspire the next generation. And if along the way it ignites a lunar economy, that's fantastic. But it costs an awful lot to get there, an awful lot to extract resources.

Q2：月球南极的"停车位"经济学 & Promise 任务

Surface area of the moon is like the size of Africa. The south pole of the moon is like Washington DC. And there's only so many good craters that have these permanently shaded regions — which, by the way, is a harsher environment than Mars itself. That's where the water ice is. But the crater cliffs can also give you near-eternal access to light for solar power.

When a vehicle the size of Starship comes down on the lunar surface, believe me, that's going to blast out little craters, send debris. So really limited parking spots.

Promise is very awesome because Promise is a radioisotope-powered rover that we built as a spare, essentially, for the two rovers — Perseverance and Curiosity — that are on Mars right now. This thing is the size of a jeep. We have some Pu-238 that's decaying right now — you only get so much life out of it. We want to take that, put it on Promise, and send it to the moon. It can go in and start prospecting in those permanently shaded regions that almost any other hardware would die in. It's a very good way to make use of taxpayer dollars that have largely already been spent.

Q3：为什么必须先于中国到南极？NASA 你接手时是什么状态？

Just to be clear: some of the best talent in this nation shows up to work at NASA every day, and they want to change the world in air and space. And for a very long time, everybody was trying to run NASA other than the people themselves who show up to work there.

Let's make everyone happy. Let's spread our resources to every congressional district. Let's collect 25 different flags to partner on the next mission — that takes something that should cost a couple billion (like going and getting samples back from Mars, potentially the most consequential discovery in human history) and layers a bunch of other people on and makes it cost more than a carrier, and then it gets canceled.

So NASA's back in charge now. We are in a space race. People are giving us the latitude to do what we need to do. And as a result, we are extremely focused on the president's national space policy: return to the moon, build a base, get underway in nuclear power, and the other things. The workforce is responding well.

On the South Pole: the Chinese and the Russians know there are only so many good parking spots. They were going to launch a mission a couple weeks ago to the Shackleton Ridge. Maybe it was mechanical, maybe it was weather related — or maybe they were smart enough to know that if they actually did it, it probably would ignite one hell of a fire and urgency in us. But that would have taken up one of a couple critical parking spots. They're going to build a base there. They've partnered with Russia. They're going to have a fission reactor there. And then where are they going next? The third space race — Mars.

Q4：到火星最关键的技术突破是什么？

There are a couple of things. Look, robotics are going to be critical.

If you chose a path that was purely chemical propulsion — vehicles like Starship are going to be incredible at that — you will no doubt have the means to send astronauts to Mars. They've already figured out habitability a long time ago, and you're talking very comparable velocities whether you're going to the moon or Mars.

The hard part is how do you come back? You're going to need to make propellant on Mars to do so. One solution: I'll have an army of robots that'll do it, and I'll have football-field-size solar panels, and the robots can dust them off from all the dust storms, and then I'll make my own propellant and come home.

The hard part is: it's really challenging to do that under one atmosphere and 1G here on Earth. You can see how many people show up at stage zero at Starbase to launch a mission. And by the way, that is the right way to kind of win the war — to put lots of mass on the surface.

NASA can help by pivoting — stop doing what industry is already doing really well, and invest in that next-giant-leap capability that has no obvious business use case today: fission power. Then you can have chemically augmented NEP (nuclear electric propulsion) spaceships / transfer vehicles and go to and from Mars, and you don't need to refuel them until they come back. And what you're refilling is krypton or xenon — you're not having to make propellant on the surface of Mars.

That's how NASA works alongside industry to invest in the capabilities that are necessary for American leadership in space. And those are the same capabilities you want to go to Enceladus, Titan, Europa — where you have oceans on two of those moons that could have life in them. We don't know.

Q5：如何吸引顶尖人才加入 NASA 而不是 SpaceX？

Right now we don't have a recruiting problem initially. We take 1% of the intern applications that go into our pathways program, which guarantees them a job at NASA.

The question is: can you retain them? If you're doing exactly what SpaceX, Blue, Rocket Lab, Stoke, ULA, and others are doing in industry, except you're doing it off 50-year-old shuttle hardware that again is not as efficient for missions like going to the moon as Saturn V was — you're going to lose that workforce.

So what do you need to do? When we have those near-impossible breakthroughs and there is a business case (as there certainly is for launch, where you can be one customer of many), you hand it off to industry and you pivot. That's how you retain talent that can only do these types of missions at NASA — which is the nuclear NASA. SR1 is just the beginning. That is our Nautilus. There will be a grand fleet of nuclear-powered spacecraft on the frontier. You need to constantly keep pivoting to the next new thing.

Q6：核动力推进的原理入门

Actually, just think of a lot of the Starlink satellites you'd have up right now that use Hall-effect ion thrusters. They're generating electricity through solar power, and then through electromagnetic forces they're ionizing either krypton or xenon and accelerating it out of the thruster — which gives you very very high exhaust velocity. So it's extremely efficient, very low thrust, and you can use that propellant for a very long time.

In space, the faster the molecule shoots out the back, the more thrust it generates for the craft to move forward. It's very low mass flow, but highly efficient.

Where that breaks down is the farther you get from the sun. Once you get out towards Jupiter, solar effectiveness is negligible. So what you're using is the thermal energy from a nuclear reactor — 100 kW, scale it up to 250, maybe megawatt class. You're going to want to run that reactor as hot as you possibly can — so that's your high-temperature materials — and then you're going to convert it through a closed Brayton-cycle power conversion unit into electricity, and that electricity is then going to power those same thrusters you'd see on Starlinks. They're just scaled up: 12 kW, then 14 kW, 25 kW thrusters.

Q7：NASA 预算与资本配置

What is NASA's budget, and if you could, what would it be?

I've said it many times: NASA does not have a topline problem. We are bad capital allocators, and have been for a long time. A lot of that is based on NASA choices, based on what other people forced us to do — and that's changed. We have $25 billion. How many entrepreneurs are in this room? $25 billion is a lot of money. You can build some pretty incredible hardware.

Q8：航空组合 & 那张"黑鸟"照片

The first "A" in NASA is our aeronautics portfolio. When you go see an F-22 fly at an air show and it wows you — the fly-by-wire technology was us. The thrust-vectoring technology was us. NASA's been contributing to breakthroughs in aeronautics — civil, commercial, and national-security applications — for a long time.

Over the years, we've been forced to spend our aeronautics budget on subsidizing high-TRL efforts from big prime contractors. An engine that's 40 years old, they want to squeak 3% more fuel efficiency out of it, get NASA to pay for it. Are you kidding? You can underwrite that investment yourself for competitive reasons.

What I want to do is get back to the radical airframe and engine designs like we were always supposed to do. You're getting a little bit of a taste for that.

Q9：为什么要送人，而不是全交给机器人（Optimus / Figure）？

It's our destiny — the same reason we cross the oceans and seas and climb the mountains. This is who we are.

Would as many people have paused from the discourse of their daily lives to look at those astronauts go around the moon on Artemis 2 if they weren't humans? I don't think so.

Don't get me wrong — we are going to need robotics, and there are some environments where, because of the radiation, we can only do uncrewed robotic missions. But we can go to the moon as we've done before, we can go to Mars, and we can continue on outward — and robotics will absolutely play a critical role in that journey.

Q10：自动化 & 空中安全

NASA's been playing a role in air-traffic safety and modernization for a long time. It was NASA that pioneered the autonomous ground collision avoidance software — saved countless lives of fighter pilots who pull too many G's and black out, the nose of the aircraft points at the ground, the aircraft recognizes it and safely recovers. That was NASA work.

And as you think about a world that's going to have millions of drones flying around delivering us medicine and other things — we have to work very closely with the FAA on that.

We are thinking about AI and autonomous applications within the missions we're designing right now. For example, one mission going to Venus — DaVinci — will not last long in that high-pressure environment. We're going to have only so much time to gather as much information as we can, and to update the trajectory of the vehicle: "this is not interesting, disregard; this is interesting, I'm turning in that direction." We've already tested this with some of our rovers on Mars. "In my last dying breath, this is what I choose to send back to the scientists on Earth to understand this environment." That's just one step towards a direction that will inevitably include more autonomy in our crewed and uncrewed spacecraft.

Q11：科学任务的资本配置

Science is approximately a third of NASA's budget. We recently reorganized. Your main mission directorates right now are:

  1. Human space exploration — ISS work, missions to the moon, building a moon base.
  2. Research technology mission directorate — shouldering most of the nuclear NASA effort.
  3. Science mission directorate.

How I think about this: you have to take advantage of commercial industry right now. No one would doubt that launch, observation, and communications are real services where NASA is one customer of many. All these great companies are printing out satellites — for national security, agriculture, Earth sciences. Leverage it. Give them the instruments if necessary, license it to them, free up resources to do what industry is not going to want to take on — like building a nuclear-powered octocopter to go to Saturn's moon Titan.

I would always prioritize getting new missions out there to unlock the secrets of the universe versus the researchers. If we get the data, there'll be plenty of brilliant people at institutions around the country who will want to analyze it. But what's the point if you can't launch those next missions?

Q12：火星直升机视频与时间线

We tested one — Ingenuity — on our last rover mission to Mars. It did fantastically well. Near vacuum on Mars — like a 10th of an atmosphere, fractional.

Now we're going to send three of these with ground-penetrating radars — which I think is just awesome. But most importantly, how it got there: under nuclear power. A true fission-powered 100 kW spacecraft that flew by Mars and released it. This will launch in '28, and it's approximately a year before the helicopters will get there.

There is so much we can learn on the moons within our own solar system. Some really shocking discoveries are just waiting for us in our own backyard.

Q13：中国与俄罗斯的能力评估

On Russia: I have a great appreciation for the history of the Russian and Soviet space program. Like I said in my remarks, they came out of the gate hot — first astronaut in orbit, first spacewalk, they've done a lot of great things and they contribute with us today, collaborate on the International Space Station. But yes, they have a conflict and they're prioritizing resources there.

On China: The Chinese are an incredible rival in space right now. Yes, they don't have the same reusable launch capabilities that SpaceX and others have. But what they do put in space — even if they brute-force it there with hypergolic-powered thrusters or hypergolic-powered rockets akin to like Titan II of decades past — what goes in space is good.

There were some pretty interesting developments that came out of AFA today — our Secretary of the Air Force and others in the Space Force enlightened the general public about how contested that environment is. The bottom line: the Chinese are extremely good in space right now. You couple that with some Russian capabilities on nuclear power — they will return to the moon, they will get to the moon, and they will build a base on the south pole.

Q14：没有 SpaceX，美国会在哪？

SpaceX is our most important launch partner. We can't send astronauts to and from the space station without them. We can't have down-mass of our science experiments from the space station without them. The Nancy Grace Roman telescope was launched on a Falcon Heavy not that long ago. We are fortunate. There are a lot of great companies in commercial space right now, but the United States would be seriously challenged in the high ground of space without their capabilities.

结束致意

"Jared, I'm not a huge fan of government. But I think NASA plays one of the most important roles for humanity that no individual organization outside of government can play. I cannot think of a better person to lead it. I think you're an inspiration to so many. I truly, honestly respect the service you've provided to this country and to the world. We're so lucky to have you. Thank you for being here."

— "Oh, grateful every day. Thank you all."

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的洞察：NASA 正在从"梦想服务商"变回"承包总工"
Isaacman 讲话中最刺耳、也最少被注意到的一句话是——"我们发明了一种叫做 dream state as a service 的东西"。这句自嘲背后藏着一个惊人的组织病理学诊断：**过去二十年的 NASA 并不是在造火箭，而是在向承包商"外包梦想"，再用政治叙事回购这个梦想**。
这与硅谷 SaaS 的兴衰曲线惊人同构：当一家公司把核心能力全部外包给 vendor，只保留 PPT 和采购部，它就从"造物者"退化成"叙事者"。Isaacman 实际上在把 NASA 从 SaaS 模式重新拉回 **vertically integrated OEM** 模式——这和 Tesla 自造电池、Apple 自造芯片是同一个动作。**太空竞赛的胜负，可能首先是一场"组织架构反 SaaS 化"的胜负**。
## 二、跨领域连接：月球南极的"停车位经济学" = 曼哈顿地价 + 石油海上钻井平台
Isaacman 反复强调"月球南极只有那么几个好停车位"（only so many good parking spots

item.title: [Lex Clips] The Nazi program to exterminate the mentally ill | Andrew Scull and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被历史顺序掩盖的技术真相

大多数人以为奥斯维辛的毒气室是为犹太人发明的——事实恰好相反。"淋浴间伪装 + 毒气 + 焚尸炉"这套后来被工业化复制的杀人流水线，其技术原型完整地诞生于精神病院内。约二十五万精神病患者的死亡不是"最终解决方案"的附带脚注，而是它的方法论试验田。这颠覆了公众对纳粹罪行的时间轴认知：种族屠杀之所以能够"高效"运转，是因为它先在"社会最无声的人群"身上完成了技术调试。历史往往不是从最戏剧化的场景开始的，而是从最没人替他们说话的角落开始的。

"无用的食客"：一种可怕地"理性"的语言

"Useless eaters"（无用的食客）表面上是意识形态口号，实质上是一个经济学-生物学-道德三层复合的会计术语。它把"是否值得活着"翻译成了"投入-产出比"。跨领域地看，这套语法今天仍在生龙活虎地运行——出现在医疗系统的 QALY（质量调整生命年）评估里、出现在福利改革"劳动能力"评估里、出现在 AI 时代关于"人的比较优势"的讨论里。真正令人不安的不是 T4 的语言多么极端，而是它多么兼容于任何一套现代管理学工具。当一种伦理灾难可以用 Excel 表格论证时，抵抗它就变得异常困难，因为你不是在跟仇恨辩论，而是在跟"效率"辩论。

治疗职业的"合谋分岔"与一个尚未消散的悖论

Scull 说了一句被采访者轻描淡写带过、但极具杀伤力的话："the same logic applies in the present for many working in the field"——现代生物精神病学与 T4 共享同一个底层假设："生物学既是问题、也是答案"。差别在剂量与包装，不在逻辑。这种"用问题的媒介来命名解决方案"的悖论并不局限于精神医学——它同样出现在用碳市场解决碳排放、用监控技术保护隐私、用更强大的 AI 来对齐 AI。每一次这种"媒介重命名"都会产生微小的伦理位移，位移累积就是滑坡。

而"治疗职业"面对"无法治愈"时的两条路——降格为看守（glorified boarding house keeper）或升格为解决者（激进干预）——是一个系统性张力，并不专属于精神病学。教师面对无法教会的学生、警察面对累犯、工程师面对无法重构的遗留代码、程序员面对无法修复的用户，都在同一条谱系上。文明的成熟度，也许可以用一个残忍的指标来测量：这个社会是否为"与无法解决的问题共存"保留了尊严的空间。当"共存"不被承认为一种合法姿态时，看守就会滑向解决者，解决者就会滑向 T4。

📝 转录文本

The T4 Program: "Useless Eaters"

What happened in Germany once the Nazis came to power is they seized on these notions — the idea that the mentally ill, or as they put it, "useless eaters," people consuming resources but never going to get better, just a burden on the state, their lives weren't worth living because, after all, they had this serious mental illness.

So first you sterilize, and then you go, "But we're still supporting all these people." And so Hitler started something called the T4 program, after the street name of the house where this was concocted: Tiergartenstraße 4.

The Mentally Ill as the First Victims of the Final Solution

The mentally ill were the first people to suffer from the Final Solution. It was in the mass killing of the mentally ill — which may have been as many as a quarter million people — that the technology of the gas chamber was developed, and the technology of disguising the gas chamber as showers was developed.

And so the patients were taken away to a number of psychiatric centers and systematically put to death. They had the crematoriums and the black smoke, and the local people talked about the buses that were bringing them in as "killing crates." So they were aware of what was going on.

American Influence and the Absence of Checks

Fridman: Were they influenced by the narratives that were born in the United States?

Scull: Yes, absolutely, about that sort of thing. And lacking the checks and balances that, at least until recently, this country had, it was relatively easy for Hitler to do that — particularly with the war looming — the idea that "we're going to support all these useless people, let's kill them." And German psychiatry, for the most part, collaborated with that process.

Who Was Brave Enough to Speak Up?

Fridman: I wonder how many people throughout that whole journey in the psychiatry profession were brave enough to speak up, like, "Hey, maybe the 'sack of puppies' kind of language is a problem."

Scull: That's the really nasty direction that that language could lead to. And it was symptomatic of the kind of stigma that tends to attach itself to mental illness, and the sense of hopelessness.

Healers, Boarding-House Keepers, and Collaborators

But if you're a healing profession — if you enter psychiatry thinking, "I'm going to do this to help people, to cure people, to make their lives better" — to just become a glorified boarding house keeper, keeping them under lock and key, or, in the alternative, to collaborate in the sorts of awfulness that the Nazis perpetrated: that's something from which decent human beings tend to recoil, and decent psychiatrists tended to recoil.

Biology as Both the Problem and the Solution

And so, still thinking as they did by the end of the 19th century that mental illness was predominantly a biological problem, some of them began to say, "Well, maybe biology, as well as being the problem, could provide the solution. Maybe we should look for ways to intervene in the biological systems of these people and make them better." The same logic that applies, I would say, in the present for many working in the field.

Fridman: But in a crude form.

Scull: But in a very different form, exactly.

Fridman: Mhm.

item.title: [YC Root Access] The AI Employee for Banks
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"共生架构"：真正的创新不是 AI，而是拒绝替代

大多数人会把 Castle 讲成"用 AI 替代银行客服"，但如果你仔细听 Nitesh 那句话——"银行不擅长变更管理，替换核心系统要花 5 到 10 年"——你会发现 Castle 真正卖的不是智能，而是共存能力。

这里有一个反直觉的观察：在高度监管行业，最有价值的技术不是取代旧系统的技术，而是能够优雅寄生于旧系统之上的技术。这在生物学里叫内共生（endosymbiosis）——线粒体没有取代原始细胞，而是钻进去成了它的能量工厂。Castle 的 AI Employee 之所以能在两年内跑到 20 亿美元交易量，不是因为它比银行原有系统更"聪明"，而是因为它拒绝了硅谷惯有的"rip and replace"叙事，选择了做寄生器官而不是替代器官。

这背后隐藏的一个真相是：一切成功的 B2B AI 公司，都在偷偷解决"变更管理"这个非技术问题，而非技术问题本身。

二、"1000 万人每月用电话还房贷"——一个关于隐藏基础设施的社会学发现

这是整段访谈最震撼的一个数据点，但它的意义远超商业机会本身。

每月有 1000 万美国人打电话还房贷——这个数字暴露出一个几乎没人讨论的经济学现象：监管强度与隐性劳动力市场规模成正比。因为 mortgage servicer 不能把电话外包到印度或菲律宾，凤凰城、达拉斯这些城市实际上成了"美国合规声音的血汗工厂"。这跟另一件事惊人相似——COBOL：全球 40% 的银行核心系统还跑在 1960 年代的 COBOL 上，不是因为它好，而是因为监管让替代变得比维护更贵。

这里的跨领域连接是：Castle 实际上做的事，和 20 年前印度 BPO（业务流程外包）产业做的是同一件事——把不可外包的劳动力，变得可以外包。只不过 BPO 靠地理套利，Castle 靠算力套利。从这个角度看，Castle 不是一家 AI 公司，它是"合规套利"产业的下一代基础设施。

三、两次归零：他们不是在找 PMF，而是在找"存亡感"

访谈里最容易被商业读者忽略的一句话，其实是 Rishi 在凤凰城机场路上说的那句——"如果我们明天消失，客户会不会绝望？"

请注意他用的词不是 "disappointed"（失望），是 "existential"（生死攸关）。这是一个非常精确的表达，也是一个跨领域的深层洞见：

  • 产品市场契合（PMF） 是硅谷的语言，它衡量的是"用户是否愿意付钱"；
  • 存亡契合（Existential Fit） 是更古老的语言，它来自宗教、来自战场、来自医学——它衡量的是"没有你，用户是否会痛苦到崩溃"。

Castle 两次归零的真正共同点，不是他们放弃了不赚钱的业务（AI SDR 已经跑到 $4K MRR），而是他们放弃了不痛的业务。这跟日本茶道里的一个概念很像——"一期一会"：如果你不能让每一次相遇都变得不可替代，那你就没有资格存在。

更令人意外的连接：Castle 卖的产品和他们创立公司的方式，本质是同一种哲学——不是替代（replace），而是深度嵌入（embed）到用户的生死之中。他们搬到 Newrez 的办公室不出来，直到系统上线，这已经不是"客户成功"，这是古代武士的"托孤式"承诺。这种承诺无法被复制，也是为什么监管行业的 AI 之战最终不是模型之战，而是信任浓度之战。

四、一个大胆预测：舞台上崩溃三次的 demo，可能才是他们能拿下大银行的真正原因

访谈里那个 demo 失败三次的故事被当成一个有趣的段子，但仔细想想——他们在评委面前经历了系统性失败，然后依然赢了比赛。

这在心理学上叫 "vulnerability signaling"（脆弱性信号）：在高信任行业，展示可修复的失败，比展示无缺陷的完美更能建立可信度。银行的 compliance 官员见过太多 SaaS 公司的完美 demo，然后在生产环境里翻车。Castle 三次失败一次成功的现场表现，反而让潜在客户看到了一个更重要的东西：这些创始人在崩溃时的反应模式。

这跟纳西姆·塔勒布的"反脆弱"、跟航空业的"事故报告文化"、跟精神分析里的"修复的破裂"（rupture and repair）——是同一个原理：信任不是建立在"永不出错"上的，而是建立在"出错后如何回应"上的。

所以，那三次失败的电话，可能才是 Castle 拿到第一个客户、拿到 Newrez、拿到 Series A 的真正起点。

📝 转录文本

Intro

[music]

All right. So, I'm excited today to welcome Nitesh and Rishi, the founders of Castle AI, who just closed a $24 million Series A led by Insight Partners. Congrats, guys.

Thank you.

What Castle Does

What does Castle do?

Yeah. No, thanks for having us, Dana. Excited to be here. So, Castle is an AI employee that automates all the operations inside a bank. We started 2 years ago, uh starting with mortgage servicing operations, and today we work with 10 of the top 25 servicers like Newrez and help them automate their customer service and collections operations across the business.

And in terms of volume, where are you guys at now in terms of processing payments?

Uh so, we recently crossed uh $2 billion in transactions processed using AI agents. Yeah, it's crazy to think that same time last year we were doing about 10 million every 2 months, and now we do that every day.

Yeah.

Why "AI Employee" Instead of a New System of Record

The interesting approach you have is that you are building a company as an AI employee. Why why is that?

Yeah. So, this is actually one of the uh interesting points that we noticed is you know, I feel like most of the problems that banks face today is that they in order to grow that grow revenue, grow uh loans, grow deposits, they also need to grow the back office. And one of the interesting things that we saw is that uh banks are also forced are really bad at change management. It's very hard for such large regulated industries to completely replace their core systems.

And so, as we built Castle, we had an opportunity to either, "Hey, do we go and execute on building a new system of record, or do we help them How do we help banks sort of adopt AI in a reliable way and deliver value quickly uh without them having to go through this entire process of you know changing their core systems which might take 5-10 years."

We were seeing a lot of um you know rapid improvements happen in like say for example coding where you know we use tools like Devin

Yeah.

and they've helped us supercharge our workflows. And we we found that the you know banks really needed something similar in order to like supercharge their own operating workflows but there was like no good solution out there that was helping them do that. Uh it was either you change the existing system of record or you had this like one point solution. So that's when we decided that hey we have an opportunity here to like really help our customers reliably deploy AI across their operations and realize that value that other industries are seeing without having to go through that rip and replace of their existing core systems.

Two Years Ago: A Very Different Idea

Now let's go back to two years ago. You were here at YC going through the batch in summer 24 and you guys actually applied with a very different idea.

Yeah.

Do you remember what it was?

I think it was real estate assistants for to help real estate agents close more loan to close more kind of deals. So AI for home buying essentially. I think within week one we proved out that we had a pilot we lost that and then we realized that this is not going anywhere and then we started talking to a bunch of more people went into the AI SDR route where we were helping essentially other companies message other businesses to source more business.

I think it was a AI SDR for specifically home buying. I think you were helping all these brokers find more leads to buy homes and you actually made progress on it. You were working on that for most of the batch.

Yeah.

It was around the summer. I think you were working on that through June, July and beginning of August and you got to about 4,000 in MRR. Just like "Okay." But something happened and you decided to kill the idea 1 month before demo day and went back again to zero. This is the second time you went back to zero.

The Phoenix Airport Moment — Killing the Idea

Yeah, I know. I clearly remember we were actually in Phoenix and we were driving you know on the way to the airport in SF. And Nitesh and I were like, "What are we What are we doing? Like we we don't really see we couldn't see ourselves like building a really large company on that idea." And most of all like we we we didn't feel that our customers this was like existential for our customers. That like if we disappeared tomorrow that they would absolutely be you know disappointed that like they no longer have a castle.

It felt like if we were like a nice-to-have for them and Nitesh and I were like we you know we we really cared about like building something for the long term and we wanted to do like go back to the drawing board no matter how painful that was and restart over to build something that like our customers like couldn't live without.

The 30-Day Sprint to a New Idea

So you were sprinting. This is only 30 days before demo day and you went on this sprint on doing a lot of user interviews. You're flying all around the country to meet people. You went to conferences for 2 weeks. And tell us about how you eventually landed in this idea of around agent home mortgages.

We went all to basically every conference that we could find. It was a lot of awkward conversations of standing outside conferences as people walked out and trying to like cold meet them and talk about their problems. But we basically did that and we actually got pretty good at it.

And got less awkward.

And less awkward at it. And so it was actually at one of the conferences here in San Francisco where we learned about 10 million Americans making their mortgage payment every single month over the phone.

You told me that. I was shocked. It's like there's people that call over the phone to pay or be reminded for the mortgages. It's like

Every single month.

I was like, what?

Yeah, and and all of these calls were actually being handled by a human agent in the contact center because, you know, mortgage lenders just don't have as much They have very highly regulated. It's very risky for them to outsource these operations to other outside countries. So, all these calls were being taken in the United States in place like Phoenix, Dallas, and is all the all that like the mortgage lenders could talk about that if someone could solve this problem for us like that would be a game-changing experience. And no one in Voice AI was like relatively like new at that time and no one was really doing it to like process payments as for such a regulated industry like mortgage. And that's that's how we got our first break.

First Customer — The Demo That Failed Three Times

Do you remember how you got your first customer? Because by that time you were running out of time. There was only 2 weeks until demo day. You got this funny insight. And

Yeah.

What what happened? I think it took another 2 weeks to get your customers.

Yeah. Yeah, so we we were like, okay, how do we speed run this? So, we went to another conference where it was actually we found out about this pitch competition. And it was in San Diego. Before our time on the stage, the teacher was in the background. You want to talk about that?

Rishi was still going on the conference trying to meet people and I had found a corner of the auditorium and was just kind of finish our demo in time. And we went up to the stage. We started the demo. It was a phone call and just to show whether we can take a payment.

First time he called in, it didn't work.

On stage.

On stage.

In front of hundreds of people.

So, we blamed it on his phone. We said, okay, it'll work with my phone instead. So, I gave him my phone. Second time we called in, it didn't work. And then I said oh I forgot to turn it on. And then [laughter] the third time we called in, it actually ended up working.

And we we were really scared that, you know, this didn't go as well, but uh turns out we actually won that competition. And that created a ton of inbound for us and helped us land our first customer.

In spite of the demo malfunctioning, that's a that's a cool story. So, you got a bunch of inbound from that. And I remember you guys just closed on Nica Time, your first customer just few days before demo day.

Yeah.

Moving to Phoenix — Landing Newrez

Cool. Then you went off to the races. And then after that, you guys went into build and close one of the largest servicers. Couple months later?

Yeah, so we had a few early customers that we were prototyping with. And then we got in touch with Newrez, which is the third largest servicer in the country. This is the time where we, you know, they had a similar problem. We knew that they had this problem. So, to actually make them live, we moved the entire company to Phoenix. And we moved in to their offices and, you know, I didn't come back until they were live.

So, you were cranking it until you went live.

Yeah.

The Next 5–10 Years

Now, fast forward. Now that you're live and now processing 2 billion in transactions, where does Castle go in the next 5 to 10 years?

What we've been able to do is prove that applied AI autonomous agents can work in one of the most regulated operational environments uh in financial services, which is mortgage servicing. And as a result of that, we've actually built a lot of technology underneath it that allows these agents to be highly effective in real-time settings.

We've basically taken that operating model and that technology and now applying across the consumer lending life cycle and across like a bank's operations. So, we initially while we initially started with mortgages, we now have large banks using Castle's AI employee to service auto loans, credit cards, personal loans, HELOCs, but also like originate loans.

We think 5 years from now that, you know, Castle can be the the number one AI employee that works as a co-worker across every operational financial institution there is doing the work alongside human agents and automating the the high-volume labor-intensive work and freeing up time for complex workflows to be handled by human agents where they where they need the judgment.

And this is essentially like to say that like there is a ton of demand for financial products and banks want to be innovative and lend to their community, build better experiences for their customers. The only thing that stops them from doing that is them not having the operational bandwidth or resource in order to, you know, provide personalized experiences for each of their customers. And Castle's AI employees unlock that.

Determinism in a Non-Deterministic World — and Hiring

So, one of the other things you've done is basically you are enabling your customers to basically prompt the agents, but inherently these agents run LLMs which are non-deterministic, but you're working in a regulated industry. So, somehow you built a hardness that makes your customer changes be deterministic and be compliant. That's pretty hard to do. And you guys are growing a bunch, so you're hiring a bunch of roles. Tell us about what are some of the roles that you're hiring for.

Yeah. So, we're hiring across the stack with the Series A, we're now starting to work with, you know, some of the largest banks across the country. So, we're investing a lot in like applying AI in the real world and building these systems around it. So, we're growing our applied AI team, growing our product teams as we get into like multiple different products. And and also scaling our infrastructure teams.

Outro

All right, guys. Thank you so much for coming and congrats again on the Series A.

Yeah. Thanks so much, Anna. Appreciate it.

[music]

item.title: [Lex Clips] Why psychiatry doesn't work - historian of psychiatry explains | Andrew Scull and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的深层反讽：精神病学的"软件版本号"暴露了范式危机

注意 DSM-V 那个耐人寻味的细节——他们把罗马数字换成了阿拉伯数字，因为"以后修订可以像 Windows 10、Windows 11 那样迭代"。这不是无害的排版选择，这是一个学科在潜意识层面承认自己已经放弃了追求"真理"，转而拥抱"迭代"。

医学的其他分支从不这样命名疾病手册。你不会看到《肿瘤学 12.0》。当一个学科开始用软件更新的隐喻描述自己的知识体系时，它其实在承认：这些分类不是被发现的，而是被制造和维护的。这与库恩所说的"范式危机"的征兆惊人一致——当学者开始用另一个领域的比喻来重新描述自己的工作时，往往是原有范式已经失去自我辩护能力的信号。

二、意外的跨领域连接：DSM 的困境与 18 世纪的"水肿病"是同一个认识论陷阱

Scull 顺口提到的类比其实是整段访谈中最锋利的一刀——今天的"重度抑郁症"在结构上等同于 18 世纪的"发烧"或"水肿"。18 世纪医生把"发烧"当作一种疾病，因为他们只能观察症状；后来生物医学发现发烧只是几十种截然不同病理过程的共同外显，"发烧作为疾病"这个概念就消失了。

而 DSM 正在重演这个错误，但代价更高，因为它同时被三个利益结构锁定： - 药厂需要稳定的靶标来申请 FDA 审批； - 保险公司需要离散的编码来做精算； - 患者家属需要一个"名字"来对抗混乱。

这里出现了一个惊人的跨领域现象：分类系统的稳固性与其科学有效性成反比。越多的社会经济结构依赖某个分类，这个分类越难被证伪——这与经济学里的"路径依赖"、法学里的"僵化的判例"、软件工程里的"技术债务"是同一种病理。DSM 不是被科学证据锁定的，它是被"三边网络效应"锁定的。

3.更深的洞见：Insel 的 200 亿美元失败揭示了一个还原论的隐蔽假设

Thomas Insel 承认花掉 200 亿美元后精神病患者的处境"一丝一毫都没有改善"——这可能是过去半个世纪自然科学最重大却最少被讨论的"负结果"。它的量级不亚于粒子物理学在标准模型之外一无所获。

但真正值得警觉的是 Scull 只是暗示、没有点破的东西："大脑疾病"框架的失败，可能并不是因为神经科学不够先进，而是因为"心智"这个层次的现象根本无法被完全还原到神经元层次——就像你无法从晶体管的物理状态去解释一个 Python 程序的 bug，虽然它"最终"确实发生在晶体管上。

这里的跨领域连接指向复杂性科学中的"层级涌现"：意识、情绪、意义都是在"叙事"和"关系"这个层次上组织起来的，试图跳过这一层直接到神经生物学，就像试图不读代码只用示波器调试软件。Bush 总统 1990 年宣布的"脑十年"是一个可以被历史标注的错误——它不是错在投入方向，而是错在其形而上学预设：它假设了一个可以被跳过的层级。

而这个预设之所以能主导 30 年，是因为它同时满足了另一个不为人知的动机——医学院院长对"数据"的偏爱。这句话看似平淡，实则残酷：一整个学科的研究方向，最终可能是被"哪种研究更容易在 PPT 上展示图表"决定的。这与学术界的评估机制、期刊的图片偏好、grant 评审的可视化偏见形成了一条隐蔽的因果链——精神病学的悲剧，部分源于学术资本主义对"可视化数据"的美学偏好。

📝 转录文本

精神病学面临的多重危机

Now, in terms of the crisis psychiatry faces at the moment as I see it, there are a number of strands that point to this.

DSM 诊断系统的起源

Psychiatry's diagnostic system, uh that is still used on — I mean the fundamental basis of psychiatric diagnosis today was really first formulated in 1980 with the third edition of the diagnostic and statistical manual of the profession.

DSM-III

DSM-III, and then there's been DSM-IIIR, DSM-IV, DSM-IV-TR, and now DSM-V. Finally, not with a Roman numeral, but with an Arabic numeral. So, they thought uh with DSM-V, when they needed to modify it, it would be like a piece of software. You have Windows 10, Windows 11, and so on, right?

为什么需要 DSM-III：诊断的混乱

Now, that diagnostic system came into being because psychiatrists had a very hard time agreeing with one another about what was wrong with somebody. And that became embarrassingly clear — first in the professional literature, which outsiders didn't read, and then via a very famous study that's a scientific fraud by David Rosenhan called On Being Sane in Insane Places, where he claimed to have sent in pseudo patients to the hospital, and they all were diagnosed as schizophrenic. All but one of them diagnosed as schizophrenic, the other as somebody with bipolar disorder. And they were fake patients.

So, almost in a panic after that study appeared in Science — and because there was an abundant professional literature from the 1960s showing the same thing, that diagnosis was a very erratic process — the DSM-III task force led by Robert Spitzer, who was at Columbia, was explicitly set up to try to create a sort of tick-the-boxes approach to deciding which box a patient belonged in.

Were you schizophrenic? Were you this type of schizophrenic or that type of schizophrenic? Were you uh manic depressive or bipolar? Uh did you have various forms of depression?

症状清单式诊断的建立

And to construct those boxes, what they relied upon was a list of symptoms. And if you had more than a certain number — if you had more than six of 10, six or 10 or more symptoms of a certain sort — you could be diagnosed with major depression, for example.

So, that system came into being. It was partially embedded because: - it appealed to drug companies who were developing drugs to treat these various disorders; - it appealed to insurance companies, because it gave them a stable base to look at; - it appealed, as diagnosis always does, to patients and their families who are scrambling to deal with these enormous upsets in the mental life of either themselves or a family member.

So, provided some sense of certainty around diagnosis.

18 世纪式的诊断逻辑

But, that was always based simply on symptoms — in the way an 18th century doctor might diagnose dropsy or diagnose some other kind of dis- or fever, for example. Well, fever and other diseases they talked about in the 18th century are really a constellation of very different things under one label. And I think that's what is turning out to be true of the DSM labels.

But, that approach was really all that psychiatry could come up with if it wanted to make sure — whether you were in Walla Walla or New York or San Francisco or Atlanta — you reached the same conclusion faced by the same patient. That you had a reliable diagnostic system.

可靠性 vs 有效性

That didn't mean necessarily it was a valid diagnostic system, if you understand the distinction between validity and reliability. Reliability means you and I, faced with the same sets of facts, reach the same conclusion, but that conclusion may or may not reflect the underlying reality of things, right?

So, you had this diagnostic system and it went through various iterations. Each time it went through an iteration, the number of possible psychiatric disorders you could get grew and grew and grew. And it became difficult to believe in some of those categories, shall we say — that they were really illnesses rather than some sort of social construct.

精神病学向"脑科学"的转向

But beyond that, psychiatrists wanted to be more like other medical doctors — to root their diagnoses in an understanding of the underlying pathology of the disorder. What was it that caused people to become schizophrenic? The sense was: if we could grasp that, we'd have a better handle on how to attack it, how to treat it.

And when DSM-5 was mooted — the fifth edition, in the early 2000s — NIMH, then under the leadership of Steven Hyman, who's at Harvard now, and succeeded by Thomas Insel who ruled NIMH for about 13 years, the two of them had pushed psychiatry and psychiatric research in a very particular direction:

  • On the one hand, towards understanding the genetics of mental illness.
  • On the other, to looking at what the new discipline of neuroscience could contribute to understanding things.

Both of them were heavily invested in the idea that mental illness was brain disease. And if it was brain disease, then the question was: what was making the mechanism here go awry? What was causing people's emotions, or their cognitive skills, or their sense of the world, to become so disordered?

Insel 的坦白：200 亿美元的失败

And they invest a lot of money in that approach. When Insel stepped down, he gave an interview actually to somebody at MIT. And he's repeated it since in a book he wrote about his experiences. Where he said:

"Well, you know, as I look back on my 13 years, I funded an enormous amount of scientific — really cool scientific — research. I funded geneticists and I funded neuroscientists and they did a lot of really interesting science. And after spending 20 billion dollars, the lot of the mentally ill has improved not one bit."

Wow.

Which was a pretty devastating statement, I thought.

And I imagine... National Institute of Mental Health.

National Institute of Mental Health, yes. I shouldn't resort to jargon.

[laughter]

NIMH 的使命与"脑十年"

But the National Institute of Mental Health had been founded in the late 1940s with the goal of improving — doing basic research, training people in the field, advancing the care of the mentally ill, and producing, obviously, cures and advances.

Its mission has varied widely over the years since, but starting in the 1990s — the period when the first George Bush declared the "decade of the brain" — NIMH increasingly focused on the idea that mental illness was purely a brain disease. And there's something to that, and there's also some mistake in thinking about it that way.

大脑 vs 心智：两种研究范式

This is, by the way, as we'll talk about — this distinction between seeing mental health and maladies of the human mind as a problem of the brain, like neurobiology, neuroscience...

Right.

...versus the problem of the mind, which is more in the cognitive science, psychotherapy — these more less amenable to scientific rigor. So, I think what's appealing about studying the brain in neurobiology, neuroscience is there's data.

Yes.

It's more rigorous, you could do science.

It's the kind of thing that really appealed to medical school deans.

Yes.

Because once NIMH — and the drug companies, too — were funding basic research on neurobiology and basic research on genetics, the money flooded in. And psychiatry, which had been something of an orphan, became much more popular.

多重因素的交织

And we should say that this is something you write a lot about — that there's all these factors to consider. So, there's the cultural elements.

Yes.

There's the political, public policy elements. Then there's at a certain point the drug companies and the insurance companies come in.

Yes.

Of course, all the human beings around somebody who is suffering with a mental health issue. So, the family factors, and that's connected to the cultural stuff.

It's a very, very complicated area, and oversimplification is a real problem, I think.

Mhm.
