item.description:
## 一、被忽视的深层反讽：精神病学的"软件版本号"暴露了范式危机
注意 DSM-V 那个耐人寻味的细节——他们把罗马数字换成了阿拉伯数字，因为"以后修订可以像 Windows 10、Windows 11 那样迭代"。这不是无害的排版选择，**这是一个学科在潜意识层面承认自己已经放弃了追求"真理"，转而拥抱"迭代"**。
医学的其他分支从不这样命名疾病手册。你不会看到《肿瘤学 12.0》。当一个学科开始用软件更新的隐喻描述自己的知识体系时，它其实在承认：这些分类不是被发现的，而是被制造和维护的。这与库恩所说的"范式危机"的征兆惊人一致——**当学者开始用另一个领域的比喻来重新描述自己的工作时，往往是原有范式已经失去自我辩护能力的信号**。
## 二、意外的跨领域连接：DSM 的困境与 18 世纪的"水肿病"是同一个认识论陷阱
Scull 顺口提到的类比其实是整段访谈中最锋利的一刀——**今天的"重度抑郁症"在结构上等同于 18 世纪的"发烧"或"水肿"**。18 世纪医生把"发烧"当作一种疾病，因为他们只能观察症状；后来生物医学发现发烧只是几十种截然不同病理过程的共同外显，"发

item.title: [Business of Sport] The Fall of Nike, Sydney Sweeney, & Infantino Consolidates his Power
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个意外的系统性观察

1. Nike 的悖论：它不是"输给了政治正确"，而是"输给了自己解锁的信任门"

表面叙事说 Nike 是"go woke go broke"的典型。但真正的系统性真相埋得更深——Nike 的崩塌是"直销革命"和"文化站队"两个独立决策在同一个时间点形成的死亡交叉。

想想这个隐藏的机制：当 Nike 把消费者从 Foot Locker、JD Sports 的货架上拽到自己的 App 里时，它其实是在做一个惊人的信任赌注——"你必须已经决定要买 Nike，才会打开这个 App。" 这意味着 Nike 主动放弃了"被偶然发现"和"在竞品旁被选中"的权利。

而恰恰在这个时刻，它选择了 Kaepernick。这就形成了一个致命的系统耦合：当品牌需要消费者"预先决定爱你"时，你却给了他们"预先讨厌你"的理由。 传统零售渠道能吸收政治争议——因为消费者是在货架前做冲动决定的；但 DTC 渠道放大了品牌"信仰门槛"的成本。这是两个看起来独立的战略，在心理学层面形成了乘法效应的灾难。

2. 跨领域连接：Sydney Sweeney 广告与 FIFA 权力结构惊人地同构

这两个话题看似风马牛不相及，但它们共享同一个深层机制：垄断者试图定义"谁有权代表某个类别"。

  • 女性运动员愤怒的不是"性化"（她们自己也在做），而是"未经许可的类别占用"——"只有我们才能与运动+女性身体产生商业连接"。
  • Infantino 和 UEFA 之争的本质，也不是钱的问题，而是"谁有权定义'足球治理'"这个类别。

更深一层：两者都揭示了"稀缺资源不是产品本身，而是'话语许可权'"。市场早已不是产品的竞争，而是"允许谁进入这个符号空间"的政治学。这解释了为什么 Charlie Hull 靠打球赚不过 Sydney Sweeney 摆姿势——因为运动明星以为自己在卖运动，其实她们卖的是"与运动相邻的符号许可"，而这个许可不是排他的。

3. 反直觉的洞见：世界田径锦标赛的成功证明了"体育与娱乐的真正分界线不在内容，而在信息密度"

大家都说 Ultimate Championship 成功是因为"少即是多"。但我要提出一个更锋利的观察：这场赛事真正做对的事，是它意识到当代观众的问题不是"没时间"，而是"注意力无处安放"。

传统田径为什么衰败？因为它让 200 米预赛、铁饼资格赛、跳远预赛同时进行——这是给"专业观众"设计的信息结构。而 Ultimate Championship 把它变成了"给算法时代观众"的信息结构——每一刻只有一个焦点，就像 TikTok 每次只给你看一个视频。

这里有一个跨领域连接：这与 Netflix 早期算法的洞见如出一辙——不是给你更多选择，而是替你消除选择的焦虑。 世界田径的胜利，本质上是"人类注意力的经济学"胜过了"体育项目的公平分配学"。这个洞见如果被 FIFA、NBA、任何大型体育组织真正吸收，未来 10 年的赛事结构会被彻底重写。

一个额外的预测性观察：Infantino 的困境和 Nike 的困境共享同一个隐藏结构——他们都在"扩张规模"和"维持核心身份"之间做了错误的取舍。Infantino 用 FIFA 的合法性换取小国选票，就像 Nike 用品牌纯度换取 DEI 站队。两者都会在下一个决策周期爆发同样的反噬。看着吧。

📝 转录文本

开场：一周关键议题速览

Nike shares are down by 80% — 80%, $220 billion. Just think about that. Now, you'd assume that that's because the company's losing lots of money, but it's not. It's not losing lots of money.

This is a sport — women's professional golf — that's doing things in a gradual way, is mostly being more and more successful in what it does. They could have tried to create a breakaway female league, but instead they've invested in events and the prize money on the European tour to try and elevate the value of that.

Here we are. We're 6 months out from the election for the FIFA president and the battle lines are starting to be drawn.

There is most likely one way that you are going to have to do this and it's going to have to be the ugly way.

And also don't forget that what Infantino is going to do is he's going to say, "Look, I've already said that I'm not going to come back with that particular scheme." So you made your point. Hands up. I should have dealt with it better. Does that mean that you want UEFA running FIFA?

Moving from the ghoulish FIFA boss to — I think I could say objectively — rather more attractive figure of Sydney Sweeney.

I don't know Charlie, that's quite — you could be canceled for that. I think — Who by? You're the only person who can cancel me. True.

主持人闲聊：搬家、蚊子与周末观赛

Good morning Charlie. Hi Charlie. You just said you're pumped. Why? I'm pumped. Well, I'm pumped because I've just seen the list of topics that we need to discuss today and it's a pretty meaty shopping list. It's pretty tasty, isn't it? Well, it's tasty. There's just a lot to get our teeth stuck into. So rather than our usual bollocking around how our weekends went, I think we need — We care. Everyone cares. Yeah, but well actually — How was your weekend? It was fine, thank you very much. Unpacking boxes in my new house. Still? You've been moving in for a few weeks. Two weeks. Two weeks. Yeah, two weeks, but it was slightly interrupted by a two or three day period when we had to vacate the place for a mosquito infestation. And obviously touching on sore topics given your recent encounters with biting insects. Oh yeah, that's true. Very true. I had a slight twitch when you were saying that.

But I did still find time, as I'm sure you did, to watch some sports over the weekend. Because — I know we're in the football season and football, football, that type of stuff — but I thought that the two biggest events of the weekend were World Ultimate Athletics Championship on the one hand and the Solheim Cup, the professional tournament between Europe and the USA for female professional golfers. I thought those were the two real sporting centerpieces of the weekend. What did you think?

第一部分：Solheim Cup 与女子高尔夫的商业模型

观赛体验：像 Ryder Cup 一样精彩

Do you know what I thought? Ryder Cup is one of my favorite things to watch across every sport. I absolutely love it. For the first time ever, I had the opportunity to cover pretty much three days of the Solheim Cup just because I didn't have anything on and we were at home and the baby is being potty trained so we couldn't leave the house. And so the TV was on and the Solheim Cup was on for the whole time. And I watched all of it like I would have done the Ryder Cup.

So my first thought was — I can watch the Ryder Cup every year because I thought it was so good. I thought it captured a lot of the elements that make the Ryder Cup very special without some of the massively boisterous elements of the crowds. The talent on show from a golfing perspective is exceptional, and there's just something beautifully competitive — as a fan, a highly exciting way between a red team and a blue team, and different people going out representing those teams trying to one up each other for a few days. It captured the best elements of sport.

对阵赛（Match Play）作为电视节目的独特价值

Yeah. I think what's quite interesting about that is that there are two elements of the Ryder Cup and the Solheim Cup which do not apply to the general professional golf that's served up to us.

I've always felt that there was room for more match play golf. Now I know — interestingly — we discussed the end of season tour championships in the US two or three weeks ago, and I note that recently the USPGA announced that was going to move to a match play format. I don't know if you saw that. So there's clearly some thinking going on around this.

The compelling nature of head-to-head golf as opposed to stroke play golf — it's much easier to guarantee excitement. We used to have a massive event in my youth, which probably only finished about 15 years ago, called the World Match Play that used to happen at Wentworth. And it was effectively owned by IMG actually. It was an invitation event, but most of the top golfers in the world did play in it. I remember when I was a journalist going inside the ropes and watching 36 holes of Tiger Woods against Colin Montgomery one year and it was just absolutely fantastic. And it just just seems to have sort of just tailed off rather over the last 5, 10, 15 years. Watching it on the weekend just made me sort of feel I want to see more of this.

As somebody — because most golfers, the majority of what we play is match play, right? So you're much more able to imagine that that is very similar to a situation I found myself in last week or whatever it might be. 72-hole medal golf, which is of course the ultimate challenge cuz every shot counts, is not something that the rest of us play very often.

And that's just to be clear to anyone listening who isn't a big golfer. Match play is basically — you win a hole, you go one up, you win another hole after it, you go two up, you lose the next hole, you're back to one up.

Yeah. The best golfers, the ones that play seriously — what Charlie has described as medal golf — that's when you're watching the majors and every shot you play stacks up to an eventual score. So for us amateur golfers — Right, the part-timers. This type of golf, you say, is something that we can relate to. And remember, we talked last week about participation with the NFL and the importance of being able to relate to the experiences that you have personally playing a sport. This is the best example, as you say, of why golf like this is so attractive.

LPGA 的营收结构与循序渐进策略

Maybe we can do it properly at another time. We're going to talk a lot about women's sports today, but it actually led me to just have a look at the broader economics of women's golf, because I was keen to see if this fantastic event actually translated into commercial — a business.

And I think it's safe to say it is, with some development that still needs to be done and is going on. But the LPGA, the ladies PGA, had a total revenue of $252 million in 2024 — the last accounts. That's a significant amount of money, of which $132 million of that across 33 events was prize money. So basically $4 million per event.

We're going to come on to another sport a little bit later, which doesn't have the money to elevate its prize money, but is still trying to do so. The model they've put into golf, the balance they're finding between commercial interest, broadcast deals — they're still tied in in the US with the PGA Tour on the broadcast side, so they haven't been able to separate this. But this certainly looks like a sport from an evolutionary perspective, as a women's entity, that is doing things in a way which actually give it a chance of long-term success.

They're not trying to do things ahead of their time. They're not trying to jump a hurdle that they're not ready to jump yet. And you have stars within that game that they can leverage. Of course, Nelly Korda is one of the top 10 most marketable female athletes in the world — one of the few outside of tennis. You saw a number of players I think within that Solheim Cup format who I would imagine over the next year — because I do think this was quite a flagship tournament — it just felt it will probably come a little bit more into the mainstream of sport. Can they capitalize on this?

Ladies European Tour：紧张的现金流与沙特资金

So, I guess the question is — it'd be really interesting to see when they eventually come out, which they haven't yet, so we need to keep an eye on this — what the qualified TV viewing numbers were for the Solheim Cup and therefore whether it's able to capture significant media rights value going forward.

It's owned by the tours I think.

Yes. I.e. the LPGA tour on the one hand and the women's European tour on the other hand. The women's European tour is perpetually strapped for cash. Yes. And the prize money on the women's European tour is $45 million compared to $132 million.

But interestingly, of that $45m, $35m give or take comes from money put from the LPGA into a couple of majors, the AIG Open and one other, and then another $10m or so comes from a five-series Saudi PIF series of which there's $10 million in prize money.

You're talking about LPGA media rights. No, no, no. So, the Ladies European Tour has prize money of $45 million. Yeah. As part of Ladies European Tour that includes two of the majors. Yeah. And a Saudi series. Yeah. You then on the side have a number of events — everything else apart from those ones I've just described — which is basically 20 events that have $10 million in total. Which means that those events have prize pots of about $3 to $500,000, not $10 to $15 million.

So the European tour, the Ladies European tour — the prize money at $45 million is good and has been going up, but it is highly weighted towards very few of the top events.

沙特模式的意外正面案例

But in an era where we're talking — and we'll talk about it again today — of Saudi pulling money out of a lot of things, the Ladies European tour is actually the one place where they've upped an investment this year. As part of their PIF series, the five tournament series which plays in Saudi for one of the tournaments, then goes to Seoul, Aramco, China, they play in London or the UK — they've added $2 million this year onto the prize pool taking it up to $15 million. Again, movements in the right direction. A massive gap between the two, but I also think it's far more recognized and accepted that the Ladies European tour is a feeder to the LPGA. So many acronyms.

Yeah.

Rather than fight against each other, what I did enjoy on the Saudi piece was what they've effectively done here at the PIF is do what we wanted them to do on the other side. They could have tried to create a breakaway female league, but instead they've invested in events and the prize money on the European tour to try and elevate the value of that. So that captured my attention.

女子高尔夫的明星缺口

As I said, you need events sometimes to really capture attention, right? This creates a moment where I am now actively interested to see what Lottie does on the next event. It does feel like the sport is in need of a few stars.

Now, this is something that tennis has been in some ways quite fortunate in — and I guess you get a lot of head-to-head combat in tennis which makes those rivalries easier to identify when you're seeing the same players playing in finals against each other on a very regular basis.

If you think about women's golf, really as you say, Nelly Korda has come to the fore in the last five years as both a top player but also marketable as they would say. Ironically of course, her father was a top professional tennis player, and her brother —

And her brother, another story — Grand Slam winner. Petr Korda, yeah, won the Australian Open. Yeah. So good genes. Yeah. Good genes if you can say so. Well, we'll come on to that later on as well.

Anyhow, but the bottom line is — you go outside Nelly Korda, and what we've basically been lacking in the last decade or so really is a really marketable European player. If you go back 25, 30 years, when Laura Davies was one of the top three players in the world, multiple Grand Slam winner, big character, was very famous in this country and throughout Europe. And Suzann Pettersen does a huge amount of the broadcast now, both on the men's and the women's game. So she was a sort of national figure in this country and very well known throughout the rest of Europe and indeed in America.

Haven't really had that since. You need to have somebody who is both a character and successful. And probably the character who European golf would love to see become that is Charlie Hull, who is a character but hasn't nailed the majors yet. I mean, she's absolutely in the top 10 in the world, but hasn't yet nailed those big major winning moments that break you through onto the big stage.

And then you got Lottie Woad, as you mentioned, who's much younger. Yeah. I think she's only about 20 odd.

Pro for 13 months, I think. Yeah. So she's come up to the top table very very quickly.

But in general terms, I agree with you. This is a sport, women's professional golf, that's doing things in a gradual way, is mostly being more and more successful in what it does. There seems to be a clear understanding, as you say, that the European tour is a feeder to the US tour. You hear about equal pay to the men's golfers — they're very focused on "well, what can we do for ourselves" rather than leeching off other entities.

So all the things we talk about is stuff which women's professional golf is kind of doing. But at some points sports need a bit of luck. Where would women's professional tennis be now without the Navratilova–Evert rivalry? It needs these moments of superstars where you cut through into the broader public. So I'm going to be really interested to see what the TV ratings were on it, both in Europe but also in the US where the big commercial markets are.

Overall, a terrific event. And of course very pleasing for those of us on this side of the pond that Europe won.

第二部分：世界田径 Ultimate Championships——赛事策展的教科书

免费直播 + 顶级场馆 + 极致聚焦

Another big event on the weekend was the athletics. Now I made a deliberate point of watching quite a bit of this. In this country, it was on the BBC, and it's been a sort of long-standing obsession of mine that too many sports try to obtain money for their media rights when it's a relatively small amount of money, but somehow it makes the executives feel good that they are being paid — when actually going free-to-air is what hits a much bigger audience and really enables you to break through, which then is what achieves the big commercial numbers, but also brings the eyeballs which you then have the ability to sell to one of the pay TV platforms for a lot more money.

So I thought this was absolutely spot on. And the staging of the event was —

Outstanding. It's cool, wasn't it? I love like the black in the room from the track. Everything was cool. The stadium — I mean, amazing venue just as a stadium. It made athletics seem cool. Yeah. And that's not necessarily a given.

Right. But even when they were introducing the athletes at the start of the whole games, and they were all wearing quite cool fashion outfits, and the spotlight being on them and all this stuff — so I just thought the whole thing was delivered brilliantly.

The atmosphere in the stadium — the way in which they often in athletics meetings, you get a bit of this when you watch it on TV, but if you go live, you really get it — is you can have two or three events happening at the same time. So different parts of the stadium are looking at different events. Now, if you've got loads and loads of events and loads and loads of athletes, that's the only way to cram them all in. Right? If you're having to run the heats for the 200m at the same time as the qualifying for the discus at the same time as the qualifying for the long jump, you need to get all these events in.

So what they did in this event is they said, "Right, we're going to cut down the amount of individual events we have. Number one. Number two, we're only going to get the very top athletes to come along. So we're not having to run lots of heats and all the qualifying sessions and all this type of stuff."

So every single bit mattered and every single event had the spotlight quite literally on it. And I don't know — it just for me, that's the best I've seen athletics, that's the best presentation of athletics I've seen.

少即是多：奖金结构与赛制创新

Do you think it's because less was more? Definitely.

There was $10 million in prize money put towards this. Seb Coe, when he came and spoke to us on the show — this was something that came into the conversation when we spoke about the earning opportunities for athletes. We've often spoken about governing bodies having to do more in sports where it's harder to make money, but also within the boundaries that they can, i.e. not extend themselves too far.

World Athletics recognized there was a gap in the calendar. They recognized without a World Championships and an Olympics in a year, there had to be some form of showpiece and they had to try and make it appealing to you and I who sit here — as we've talked about again — watching moments, watching great things from athletes, and then having nowhere or no idea where to go to follow them.

In something again rather than a breakaway competition, this was a governing body recognizing that they could control and do this while finding a budget. I mean, it took certain elements out of Michael Johnson's failed thing last year, didn't it? In terms of cutting down the number of events, in terms of the spotlights on individual events and individual athletes — there was quite a bit of "let's take the best out of that idea and then let's apply it in a more systematic, fully backed way."

Absolutely.

用现有 IP 创新，胜过创造全新 IP

And I feel like a consistent narrative you and I have here is — we're not saying you can't create new IP, but we're saying quite a lot of the time you can innovate within the existing IP to offer something that actually does what new IP is setting out to do.

Us as athletics fans didn't need to go and follow a brand new tournament to follow this. This was put on by the same people that put on a World Athletics Championship. This was distributed on the same channels, so I knew where to watch it. I could flick on my TV just as I'd expect to in a traditional athletics competition. I could find this just as I could find anything else. They made it easy for me as a consumer.

We spoke of LIV Golf — sorry, I only mentioned the distribution element of it and their big challenge being people not having access. When you create these new tournaments, they've leveraged their existing broadcast relationships highly effectively so that you and I can sit down and catch it on a weekend where maybe we weren't even aware it was on.

I'll be honest, I was a bit skeptical — and I can say it now. Seb, World Athletics, when they came in and they said, "We really want to talk about Ultimate Championships cuz it's going to be a great thing." There's a part of you that goes, "Oh, okay. Yeah. Okay. Well, can we keep that down to two minutes?" But this totally lived up to that.

第五部分：Nike 的陨落——一场市值蒸发 2200 亿美元的解剖

从 S&P 100 到崩塌

Moving on to cancellation — or perhaps not quite right is the phrase — which has now become known in the general business marketplace as "go woke go broke." And this is something which is very much in the sports industry mind at the moment with regards to the biggest sports merchandise brand of all: Nike.

Now, Nike has had a phenomenal run of it. Absolutely phenomenal run of it. Really, there have been a few ups and downs in the meantime, but over 40 to 50 years they've barely put a foot wrong during my lifetime. They are the behemoths of the sports merchandise space, and they're a quoted company — which means they're listed on the stock market in the USA. And by sort of the time just after Covid, they were one of the biggest companies in the world. They were in the S&P 100 — the S&P 100 is the list of the hundred biggest companies on the US stock market. And because the vast majority of the biggest companies in the world are American, it's not far off being a fair denomination of the biggest companies in the world.

That was about 2021, 2022, that type of period. Anyway, since then Nike shares are down by 80% — 80% or $200 billion — $220 billion, £160 billion pounds. Just think about that. That's the reduction in value at that business over the last four years.

Now, you'd assume that that's because the company's losing lots of money, but it's not. It's not losing lots of money. It's lost a bit of revenue. So, at its absolute peak in 2023-24, it got up to $51.5 billion in revenue, and it's now down to more like $45 billion. So, it's lost 10% of its revenue during that time. And that's, by the way, really bad for an established company — all the stock market analysts will be crawling all over that saying, "Oh, hang on a second. What does that mean in terms of your cost margins? What's that mean in terms of your EBITDA? What does that mean in terms of the dividend you're going to be able to pay?" — and therefore putting out sell notes on it.

There's no doubt that this is partially driven by revenue. But it's not just driven by revenue. It's driven by market sentiment as well in terms of where Nike has got itself to and whether it still feels like that brand that everyone can love.

Nike 品牌的历史意义

What's Nike meant to you? You've been — and please this is not an age joke, right — you've been around for closer to the time of Nike existence. What did it mean to you?

I think what it meant was and what it has meant is: it is always up with and just ahead of the trend. So, Nike sets trends and decides — it slightly makes the weather, right? You've got the big merch companies who chop out their merch, do it as cheaply as possible and sell it to you as expensively as possible. And sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't work. Adidas and all these types of guys.

And then Nike are the ones who have been able to somehow, despite becoming massive, still maintain a bit of the energy of a challenger brand. That's been their genius. That Nike swoosh, which is just the most wonderful brand logo — that swoosh with the uptick — has always looked towards the future, has always somehow signaled a sense of "we are part of the future, and therefore by buying our brand, you are buying into the future."

And some of the decisions they've made in terms of, obviously, their legendary partnership with Michael Jordan — they've just made so many good judgment calls to keep their brand in that place.

Kaepernick 与政治站队的转折

And then it seems like around about the time of Covid or just before Covid — the pandemic and then since Covid — they took a corporate level decision that they were going to ally themselves effectively with progressive politics. All of this package of things that left-wing political people have put at the forefront of what they've been trying to sell/preach to the rest of the world for the last half decade to a decade — and Nike decided very conspicuously. It's almost hard to overstate how conspicuously they decided to ally themselves with that.

Now, the cornerstone of that was the decision to go into partnership with an American footballer called Colin Kaepernick, who became famous in the US for refusing to stand for the US national anthem. And the amount of controversy that generated in the US was absolutely huge — with a vast chunk of the country feeling totally affronted by it, and then also a very good chunk of the country saying, "You know, good for him, he's standing up for those who the American state has oppressed or has not been run for the benefit of," or whatever it might be. But it was a very polarizing thing. And then for Nike to enact a partnership with that was a moment in time when a good chunk of middle America — which is where the real spending power lies — went "Well, if that's what Nike is about, that's not for me. I'm proud of the USA," and Nike had up until then always been roughly associated with America.

Phil Knight 与"Shoe Dog"里的初心

Right. So, coming back to the question I asked you — to me, it's always been about excellence, the pursuit of excellence, being the absolute best you could be.

Phil Knight, the founder of Nike — have you ever read Shoe Dog?

No. Read it. My god, it's one of the best books.

The fundamental reason I loved it so much was because — from someone that has only seen the later years of Nike, I've only ever seen Nike as this massive success — but the story of creating this business and how he created it is absolutely extraordinary. And 90% of the book is that. It's not about how great we are and have been over the last 30 years. It's about what it took to get there. And what it took to get there is what they've lost now.

I went back to the book. I was interested as I was reading through it a few years ago what I'd highlighted, and there were a couple of quotes from Phil that I think Nike need to remember and bring back into some of this. One of them is: "What if there was a way, without being an athlete, to feel what an athlete feels?"

In other words, through our brand, you are going to feel like the people that you look up to, and we're going to make you feel like that. Whether that's wearing Michael Jordan's shoe, whether it's dressing like Roger Federer, whether it's walking out on a golf course wearing your red Nike top like Tiger Woods — we will put you in those positions, and we will leverage talent to do that with brilliant product, top-of-the-range product. So, not only do you feel good, but you feel like you are the best prepared you could possibly be.

Wow. Now, to me, that is the best sell as a consumer looking at a sports product you could give me. What do I not care about? I don't care about buying another lifestyle product that pitches itself in the middle of a discourse around broader global politics.

Also, Charlie, I think what's really important about that — because I totally agree with everything you've said — is that sport is the place we go to to forget about those debates really. You sit around the dining room table, you listen to the radio station, you read the newspaper, and you're in the middle constantly of these political and cultural debates. Football — a cultural debate. That's not sport. Sport is for its own. It's a recreation.

For Nike, it's been about participation. It's been about getting involved. They've replaced participation with inclusivity. And this is not the place for me as a wearer of Nike, as an aspirer to athletes, where that is the front and center of my mind. My mind gears purely towards how do I get the most out of my buy? How do I get the most out of resonating with a brand?

Now, if victory, if winning, if excellence is that North Star of the brand, that is the one thing they should always stick to no matter what they do. You look at the biggest businesses — they can make lots of changes, but they always have one North Star and they do not compromise from it. That again is why that book is so fascinating.

Because with Phil Knight's obsession — he was a runner, so it started very much as athletics, right? It was about the best running shoe you could ever create. Whether it was going to Japan in the 70s, making a flight and a trip that was far more complex than it is today with Onitsuka Tiger, trying to figure out how they created and captured the power of their running shoe and bringing that into a US market. Whether it is moving into sports and recognizing emerging talent like Michael Jordan — because that for Nike, as everyone knows, has been an incredible partnership, but it started long before Michael Jordan was Michael Jordan. So the things that made them great have kind of fallen a little bit by the wayside.

领导力失误 (一)：从体育垂直到男女童分类

Now with that comes leadership challenges. And I've written, as we were going through this, kind of a list of a few things that we should cover off as part of this. Because you have this overarching theme, I think, that you can definitely say of "go woke or go broke" linking to the demise. But there's also things that have actually directly happened off the back of that that have created it.

One of which that we can directly link to that was this move from verticals — sporting verticals, athletics division, football division, basketball division —

Yeah. to men's, women's, and kids. Yeah.

So again, if we're going back to why I go to Nike over other things — I go to Nike over other things because when I want to buy my pair of football boots, they're the brand. If I want to go and buy my golf clothes, I want to look like the guys. I want to win. They're the best products. I don't go because they have a good men's range. Broad, unspecified, lack of focus. That's not why I shop with Nike.

The leadership that they had, John Donahoe, who was the chief executive from 2020 to 2024, made changes here that are now being unpicked. That is one of them. Nike now moving back to the sporting verticals.

领导力失误 (二)：从批发到 DTC 的过度转身

Another major one — and John Donahoe elevated it and accelerated it, but it actually started under Mark Parker who was the CEO previously — was a move from very strong wholesale retail partnerships. I think this is probably the biggest single factor actually. To a direct-to-consumer [model].

Do you like — explain? Right. Okay. What Charlie just said there was probably — notwithstanding what we just said about go woke go broke — probably the single biggest decision, and might be put under a different banner, which is Nike got too big for its boots.

So in other words, the way in which most merchandise brands sell their product is by having very strong relationships with the big retailers. Those retailers will get some pricing power because they're buying in volume. But in return, the big merch producers exert power over how their product gets displayed, how they market it together and all these types of things.

Nike decided they got themselves into such a powerful position in the marketplace — people like me and Charlie could just go online and just buy direct from Nike. And that came at the cost of certain B2B relationships which started to be downgraded or degraded effectively. And the problem is that the B2C — that's the business to consumer direct market — had not yet sufficiently developed, and may indeed never do so, to replace what they were losing on the B2B side. And there's absolutely no doubt that that was a massive factor.

It's a huge point. Look, first, if DTC was easy, everyone would do it. Okay. You have much higher margins. You get 100% of everything you sell. You get all of the data from it. You can leverage your consumer experience from the first time they access the brand to make a purchase. Brilliant. When you are a truly global business, to own every single point of that relationship is incredibly expensive and incredibly hard to do. It is also, no matter how big you are, never going to put you in front of as many people as you could be put in front of.

Hence why going wholesale retail in your JD Sports, your Foot Lockers, your massive US stores — that is worth the 50% cut that you may take on your end sale price. Because you are firstly selling stock in bulk, so you're selling a huge amount in one go, you are also giving someone else the job of shipping, of managing the customer experience that is maybe not the easiest part of a job.

Now, I get it. I get it from Nike. I do understand why they wanted to do it. And particularly from a world where we always talk about experience, and customer experience — and connecting to want to own more of that makes a lot of sense, especially when they've tried to bring a lot more innovation and creativity to, as you say, the digital studio there. The experience when you go into the Nike store — the Nike app is excellent. It's a really good app. But I still have to go on to that Nike app. I don't come across that Nike app by chance. It is a decision that I make consciously.

And to make that decision, Charlie, you have had to have pre-decided "I am definitely going to buy Nike." Yes.

无法承受的品牌信任门槛

Now this is the biggest issue I think in the wholesale versus the DTC thing — which is that the vast majority of people who buy Nike are not solely Nike buyers. Nike has to back itself that in a competitive marketplace, people will choose their product.

So, I actually currently — my current trainers are tatty and I need to go and get some more today. So what I'm going to do is I'm going to go off on my way down, walking down through town, I'm going to go to Hamleys, and I'm going to go in there where I know that there will be a large selection of different brands.

Sorry, Hamleys? Sorry, not Hamleys. I mean, I'm going to go to buy some Playmobil. I'm going to go — Whiteleys. Lilywhites. Sorry, Lilywhites. Charlie. Oh dear. When you get to — This is not the drunk down. Just so we can — it's not too big. There's a certain moment in time. Yes. I'm not going to go to Hamleys — well, I might go to Hamleys, but not for this purpose. Say your daughter will be delighted. My daughter will be here. I'm going to go to Lilywhites at Piccadilly Circus, where I know that I will find a great selection of trainers.

Now, because in the past I valued Nike as a product, my eye will be drawn more naturally towards the Nike products, and I am more likely to make a Nike purchasing decision. But for me, that's a really easy marketplace. I don't have to go on lots of different apps. I don't have to go onto the Nike app first and then onto the Adidas app. Here I can go into a shop and see all of them and therefore make what I regard as being an informed decision in so doing.

Now, Nike have to back themselves that their brand is strong enough that once I put myself in that multi-product situation, that I'm going to choose Nike. But effectively by asking me to go on the app, they effectively are telling me you need to have already made that decision before. And that slightly puts you under the headline of "mug" — because then they can start exerting pricing power on you. They can say, "Well, since you're here anyway, and since you're plainly planning to buy Nike, we can then start to push the price a little bit."

So I think you're right. I think betting in stuff that you're going to actually wear — clothes, shoes, socks — putting yourself in a situation where you're expecting people to simply make that decision always to go with you, is strategically a very risky thing to do.

产品质量的隐性衰退

If they were going to do this properly, what they had to do is they had to double down on the core identity of Nike. As a DTC thing, they had to bring me more into the "I need to feel like an athlete" than I've ever been before, if you were going to own that relationship.

The fact that they had category changes like they did — removing verticals and then asking me to go and make purchasing decisions on a site which I actually stopped understanding with the clarity that I'd always had with that brand — was a horrible combination of factors that worked together.

And when they go into this period, they made quick careless decisions about which products they really doubled down in to try and ensure that the revenue didn't take a hit. What do I mean by that? They went all in on what we would call the classics — Air Force One, Jordan, those brands that they could shift in their mind a huge amount of inventory for very quickly because there was a demand. But the demand for those brands had always been built on one thing, and it was exclusivity. And in doing that, they stripped out a huge value of what a lot of those classics, that heritage product had done.

They deviated from the quality of the core product to the extent where — I don't know about you — but since that has happened, I've had a few pairs of Nike running shoes, they fall apart like that.

Really? That's really — They have a foam thing at the moment and what you see in this foam thing is a lot of them have a line through the foam sole, and that foam sole is actually clearly glued on. After I reckon for this pair of shoes, I'm thinking I probably ran in them for 3 months — separation in the sole. They were pretty much unwearable after that.

The product — that running shoe that Phil Knight strived to build, that was better than anyone else — had suffered.

Now, if you are creating a verticalized strategy with developers who know they're coming in to create the best products, because "I am creating a running shoe," that doesn't happen to my product. If I've got a load of developers in there saying, "We're creating men's, women's, and kids products, and then we're going to sell them in a new retail — well, sorry, a new sales strategy" — that developer is not going to have that specificity, that focus to create the best product to then sell in your new environment.

Elliott Hill 与复苏的可能性

So I honestly, the reason I wanted to drill into that piece was because I think that's a really important part. But what is notable to say just at the end of it is that Elliott Hill, the new CEO, who they had to bring out of retirement — he'd been at Nike for 32 years and has now been pulled out of a four-year retirement to come and unfuck this. Basically, he is now trying to rebuild these relationships.

And it is worth saying that 2026 wholesale is up 6% to $27.5 billion. It is moving back in the right direction. It will not change quickly enough, anywhere near quickly enough, to move that share price to the extent that that will get them back into a kind of top business conversation in the next few months. But if they can do it properly, can they recover from this? Absolutely. Can they get people back buying to it? Yes. But I do think they need to get that North Star, that core piece.

中国市场的崩塌

There are other problems. There are other problems. You mentioned other problems as well. Tap China straight away. Mentioned that. The trading relationship between the US and China over the last 3 years has been significantly impacted by the imposition and then removal and imposition of various tariffs. And that is having an impact on lots of different brands and lots of different situations. Because even if the tariffs get put on and then removed, in the meantime you're removing B2B certainty. So that's obviously caused significant problems.

Have you got the numbers there in terms of what's actually happened, Charles?

So, you mentioned financial year 2021 as being a major year for the value of the company. High watermark. Yeah. The revenue in China was $8.29 billion in 2021. The revenue in 2026 was $5.85 billion.

So that's minus 30% of their Chinese revenue gone in 5 years — in a market where sportswear spending has actually grown by about half in the same time period. Why? What it has seen is the rise of Chinese domestic challenger brands capturing a huge amount of this market. Anta and Li-Ning being two in particular — domestic brands that are slightly more affordable. I mean, Anta alone now hold 21.8% of China's sportswear market, where Nike previously would have captured far more of that.

And if you lose your quality differentiation in the meantime and then a local challenger brand comes along — what's the normal charge that you would make against the local challenger brand? You say, "Well, probably the quality is not going to be all up to all that much." But if you yourself have not kept up your own quality level, and a local challenger brand comes along, then you lose that bit as well.

Guochao：民族自豪与本土品牌崛起

Guochao — you know what Guochao is? I think I pronounced it right. State-encouraged consumer pride movement. Basically it's this "buy Chinese." Buy Chinese products. Support the industry, invest more, and we'll be able to do more.

Why have Anta and Li-Ning in particular been very good? Well, they've created the foam type running shoe that I was talking about previously — that Nike would have marketed as what made them different and the best in their markets. And they've said, "Hey, look, we can do this and we can do it for 80 quid rather than 280 quid, which is if you look at those top running shoes, what Nike will charge for them."

So, product innovation through national pride in the brands that they want to start promoting has basically given a Chinese public a different opportunity, a different alternative.

Yeah. So if you're looking at the diminution of revenue from peak to now, to being about $5 billion a year, about half of that's from China.

Do you know what's interesting? Nike is also terminating its online distribution deals with thousands of Chinese retail partners from the 1st of January 2027. They're consolidating their own site, their own app. What they're stripping back in all the other regions they're actually rolling out in China. In China, they want to basically be DTC.

But it does talk about the challenger element to it and the rise of other brands, because it's very hard to keep on being the challenger when you're 50 years into your evolution.

联邦调查与更宽的挑战者市场

And there's one final bit I just wanted to bring up, which is that they are actually currently under investigation by the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. This is investigating whether Nike has discriminated against white employees and applicants for employment. So, in other words, in their manic drive to be DEI and all this type of stuff, there have been a sufficient body of complaints, evidence, to support a fairly significant investigation into whether they've actually practiced systematic discrimination.

You don't want to be investigated by the US federal government. It's just a horrible, horrible place to be. Those cases can go on for a long time, can cost a vast amount of money, and the fines that tend to get levied by the federal government in the US are vast and they're absolutely huge. So it wouldn't surprise me if part of the current share price problems that they're facing is when you've got a company that's under investigation by the Feds, you're not in a good place.

So I think loads of different things. But in the meantime also, you have a very strong market that doesn't have one company that has grown up and been competitive. It's got a number of companies that have been competitive. And while you've left retail, that leaves a lot of shelf space, and that's been filled by the likes of Hoka, On Running, more of Adidas, New Balance is — doesn't publish its figures but is significantly up.

There's been a huge elevation in alternatives to people. So it's far harder for Nike to go, "I identify one challenger, we're going to grab that market share back," when a whole number of businesses have come to grab that from them.

And just finally, I think — because there's a real question here as we end up — of are they terminally screwed or is this recoverable? Those companies I've just named, everyone looks at and says, "Oh, haven't they grown in the same time?" They've also — and are also — having significant challenges. On [Hoka's parent] shares fell as much as 22% by August 2026 on a revenue miss. Public company. Hoka's growth decelerates into single digits. So, we're not saying the market is booming. There are real challenges out there for everyone.

And if the running boom is entering kind of a normalization phase, then in a flat market, Nike are going to have a far better opportunity, I think, of grabbing some of that market share back than they do in an accelerating one. They just really need to sort out who they are and remember what the business was. Read — every single person making a decision at that company should just go back and read the book that their founder wrote as to what it means to wear Nike.

Yeah. Good.

收尾：Substack 预告

Right. Well, we have another massive segment that we want to talk through — we're going to move on to Substack now on women's tennis, WTA.

Did you for the audience — did you watch the women's final in the US Open?

I actually didn't. I'm ashamed.

It was excellent. Yeah, it was excellent. But there are far bigger talking points happening within the women's game that we need to pick apart. So, we're going to do that on Substack. For those of you that want to come over, please do. For those of you that don't, thank you as always for joining us and we will see you next week.

Thanks very much.
