四、Warehouse Risk：做市商的"仓储"逻辑

Q: In situations like DeepSeek or July, would you ever make a directional punt on one of the names?

For me at our particular seat, the mandate was much less to take an explicit opinion on markets. It was much more: identify who IMC was trading against, and if we believe the trades are against a benign counterparty, we should warehouse off that risk — actually carry on more of that risk and try to get more of those trades.

做市商的"矩阵思维"

Typically when an options market maker like IMC trades against an option, this option is added to the firm's book. We identify the risks — deltas, vegas, gammas, thetas, expiration risk, exotic stuff. This risk is netted in a massive matrix against the risks that we're holding on all the other options we're trading. If there is an accumulation of specific types of risk, eventually the firm externalizes their risk — trades it away.

This is what you imagine when you see a market maker: they're pricing it such that people are buying and selling, and the market maker is taking the spread. The way the market maker actually does this across many instruments is to put all those risks together in a massive matrix or similar structure, and adjust the valuation of their pricing such that over time the risk would even out.

For us, when we traded against counterparties at prices that we thought were really good, carrying risk that we thought were benign — we could just warehouse that risk. Screen and say: "Hey, we don't actually want this thing to go into the firm's model that affects the pricing of every other instrument. We actually just want to hold on to these options till expiration." Maybe we delta hedge them over time with a half-life, or once a day. In general, we're happy to just warehouse this variance because we thought these were really good trades. And if we see more of those trades coming, we can be like — hey, let's try to get more onto this flow.

But very rarely are we like, "hey, in the absence of flow, we think the market at its natural state is inefficient, and we want to directionally take a punt."

五、七月是怎么被交易的？Leopold 与"退出流动性"

Q: How would a desk like yours handle a month like July?

Talking to a few of my IMC coworkers, July was actually a pretty decent month for them. What happened among a lot of the trading firms was people started realizing someone was getting liquidated, because prices were getting to somewhat absurd levels — there was just consistent selling flow.

One indicator that a lot of trader friends point to is Intel earnings, where they gave a monster guidance, smashed earnings, and then the stock popped. But then it sold off the next morning — showing that someone was using this positive earnings as exit liquidity. Then it went below where the price was pre-earnings, and this was in the absence of any other major catalysts.

Don't quote me, but at the time the upside calls were very cheap across a lot of the semi stack — partially due to deleveraging effects. My previous desk was able to pick up a lot of those upside calls, which realized very well when it came out that it was Leopold's fund, Situational Awareness, that blew up. They got bought by Ken Griffin. People realized, hey, this selling flow is probably going to stop now, because it's captured by someone who actually has balance sheet. And then all of those stocks pumped up 20–30%, and the upside calls also got bid up — because when stocks go up that much, the entire vol surface also elevates.

六、"座位比人重要"—— 期权做市的信息拓扑

Q: Was there a misconception people had about what you were doing?

I would say the thing that my desk was doing is a very similar job that a lot of single-stock options desks had. So a lot of trader friends were actually sitting in a very similar seat.

There is at times a larger difference on how wide the mandate is. Some firms have very confident analysts who can make decent projections around events like earnings or major announcements, such that they would actually take positions. Certain desks — the rest of firm may have a better OTC business and have better access to flow information. IMC at the time was expanding its block trading and OTC trading business, but still most of the flow information was from public exchanges.

If your firm has direct trades with, say, pension funds that would affect pricing, obviously you have a fuller picture. But the general principle of buying cheap, selling expensive, warehousing good risk, and occasionally reacting to news events or special situations — all of those are roughly the same set of skills.

座位本身就是杠杆

Q: Did that seat give you a differentiated perspective on where markets were going?

In some sense yes, because you're sitting in a seat with more information. But now that I no longer have access to a lot of that flow information, I don't think I am currently better at predicting where the market is going to go.

A lot of times on these seats, the value of the seat by itself is already very high, because you're already in a highly leveraged position where you have access to information that the vast majority of the market doesn't. If you're looking at options volume data in the United States, probably the top-five options market makers do 80–90% of the liquidity provision. So when we say that maybe just a few dozen people on the entire planet have that view — I think that is quite literally true.

You are among the few dozen people on the planet that actually have this full view of the market, and you're uniquely able to take advantage of that. But that skill set doesn't necessarily convert as well to personal trading. I do some personal trading based on general principles of buying cheap, selling expensive, but a lot of it doesn't have that much to do with the job.

Well, not more valuable than the person — the seat itself being high leverage. Like the CEO of Google is an extremely high-leveraged seat, but the person can still be extremely valuable by leveraging the seat to create even greater value.

七、交易公司的组织学：谁坐在谁旁边？

Q: What are some of the ways trading firms design ops and training so that people can have insane competitive advantage?

That is kind of the central question of how you build a trading firm. Even when I was at IMC, they had rearrangements of how the teams actually worked. I think there were a few over the years. Friends at Jane Street say they have teams being rearranged over time as well. Same with HRT.

The fundamental question of who in my company should be sitting next to who else, who should they be talking to — how do you organize the communication, the actual floor plan, the people, the machines in such a way that you make the most amount of money — is probably an unsolved problem.

共同的模式：不给固定座位分配

Some common trends: it's very rare for people to get direct seat assignments from the internship at large trading firms. Usually they go through new grad training, and seat assignments are made after some sort of evaluation process. Being able to do a lot of mock trading or even real trading and projects to see what each person is best at, and then putting them into that position — that's a very common trend across all trading firms.

This is somewhat counterintuitive to a lot of other companies where, as a new grad at most normal companies, you apply for a specific job and get that job function. Trading firms take a lot of time to monitor and evaluate — not only whether you should be working at the firm in the first place, but also, if you're working at the firm, what is the best use of both your time and the firm's time.

IMC 特有：一个巨型系统

Q: Anything specific to IMC?

For IMC, we spent much more time with the firm's systems. Roughly half or more of the training process was about learning each part of the firm's trading systems — which is like one giant machine that I probably should not go too deep into.

But in terms of firm's architecture, it's well known that IMC has a long history of being very systematically driven. The systems interact — one part of the system interacts with the other part in very special ways — that it's like firm-internal knowledge to know this really really well. Some people can argue this is not the best thing that you're stuck learning this system, but on the other side, it is a very powerful system, and the people who are very good at it are able to leverage it. This is something that's somewhat IMC-particular.

八、Trader Group Chats：AI 押注、群体贝塔与 30% 中位回撤

Q: How do you see the AI landscape, having sat in a seat with much higher-quality information?

Are you punting?

Am I punting? I think both myself and the majority of my former co-workers, and the majority of the people who I graduated with, and the majority of the traders who graduated after me, are all punting and extremely bullish AI.

I have a few group chats on my iMessage with just trader friends. I think the average beta of these group chats is like probably three to the S&P, and I think group chat median drawdown during July was at least 30%.

Median.

So the boys are very bullish AI here. And me too. Part of it is a bias on the fact that I think trading firms are some of the most AI-native enterprises on the planet.

Not sure why — I saw this on Twitter and I'm not sure if it's 100% correct — but it does seem plausible that the three largest uses of AI right now in terms of token consumption are:

  1. The frontier labs themselves — training, inference, post-training
  2. AI B2B SaaS enterprise auto startups
  3. Trading firms — I think the third largest user of AI throughout their entire work stack

From optimizing internal tools for traders, to firms like Jane Street or HRT which have GPU clusters that do deep learning (not necessarily purely based on large language models but nonetheless still consumes a lot of compute power) — AI is being used everywhere in trading. Firms which embrace AI first in trading — such as Jane Street — are doing really really well right now. It's actually one of the largest mistakes from a lot of firms maybe five to six years ago to not have invested in their AI infrastructure as early.

九、"整个 Stack 都买"的组合逻辑

Q: What specific parts of the stack are you riding right now?

For me, it is all parts of the stack. It is very hard to guess where the value of AI is going to come down to. Let's say AI generates hypothetically 10 trillion dollars of value on some year. First, it's difficult to tell how much goes to consumers, how much goes to corporate earnings in the first place. Of the part that goes to corporate earnings, you don't know which ones go to:

  • The labs
  • The GPU designers
  • The data centers (something like a CoreWeave)
  • The fabs that actually make the chips (Intel, TSMC)
  • The tool providers to fabs (Lam Research, Applied Materials, ASML)
  • Connectivity between data centers (Lumentum, AOI, Coherent)
  • The materials and substrates on the chips

There are all these parts of the stack. It is difficult to tell where value will occur. So I'm doing the simple thing of just investing in all of them. Which is why right now my personal portfolio is like 50 random chip/AI stocks that pretty much covers the entire stack.

Q: In the group chats, is that the consensus?

Having some exposure to this seems to be the consensus. Having exposure to this exceeding the S&P is the consensus. The particular level of leverage that I've chosen is not the consensus, and the lack of diversification into other potential themes is also not purely consensus. But it is consensus that most people are underallocated into AI, just judging by the S&P 500.

十、"永久底层阶级" vs 泡沫：如何选择站队？

Q: Are you a proponent of the SF AI-pilled worldview?

If you don't have any AI exposure in your career or in your portfolio, you are going to be the permanent underclass. A slave for the entirety of your life. Working dead-end jobs, useless skills — it's funny because we're laughing about it, but people seriously believe this.

It is a possibility. I assign some non-zero probability to this.

年轻人该怎么打这手牌？

Q: What's the best way to ride this trend?

The most obvious way is to just buy AI stocks. People discuss how there is rising inequality in the US and a lot of this is driven by the rising asset prices. There are moral statements you can make about this, but that trend is probably going to continue. If anything, if you truly believe AI is going to create value, more value is going to accrue to capital — which probably means that you should invest in AI stocks.

Also — if you're really young, let's say 18, 20, 22, before you're 30 — you don't, you're not married, you don't have kids, you don't have real responsibilities. There's no particular reason that you shouldn't probably be at least a little bit leveraged.

This is not financial advice for legal purposes. But one example I like to give: consider how much the average college kid has in savings by the end of their senior year — probably not that much, few hundred, few thousand. Then consider how much they will have after working a job for a few years — significantly more. As your career progresses and your human capital compounds, you're just going to make exponentially more. Which means that, especially super early on, most people are extremely underallocated into capital. Because you shouldn't really just invest how much money you have right now. You should in some sense invest how much money you're ever going to have.

This example is made really clear in trading, where kids going into trading get an offer between $600K to $1M a year. They're starting off with a portfolio of $50K to $100K from internship money. By the end of the year, they're guaranteed to at least 4x–5x that. There's no reason why they should not be 3 to 4x leveraged.

On the older side

I'm personally not a massive AI doomer. If you look at employment data — there's a recent article from the Economist — AI seems to mostly be creating jobs. We're not having massive unemployment right now even though AI adoption is increasing.

It seems like the best thing to do is to learn to use this technology. If you're working in a company that's already embracing AI, use more AI in your workflows, automate more of what you're doing. If you're in a company or a position where you feel you're not able to use AI or grow along with the technology — it's never been easier to start a business.

On Twitter people are calling it the age of the idea guy. Because if you have a good idea, and it truly is a good idea, you could get the AI to just build an app, submit it to the app store, get it past review. And I think if anything, AI is showing that most people's ideas are just not that good. There is nothing stopping anyone from building anything that is merely software, and yet most people don't actually seem to be building great software — which probably suggests we have to work on the idea section.

十一、护城河 vs 增长：一个反直觉的选择

Q: Do you think the optimal way to take risk today is in tackling extremely difficult problems where you can build an actual moat?

One of the Stripe founders — I think it was John — said that the ideas one should work on today are the ones that are extremely difficult.

I think we have to get a little bit deeper. Generally people should solve hard problems. But is everyone going to be able to solve hard problems?

提问者自述

Something I think about a lot is how to build a moat around one skill set. The reason I focus on a podcast is because I know there's a moat around brand. There's a moat around connections. Intellectually I'm also building a moat around myself where I'm learning from every guest. That is my personal bet, and then I'm long AI in my portfolio.

Many people today do not really have strong moats around their skill sets. What is the optimal way to play that hand without the moat around one skill set?

Okay, that puts a lot of things in context. That probably should change a lot of the ways I answer.

Moat vs Growth：一个不同的框架

The way I actually see the whole situation is maybe a little bit less around moat and a little bit more around growth. Moats are useful — or not just useful, they're necessary — in a competitive environment, and they become more important if the environment is closer towards something that's like a zero-sum game.

Zero-sum industries: manufacturing, restaurants. Restaurants are actually a really good example. People only need a certain number of meals a day. Restaurants highly competitive, very difficult to get a moat. If you can have some social prestige around your restaurant, it's great. That's very important, but it's very hard.

Versus on the other side, if you're in a fast-growing industry — again like AI — look at a company like Cursor. Did it have a moat? Not really. But I forgot which VC partner it was that said, "Yeah, we kind of thought this company had no moat, but it was just growing at such a ridiculously high rate that we're going to do like pass on your round."

Potentially it's going to be the same thing with AI — at least in the bull case — where moat is a secondary consideration to opportunity and growth. It could very well be the case (and probably would be the case for the majority of people) that there isn't going to be a very concrete moat around any skill set — because it's impossible for everyone to have a moat, by symmetry. But because of how fast and how much leverage AI gives people, the quality of life, income, and experience can still increase because of growth. Competition is less of a concern.

人性化的护城河

Otherwise we're looking at trying to guess at things which AI fundamentally cannot take — which if you believe that it is truly a sort of general intelligence, if you can scale intelligence you can scale anything — has to be things which are uniquely human. As you've talked about, probably boils down to relationships and brand.

A lot of times people don't want to put themselves out there on a platform like LinkedIn or Twitter and basically make themselves more recognizable, have a stronger personal brand. This is probably a mistake because it's not a super high-effort thing, but it is very helpful.

案例：Quant Recruiting

One example again is quant recruiting. Most people just apply to jobs, which is not the right way. You're not taking advantage of potential connection moats and personal brand moats. I was actually pretty strategic when it came to trading recruiting back in college. I was part of the exec of our quant trading club, so I was responsible for outreaching to a lot of these firms and helping them host events. That means I would personally know the recruiter from most of these firms.

When it came to application season, I was sending my application but also sending an email — "Hey, great talking to you at this event, yada yada yada, I just applied to your firm, would love it if we can set up a first round interview." I wouldn't say 100%, but 95% of them responded, and I did manage to get first round interviews at almost all the trading firms I applied to as a result. This requires a little bit more planning, higher agency, but it's very high value.

In the age of AI it's very easy to just send a resume out there. So relationships, brand — and a lot of times they're not built in the most obvious places. You have to think about what the particular situation allows.

十二、离开 IMC 创办 Freeport 的心路历程

Q: What was the moment while you were at IMC where you decided to leave and start a perps exchange?

If I had to pin it down, probably when we got YC — kind of have to make a decision there. But it was probably a slower thing. When I was in college, I was the head of our trading club. I was also the president of my fraternity AI for two years. Both of these positions I took pretty seriously — growing a club or leading a fraternity was very exciting for me. Also a very high-agency position.

Going from that to working for a very large corporation was a shift. There was basically an itch. An itch to do more, which working at a job did not really satisfy. I want to be very careful — I'm not trying to say anything bad about IMC. I actually really enjoyed the job itself, the people were great. But there was an itch inherent to working for another company that was not being scratched.

During this time, because of trading restrictions you have as a trader, I started getting more involved in perps exchanges and started talking with a lot of other trading friends. Which is this issue — how do I in some sense legally bypass my trading restrictions? When I describe what I do right now, people are like — "perps exchanges on blockchain sounds really sketchy." The actual jurisprudence is: there's literally no regulation. It's neither legal nor illegal, it's a gray area. There are no laws against it. In general, in the US, firms do not monitor this.

A lot of my friends were also interested in this. So I was like, hey, it seems like there is a market here. Let me have a conversation with my co-founder. We talked about this for multiple months, applied to YC, got it, had to make a decision within 24 hours. And at that point, you kind of have to just go for it.

Freeport 的差异化

Q: I've heard of a million perps exchanges. What is differentiated about Freeport?

Instead of just being a place for people to trade and make their own decisions on what to trade, we want to specialize in a particular way of trading — which in our case is event-driven. If you're looking at trading around specific earnings, specific narratives, macro events, tweets — these are things that we integrate into our app to assist you with that trading.

The two biggest things:

  1. Access to different assets. One of our taglines is "buy OpenAI and Anthropic before the IPO."
  2. Tradable Twitter feed. Twitter, podcasts, Substacks, Reddit — whatever information sources you're already looking at, we can pull directly, have an AI agent evaluate whether this thing is potentially useful for whatever narrative you want to trade, and then send you notification or put it on your feed.

This workflow is inspired by our experience at a trading firm, since a lot of what our analysts did was track a lot of these sources and give us what's relevant in a timely and concise way.

交易台工作流如何被 AI 复制

Q: Can you break down that agentic workflow?

At a trading firm, there is a defined, curated list of data sources that you feel is relevant. A lot of times before the day, overnight events happen — so you go into a meeting or send an email to give traders a briefing on what you think is going to happen during the day. Throughout the day as events are happening, you may shout to traders, send more emails, ping them — communicate additional context that people need.

If someone is running a book, what are things they need to know, and you just get it to them. The problem with the trader themselves doing this is there's so much trash out there. Just going through all this information — both curating and aggregating and processing into some sort of model or thesis — is itself an incredibly value-additive job.

AI in some sense can replicate that workflow. Maybe not to the extent that a trading firm would need, but much better than what a lot of retail users are already getting.

For our AI: you log in, we ask what you're interested in, what markets you trade. You select your markets, we give you a default feed pulling from authoritative sources we have curated. You can manually add more sources. Data comes in — breaking news, Twitter, podcast — and we first do a classifier: is this something we need to process quickly, or slowly?

  • Fast: news like US bombing Iran, or CPI — goes through a really fast inference model. Between it coming out and being a notification on your phone is less than a second.
  • Slow: a Katrini Substack about the AI photonic supply chain — gets processed by a larger reasoning model that breaks it down into 7–8 pieces over 3–4 minutes, then gets put under your feed.

That's the rough architecture of what we're building.

用户画像

Q: Do the people who trade on Freeport tend to be traders at top trading firms?

Right now we have a little bit of everything. Very strong product market fit with financial professionals who want to move part of their money into a no-KYC environment where they have a little more privacy, as well as people who just want the leverage that perps provide and the access to both pre-IPO and international assets.

The typical average person probably doesn't have a super strong desire to buy futures on Anthropic pre-IPO or Chinese frontier AI labs or Chinese robotics labs, unless they're actually following this. Conditional on actually following this, they probably want an AI to also partially follow it for them. That is one group.

There's another group where they're in it more for the leverage and less for the access and information. We're happy to provide to both.

十三、基础模型交易能力评估

Q: How good are these models currently for trading?

The foundational models themselves are probably good enough to trade in a way that beats the average retail trader. There is a plausible argument that foundation models are good enough to beat the S&P 500 on a risk-adjusted basis.

However, the only way you can do it is probably with very well-designed harnesses around those foundational models, and the design of those harnesses is pretty non-trivial. I do not think I can personally currently build a harness — let's say just by myself — in a few months, that leverages a frontier foundational model to reliably beat the market on a risk-adjusted basis. With a team, I'm much more confident I can.

But obviously if you look at a professional trading firm that has all the resources — they're good enough.

十四、Perp DEX 的赛道格局

Q: Where do you see the perp landscape going?

On the pure exchange side, liquidity is itself a moat. If everyone trades on one exchange, other people would want to trade on that exchange. Liquidity is also fungible — a particular Nvidia perp is not too different from another Nvidia perp, especially if it's decentralized and covering the same jurisdictions.

为什么传统交易所是碎片化的？

  1. Jurisdiction: a Brazilian exchange and a US exchange are fundamentally different things. If they are all on some permissionless blockchain, that reason for fragmentation disappears.
  2. Market structure: in the US we have Regulation NMS — the trade-through rule — which says when a broker takes an order and routes it to a market maker, they need to trade and get the order at NBBO or better. A subtle implication: if you build an exchange in the country, market makers have to connect to it in order to comply.

We don't have these regulatory requirements on the perp exchange landscape. In the absence of jurisdictional fragmentation and Reg NMS-style fragmentation, my personal thought is liquidity probably aggregates among a few big players — let's say less than 10, maybe 3 to 5.

Broker / Aggregator 层的分化

On the broker side — in the US, brokers exist partially because of regulation, because people cannot connect themselves to exchanges directly. But the actual economic function of brokers is partially distribution. Someone who uses Robinhood is very different from someone who uses IBKR, is very different from someone who uses Schwab, is somewhat different from Fidelity or E*Trade. Each broker appeals to a specific type of trader.

When it comes to aggregators and perp frontends — which is what we're building — I do believe there is going to be much more space for different types of consumers depending on the way they want to trade. Someone who wants to be self-directed, someone who wants to invest long-term, is very different from someone who wants to copy-trade politicians and hedge funds, is very different from someone who wants to trade the news and events. That space fundamentally would be fragmented. It's very difficult to build a $10 trillion business as a result, but you can have many more multi-billion dollar businesses.

CEX vs DEX & 监管的二元赌注

Q: Who do you currently think those top players are going to be?

For perps, centralized exchanges are still dominating the volumes. Binance and centralized exchanges probably do 70–80% of volume right now. Decentralized exchanges like Variational, Hyperliquid, Lighter are the minority.

This is very hard to estimate because it's extremely binary. The degree to which decentralized exchanges will expand is largely going to be dependent on regulation. Right now there's no rulemaking around any of this. If the SEC rules that these things are in fact legal and should be accorded some innovation exemption, they're going to explode — probably overtake centralized exchanges on volume just because of ease of access, interoperability. On the other hand, if the SEC rules that they should not qualify — that Hyperliquid should not be made legal in the US — they probably will not gain mainstream adoption within the near future.

Conditional on the bull case for decentralized exchanges, the two biggest ones — Hyperliquid and Lighter — both have pretty good chances of getting really really big. The thesis for Hyperliquid is that it is very open, permissionless, anyone can build on it. We route a lot of our flow to Hyperliquid — it's just a good product. The thesis for Lighter is the partnership with Robinhood — Robinhood has insane distribution, their CEO is a generational founder.

十五、AI 交易的具体择股与叙事

Q: Are there any parts of the stack you're overweight?

The parts of the stack I'm overweight change over time. To be perfectly honest, it's mostly going to be from conversations I have with semiconductor traders and analysts who still work at trading firms and are my friends. Not going to name the firms for obvious reasons.

I do talk with semi-traders at like five to six different firms who have more informed opinions on this than I do. I just try to grab dinner with people and be like, "All right boys, what's the newest thing we should put more money into." It does change over time.

There is some correlation between what trading firms think is good versus what Twitter thinks is good. One of my friends' sayings is: "All the alpha that's left on narratives is on Twitter and Substack." So there is a chance they also don't know what the hell they're talking about and they're just following Twitter.

There are some folks on Substack — for example one is like "Irrational Analysis" I think — who made a lot of money, but during the drawdown went to the same level as SMH. Now it's beating SMH, the semiconductor index.

Trading vs Investing

Investing is like — cuz this is outside the realm of high-Sharpe trading, closer to the realm of investing. Investing and trading are fundamentally very different things:

  • Trading: buy cheap, sell expensive, hedge away risk (or don't hedge away risk if it's too negative EV to hedge). When you diversify across strategies you're seeing at least 2–3 Sharpe on the hedge fund side, double-digit Sharpe on the trading firm side — you know what you're doing is working.
  • Investing: fundamentally you're making a statement — "I'm going to give these guys money and they're able to turn that money into more money at some compounded rate over the next 10 years." Anything in between the 10 years is purely sentiment. You could be very right about thesis but be exposed to path dependency. A lot of it is driven by sentiment, not actually driven by fundamentals. Over the long run fundamentals do matter, but you're trying to make a multi-year bet and it's very low signal.

You can trust that the people you're talking to are smart. You can trust that they're following the right information sources. You can be like, "Okay, this seems to be a better guess than my baseline of S&P 500 allocation."

当下的具体叙事

Q: What are they talking about right now?

  • Leopold is back right now, as of the time of recording. People are trying to think about how much money he has raised, how much money he potentially is going to raise, and just the pure mechanical trade of "if Leopold keeps buying, how much higher can the market go."
  • Connectivity — additional bullishness.
  • Momentum vs memory — especially Korean memory, SK Hynix and Samsung. Not sure how big of a deal it is now, but at least two weeks ago there were concerns about general governance in South Korea. On one hand Samsung, SK Hynix are making a lot of money. On the other hand, Korea is kind of an oligarchy where a lot of times the Hynix chairman can find ways to divert profits from Hynix to companies he holds more shares of. It's not immediately clear how much of the profit actually goes to shareholders. Samsung paid out large bonuses to their employees — there may be surprise interventions from the country for purposes of controlling inequality. Recent thing has been more along the optics and connectivity side, and slightly less allocation towards the memory side.

十六、信息传播时序：Conversation → Twitter → Bloomberg

Q: How do you filter media narratives into making bets?

Two distinct answers — how we think about narratives (informed by trading experience) vs how to risk-manage personal portfolio.

On the narrative side, when we talk about media like Bloomberg or Wall Street Journal — these probably lag Twitter by at least 1 to 3 days. By the time it's on Bloomberg, Economist, WSJ, it's already been on Twitter for over 48 hours typically.

Then there's the question of how you get access to information on the right accounts on Twitter. That is partially a skill and taste issue. Do you know what these people actually do? What's their background? If you're following the right AI researchers, do you know if they're legit? From these things you can guess two things:

  1. Whether what they're saying is true and should inform your trading.
  2. Whether what they are saying is going to become popular and is actually going to move prices.

Because markets are a Keynesian beauty contest. It matters eventually what is actually true, but it also matters what other people think is going to be true. Seeing a tweet and deciding whether it's going to become a bigger narrative — that requires a lot of experience and judgment. You can try to design algorithms to guess what makes a tweet more likely (or a group of tweets, a small narrative) to become a bigger narrative. But it's not easy.

更早的层级：对话

Can we get information before they even go on Twitter? Some funds probably can. IMC at least when I was there was at the layer of information where it would get it when it's on Twitter or on some formal paid newswire. But there are friends I've talked to at funds where they're very well connected with people in the industry. By the time someone has a thought, a lot of times they may be posting on Twitter before they even talk about it with friends — but it's also the case that a lot of times people talk with friends before they post on Twitter.

For our friends at more well-connected funds and semi-analysts at well-connected places, a lot of times you can get narratives at the conversation level days or weeks before they surface on Twitter at a large scale.

This is one of the reasons people potentially pay for a service like Katrini or Semi Analysis — partially for the research, but also partially for the access. This is also why I personally think Situational Awareness potentially does have edge in addition to having a lot of levered beta. Both Leopold and his wife are very well-connected people in Silicon Valley. If you look at some of the stocks they were buying — a lot of these Bitcoin miners-turned-data centers. These stocks would pump 10, 20, 30% on data center announcements of getting contracts. Who else to better guesstimate what Bitcoin miners-turned-data centers are going to get AI contracts than some of the most well-connected people in Silicon Valley? It doesn't even need to be insider trading — it merely needs to be understanding how these other executives who sign these contracts actually think.

Summary: - Conversation stage: lots of edge through lived experience - Twitter: some edge still - Bloomberg: probably almost no edge at all

DeepSeek 案例复盘

Going back to the DeepSeek incident — that thing was on CNBC Friday, but it was on Chinese media multiple days before. If you bought puts on Nvidia over the weekend, on Monday open stock down 17%, you would have made an insane amount of money. So the market is not that efficient, but it is reasonably efficient.

十七、个人风险敞口：亏掉一辆法拉利

Q: On personal risk sizing?

I don't know if I'm qualified to talk about this because I don't think I risk-manage my own portfolio very well.

I think I ran up — this is going to sound so degenerate — but like from bottom to peak I ran up like 470%, and then had like a 70% drawdown. Now we're like maybe a 60% drawdown, which is still fine. But this makes me feel like I'm not qualified to talk about risk management, so I'm going to refrain.

That's crazy.

Oh, no. It's because you can kind of do the math — how much time I've worked in trading, how much leverage I was probably on. I was texting a friend the day after June 22nd when there was the first mega drawdown. I was like, "Bro, I'm literally down an entire Ferrari today."

交易员群体的风险偏好

Q: Would you say a lot of your trader friends size like degenerates in their personal portfolio?

Multiple layers. In general, most people at trading firms act in a more responsible way. I'm a little self-selective when it comes to my friends — conditional on being my friend, they are more likely to be a little bit degenerate. Within my close friend group, I would say I'm top 20% instead of being top 10% — like risk-on, tolerance to risk and volatility.

Conditional on wanting to put your money on a crypto perp DEX, you're probably more tolerant to risk. Because these things — in theory they're both more safe and less safe:

  • Less safe: they're not insured. If they are hacked, there's no way to get your money back.
  • More safe: the government cannot take your money away from you on these things.

Their biggest use is to trade hard-to-access assets like pre-IPO stuff or country stocks from other countries, on leverage, 24/7 including weekends. Given that, conditional on having money on these exchanges, the people are a little bit more risk-tolerant.

I've seen one of our own users run up 70k to a million dollars, and then run it back down to zero in July. He texted me: "I think I'm going to take a break from perps." He has a screenshot at $1M though, so it's all good.

But we also have responsible people who longed some Anthropic and OpenAI at a responsible 2 to 3x leverage and is now up 400–500%. I want to make sure we don't make the thing sound too much like it's gambling — there is a proper investment use case.

十八、"AI 是不是泡沫" —— 更精细的回答

Q: Old-style fund managers say AI is a bubble. What would your response be?

It will really depend on what they mean by a bubble. The most typical comparison is the dotcom bubble. During the dotcom bubble, there were companies which were highly overvalued — something like Cisco or Enron. There are probably companies in the AI supply chain right now which are — I wouldn't say similar values of overvaluation, but let's say trading above 100% above what their fair value should be.

Then you have cases like Meta or Amazon or Google, where if you bought it at the top of the dotcom bubble and held for the next 20 years, your compounded rate of returns would have been higher than the index at the bottom of the dotcom bubble buying the bottom. Basically you would have excess compounded returns anyways — which suggests the stocks were returning above the equity risk premium over the long run. So the question is: is Google at the top of the dotcom bubble — was Google in a bubble — considering if you bought it over the next 20 years you would have had excess returns?

That brings us to the idea of path. When I say AI is not a bubble, I mean I do believe these companies over the long run will in aggregate generate compounded returns above normal equity risk premium. It is not a statement about path. If you think a company is fairly valued, it is still technically possible for it to experience a 50, 60, 70% drawdown because of sentiment. So — not a bubble, but I don't want to make statements about path.

那你为什么这么下注？

Q: You don't want to make statements about path. Why are you sizing your portfolio the way you're sizing it?

Because I feel the AGI deep inside.

A lot of times we don't act in exactly rational ways, and my leverage is probably a little bit high. But here's the question — let's say you're on the ramp-up to the dotcom bubble, what would have been the correct sizing at the time? This is not immediately clear.

A 2x leverage ETF on a ramp-up to the dotcom bubble and then ramping down, over the next 20 years on QQQ — 2xQ's from 1990 to now returns more than 1xQ's from 1990 to now, even though 2xQ had a significantly higher drawdown during the dotcom bubble.

If the thesis is about long-term compounded rate of growth, and you apply similar logic to the Kelly criterion, I do believe long-run optimal leverage over the entire market is something closer to 2.25. Now add my posterior about how bullish I am on AI — it's not absolutely unreasonable to say that maybe the a posteriori long-run estimated optimal leverage on AI stocks is closer to something like 2x leverage (which is what I have), than something like 1x leverage — or something like 6x leverage if you're only buying the S&P, since maybe 60% of the S&P is AI.

That's the more theoretical answer — you're optimizing for compounded rate of growth. Yes, you may have larger drawdowns. Yes, you may need to sell on the way down and buy on the way up. But over the long run, this is not unreasonable for this to be optimal, even though I'm not sure if it is.

十九、AI 与地缘：中美之外的世界会怎样？

Q: With AI and robotics — the only two nations that are competitive are the US and China. What happens to the rest of the world?

It is very intuitive to take the doomer take — quality of life decreasing, yada yada. But that's actually not my personal take.

The people who have doomer takes on emerging markets' reaction to AI are the same people who have doomer takes on the average American impacted by AI. If you are bearish on AI impact on average American, you're probably also bearish on impact on the rest of the world.

But if we take a step back — what AI allows us to do is create more with less. So the general amount of things you can do is expanding. Then there's the question of how it's shared between people.

比较优势原理

Here's where it makes sense to bring in concepts like comparative advantage. Let's take the extreme case — ASI can do everything that's an intellectual task better than a human can. Is there any use for humans? From an economic perspective the answer is actually yes, because of comparative advantage.

A few decades ago the United States basically was able to do everything better than China — probably including manufacturing. And yet, as a result of comparative advantage, trade makes both nations better off. As a consequence, over the last few decades China was able to lift about 800 million people out of absolute poverty, which is probably one of the best things from a utilitarian perspective that has happened to the world in the course of human history.

My view on AI is actually the same thing. Even in the ultra-bullish ASI case, it should actually in fact be ultra-bullish to people as well. Because if you believe people have comparative advantage — which even if they don't have absolute advantage, mathematically they must have comparative advantage — this will increase everyone's ability to produce; everyone will be able to have more resources.

Similarly, if we live in an international system that is open to trade and open to letting the principle of comparative advantage work, somehow through these mathematically conserved quantities, emerging markets will also enjoy greater standards of living, greater standards of development.

Within the realm of possibility — that we do not live under an international system that is open to trade, especially seeing how recent US and Chinese politics has been leaning. But if we choose to make the world go in a good direction, it's not inevitable that it should be bad.

二十、给年轻人的最后一句话：Post-Economic 与冒险

Q: Final question — what should be a young person's mindset for taking risk today?

Very general question. Okay — I've actually personally been reflecting on this a little bit, because a lot of times we do distribution events at universities and people ask me somewhat similar questions.

Reflecting on my past experience — one of the reasons I was able to take large amounts of risk is because I do come from a relatively privileged and financially comfortable background. I don't have student loans. I'm not really concerned about living or feeding myself, basically ever — that basically never crosses my mind. So it makes sense for me to be like, hey, I want to be building in an area I'm passionate about and building a great company.

But it's also the case that not all of our listeners and just people in the world have that luxury. Which makes it really difficult for me to answer.

一个反直觉的建议

I think a lot of the people we're surrounded with actually should probably be taking more risks — because in some sense they are living in this sort of post-economic situation where, if you really think about it, they should not be concerned about basic necessities. Even in worst case, their families probably will be able to take care of them.

A lot of friends who work in consulting, investment banking — I'm like, "Yo, you guys should be taking more risks. You're basically post-economic. What are you doing?"

But I don't know how responsible it would be for me to recommend risk-taking for someone for whom the risk is more real and the downside is more real. It's a very difficult question for me to answer.

No, that's completely fine. Thank you very much for coming on the podcast. That was awesome.

Cool. Thank you.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的洞察：他其实在贩卖"座位"，而不是"技能"
Leohan 全场最诚实、也最容易被忽略的一句话是——**"座位本身就是极高杠杆的"**。他把自己在 IMC 的工作类比为 Google CEO 的位置：一个人能创造多少价值，先取决于他坐在什么样的信息节点上。这句话表面是谦逊，实际上是一个残酷的结构性洞察：
**在期权做市这个行业，"聪明"是被稀缺的信息拓扑放大出来的幻觉。** 全美期权流量的 80-90% 被前五大做市商吃掉——这意味着地球上真正能"看见市场"的人可能只有几十个。他离开这个座位之后，坦承自己"预测能力并不比别人强"。这几乎是在暗示：华尔街大部分神话的本质，是**信息位次的租金**，而不是认知能力的溢价。
而他现在做的 Freeport，本质上是在**试图为散户搭建一个廉价版的"座位"**——把交易台上分析师筛信息的工作流，用 AI agent 复制给普通人。这是他整段叙事里最漂亮的商业闭环：**卖掉了自己曾经拥有过的信息不对称，再把稀释后的版本零售给市场。**
---

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、真正令人意外的观察：Apple 选硬体 CEO，不是"保守"，而是一次极其精准的"战场识别"

大多数评论都在追问"为什么不是 AI 专家当 CEO？"——这个问法本身就掉进了硬件时代的旧框架。真正的答案藏在 Apple 的组织重组里：AI 交给 Amar Subramanya，芯片和硬件全交给 Johnny Srouji，John Ternus 只坐 CEO。这三个人的分工暴露了 Apple 对未来十年的赌注：

它不打算成为"最聪明的大脑"，而是要成为大脑与世界之间唯一的那把钥匙。

这跟 Visa 的策略惊人相似——Visa 从不放贷、不发卡、不吸储，却在每一笔交易里抽成，因为它掌握的是"清算通道"。Apple 也一样：让 Google、OpenAI 去烧钱训练模型，让 Samsung 去做折叠屏——但 iPhone 里那个能"打开抽屉、翻你邮件、把航班加进日历"的执行层权限，只有 Apple 有钥匙。AI 模型是租客，可以随时换；iOS 是房东，永远收租。 一个硬件 CEO 恰好是这套哲学的最好代言人。

二、跨领域连接：Apple 的三代 CEO 其实是"企业约束理论"的完美案例

这是一个几乎没人从这个角度看的模式——Apple 的 CEO 更替，暴露了它在不同时代对"瓶颈资源"的判断：

时代 CEO 出身 Apple 认为的核心约束
2000s Jobs（产品美学家） 想象力与产品定义
2010s Cook（供应链专家） 规模化与全球物流
2020s Ternus（硬件工程师） 多技术栈的物理整合

这背后是高德拉特《约束理论》的教科书演绎——一家公司的最高领导者，永远反映它相信"下一个瓶颈在哪里"。选 Ternus 这个决定本身，就是 Apple 在公开宣布：未来十年的战场不是"谁的模型更聪明"，而是"谁能把 AI、芯片、传感器、电池、隐私边界，塞进一个能戴在脸上或握在手里的物件里"。这跟半导体行业选 CEO 的逻辑一模一样——Intel 长期由工程师主政，因为它相信瓶颈是工艺；一旦选了金融背景 CEO（如 Krzanich 之后），就是宣告"我们放弃工艺赛跑了"。

三、最反直觉的洞察：Apple 的"AI 落后"，可能是它二十年来最聪明的一次"故意落后"

这一点几乎所有分析师都没讲透。回头看 Apple 的历史，你会发现一个惊人的模式：它从来不是"第一个"，它是"最后一个"：

  • MP3 播放器？Apple 是第五代玩家，才推出 iPod
  • 智能手机？黑莓、诺基亚、Palm 早已在做，Apple 是 2007 年才进场
  • 平板电脑？微软的 Tablet PC 早了七八年
  • 无线耳机？Bluetooth 耳机遍地都是，Apple 才出 AirPods
  • 折叠屏？——你看，剧本又来了

Apple 一贯的策略是：让别人烧钱把市场教育好、把技术验证成熟、把用户预期定型，然后 Apple 用最好的整合体验做最后一击。 从这个视角看，"Apple 在生成式 AI 上落后"根本不是失误，而是默认剧本。Samsung 花了 5 年把折叠屏教育到 mature，Apple 直接接手；OpenAI 和 Google 正在替 Apple 教育用户"什么是 AI 助手"，等这批用户习惯了、模型成本降了、幻觉率控制住了，Apple 再用系统级整合收割。

这里藏着一个跨领域连接生物学的观察：这是典型的"K-选择"生存策略——不追求繁殖速度（快速迭代模型），而追求单个后代的存活率（把每一个功能磨到能在 10 亿部设备上稳定运行）。生成式 AI 现在还在"R-选择"阶段（快速繁殖、大量试错、高死亡率）。Apple 在等这个物种进化到 K 阶段。

但请注意—— 这次赌注有一个前所未有的风险：如果 AI 助手真的取代了"打开 App"这个动作，那么 Apple 引以为傲的"入口控制"就会像柯达手里的胶卷技术一样，突然从护城河变成沉没成本。硬件 CEO 能守住"最后一公里"，但守不住"用户根本不再走过来"这件事。这才是 Ternus 上任真正要回答的问题。

📝 转录文本

开场：Apple 的 AI 困境与令人意外的 CEO 选择

Apple and Apple have been criticized for their bad performance in the past two years. Apple Intelligence jumped in, Siri was left behind. The market kept asking Apple, where is your AI?

Apple has now switched to CEO. In theory, if the biggest problem for a company is AI, you might think that it will find a software engineer or AI expert to take over CEO. But Apple chose John Ternes, a hard-core engineer who has been doing it for 25 years. Why?

And the more strange thing is that the more expensive iPhones are, the first folding iPhone Duo is nearly $2,000 a piece. Even the most important folding screen is still bought from Samsung. Apple's folding screen is probably worth $250 for Samsung. It's super expensive. Samsung has probably taken a three-year exclusive contract.

Apple's AI is not the priority. Folding phones are also many years later than Samsung.

♪ World going wild ♪ ♪ She's the queen of the game ♪

Hi, I'm Bonnie.

频道福利环节

If you are recently paying attention to Apple's stock, or ready to change to the new Apple 18 Pro, you must take a look at the information column, because there are opportunities to get it for free directly.

John Ternus 的自述与背景

When I first got to Apple, it was my second job out of college. And the first time I walked through those doors, it was exhilarating and intimidating all at once. To be honest, I wasn't sure I belonged there. The people I met were so smart and so confident, and they knew so much more than me. But I'll always be grateful that I wasn't afraid to ask for help when I needed it. Because being around people that care that deeply, it won't just make you want to stretch your limits and see how far you can go. But they're also the best people to help you understand how to get there.

He was a mechanical engineer. He was the highest executive of hardware engineering before. For example, iPhones, iPads, Macs, Apple Watches, AirPods, almost all of our familiar Apple products are within his scope.

Always assume you're as smart as anyone else in the room. But never assume that you know as much as they do.

Apple 现况：一台超级赚钱机器

What kind of company is Apple now? Let's take a look at the numbers.

When Tim Cook took over in 2011, Apple's market value was about $3.5 billion. Now it's over $4 trillion. In 2025, Apple's revenue was over $4,160 billion, and its net profit was over $1,120 billion. The income of the service alone is $1092 billion. This number is much more than the income of Mac, iPad, Apple Watch, AirPods and other accessories.

So Steve Jobs left behind a bunch of very successful innovative products. In the 15 years after Tim Cook took over, Apple has become a famous and influential, ruthless money-making machine. Very good at making money.

Just think about the money I spent on Apple in recent years. I changed my new phone every year. I changed my computer every year. AirPods, iPad, all kinds of accessories. If you don't have them, you may spend hundreds of thousands of Taiwan dollars on them alone. It's very exaggerated.

而且妳看在看家人，我媽沒事就左邊一台 iPad，右邊一台 iPad，然後中間還在滑手機，還帶著 AirPods。It's crazy man。

Anyway，Tim Cook 他接手了蘋果之後呢，把這個供應鏈做到了極致，把 iPhone 賣到全球，然後利用這個龐大的 iPhone 用戶，繼續賣 App Store、繼續賣 iCloud、Apple Music、AppleCare、各種的訂閱跟服務。

時間快轉到現在，John Ternes 他接手了蘋果呢，財務狀況你就知道啦，非常非常好嘛，很會賺錢。但不可能一切都只有美好的事情嘛。John 他也有很大的麻煩要解決，也就是下一個十年，Apple 他到底要靠著什麼樣的創新啊？感覺已經很久沒有看到那種讓人家覺得 WOW 的創新了。

挫败一：Apple Car 十年烧钱记

Do you remember Apple Car? Apple launched a secret project in 2014 called Project Titan. The craziest version even wanted to make a car without steering wheel and pedal. It's completely automatic. They also made a Volkswagen, an old bread truck. The employees called it Bread Loaf.

This project took about 10 years. It cost about $1 billion per year. There were 2,000 people who participated. Their goal was to shrink down from the original self-driving car to the more ordinary self-driving electric car. The time of listing was repeated and finally killed it in 2024.

Apple cut off the whole plan. For decades, hundreds of billions of dollars, the last Apple car was not sold. The last plan to sell the car was cancelled.

挫败二：Vision Pro 的雷声大雨点小

Next, let's look at Vision Pro. Apple spent at least 7 years to develop this. Finally, they made a headband device that costs $3499 and needs to be connected to an external battery.

When it was released, everyone talked about it and it was very popular. But it soon shrunk production. Later, even the cheaper version of the next generation was suspended. All resources were converted to AI smart glasses.

Vision Pro has spent a lot of money and resources, but it hasn't become a mainstream product.

I guarantee you that the greatest source of pride that you feel when you're looking back, it won't be about the specific projects or products or technologies themselves. It'll be the journey of building them and the effort and collaboration that it took to make it all happen.

AI 时代的最大问题：入口之争

現在呢 Apple 面臨最大的問題就是生成式 AI 正在改變我們使用科技的入口。以前我們就打開手機打開 App，未來可能是直接跟 ChatGPT、跟 Gemini 說你要完成什麼，讓 AI 直接幫你做。

這個對 Apple——因為 iPhone 最值錢的地方之一，就是它一直掌握著這個入口。那偏偏 AI 爆發的第一波 Apple 是明顯的落後了。

所以我們又繞回原本最開始提出的問題，就是 Apple 明明知道 AI 就是最大的戰場，為什麼還是選了一個硬體工程師來當 CEO 呢？

John Ternus 是什么样的人？

John Ternes has been at Apple for 25 years. Most of his time is behind the product. He calls it mechanical engineering. Before entering Apple, he really did VR headband devices.

In 2001, he joined Apple's product design team. It started with computer screens. Later, he did the first generation of iPads, AirPods, iPhones, Macs, Apple Watch. In 2013, he became the vice president of hardware engineering. In 2021, he officially became Apple's top hardware manager.

Before he became CEO, Apple's hardware products, which are almost all the hard-to-make products, were all within his management range.

工作风格：真正的工程师

He worked in a very different way from Tim Cook. He described John as a "real engineer" with his colleagues. When he was developing the product meeting, he would focus on the small technical details. Tim Cook was more concerned about supply chain, strategy and finance. John would look at the product every day and ask how it was made and why it was made like this. What would happen when the user got it?

John 过去做对的事：iPad、Apple Car、Vision Pro 的判断

Let's take a look at what he had done before.

第一个是 iPad。 John started to participate in iPad from the first generation. At that time, iPad was basically the same as the iPhone software. It's just like the magnifier is on the iPad. 它覺得這樣根本沒有把大螢幕跟更強的硬體用出來，所以一直想要推動 Apple 幫 iPad 特別做自己的作業系統，慢慢才發展成今天的 iPadOS。

剛剛講的 Apple Car——John 他一直是保持一個很懷疑的態度，他覺得這計畫很燒錢，還會把最好的工程師從這種核心產品 iPhone、Mac 抽走。

Vision Pro 他的想法也是很保留的，因為他年輕的時候就做過 VR 的頭戴式裝置，知道這種產品雖然說好像很厲害，但是最後還是要回答很現實的問題，也就是每天到底有多少人願意把這個東西戴在頭上。

也曾做错的判断

John 他當然也不是每一次的判斷都對。像以前的 MacBook Pro 最上面有一排實體的按鍵換成 Touch Bar，John was one of the main supporters of that design. But many users didn't like it. So Apple canceled it later.

And the old, controversial "Dial-Sy" keyboard. In order to make the pen more thin, the keyboard was easily broken. Finally, Apple not only completely replaced the previous design, but also paid $50 million in settlement money for this problem.

So John also made a wrong product judgment. Oh, of course, 還有有沒有人真的會用它。

关键转型：Mac 从 Intel 到 Apple Silicon

Apple 過去十幾年最成功的一次技術轉型呢是 Mac 從 Intel 全面換成了 Apple Silicon。這一件事情呢，John Ternus 剛好又是最核心的人物之一。

Apple 的故事裡面還有另外一個非常重要的人叫做 Johnny Srouji。

Johnny Srouji joined Apple in 2008. His first mission was to develop the A4, the first system chip designed by Apple.

What's this? Is this important?

It's important because Mac used Intel chips. Apple had to work with Intel's product progress and performance. No matter how good the software design is, hardware can be installed anywhere, it's up to others.

So Apple spent many years preparing its own Mac chips. John Ternes was in charge of the hardware engineering of Mac at the time. Johnny Srouji was in charge of the chip. The software team made MacOS work with the new architecture.

In 2020, Apple officially announced that Mac would give up Intel and turn back to Apple Silicon. The result is that the M1 Mac of the first batch came out with a huge improvement in performance and the power consumption has decreased. MacBook can run faster and the battery can be used longer.

So this has become Apple's most successful technological transformation in recent years.

John 与 Johnny 的黄金搭档，与最新人事布局

你看，John and Johnny have joined forces and have proven themselves capable of doing great things.

This year, while John is the CEO, Apple has promoted Johnny to a position that he didn't have before, which is the Chief Hardware Officer. 硬體掌，同時把 John 原本管的這個整個硬體工程的部門呢，現在也一起交給 Johnny。

所以現在 Johnny 底下呢，同時要管晶片、要管 iPhone、要管 Mac 的硬體工程，還有什麼相機啊、顯示器啊、感測器、電池、數據機等等等這些底層的技術。

那這個安排呢，就開始讓 Apple 選 John 當 CEO 這件事情，好像比較有跡可循了，因為 Apple 過去這個非常成功的這一次翻身呢，就是靠硬體。

折叠屏之谜：为什么芯片自研，屏幕却外包给三星？

Let's take a look at this controversial battle. Apple spent so many years to replace Intel. The most important folding screen of the iPhone Duo, which sold for $1,999—why should you buy it from Samsung? It is even rumored that it will cost $250. This is too expensive. Why does Apple's chip have to do it by itself, but the screen can be handed over to the opponent?

Because Apple may never care about what it wants to produce. But it is said that some core technologies must master their own control. Apple's design is Apple's design. The real production is still handed over to TSMC.

Intel would limit the performance and update speed of Mac. So Apple took the chip design back to their hands. Because this is a very core and key thing. But as long as Samsung can do the best according to Apple's specifications, Apple doesn't have to build a panel factory by itself.

And Apple has been making folding phones for so many years, but they still dare to sell them for so expensive, $1,999. They may have to thank Samsung for spending years in the education market to make the folding screen and the folding technology very mature. But before Apple's folding phone came out, hundreds of millions of people who were using iPhones would not leave Apple's ecosystem because Samsung made folding phones earlier.

So when Apple launches folding phones, as long as its products are good enough, 它還是可以直接把原本的 iPhone 用戶升級上去，對吧。

但是呢 AI 也是這樣嗎？這可能就不一定。

AI 战场三层解析：芯片、模型、执行权

How much do AI have to do for Apple? How much can it hand out? Let's take a look at it in a simpler way.

第一层：AI 在哪里运行

The first thing to look at is where the AI is going to run. Your iPhone has Apple's own designed chip. There is a part that specializes in AI operation. So many simple and common AI work can be done directly on the phone. For example, organize notifications or identify photos.

Otherwise, it is not easy to understand what you are looking at. Even some text processing 也不一定要把資料送到外面的伺服器，這樣的速度會比較快，而且資料就在你手機裡面，這樣就算網路訊號不好，有一些功能還是可以用。

而且你也知道，Apple 最愛強調的就是隱私，因為你的照片、你的訊息、email 這些資料，不需要每一次都先傳出去給別人的雲端處理。所以 Apple 很重視自己掌握晶片這一層。

第二层：谁负责回答你的问题

第二個要看的是誰負責回答你的問題。比如說你問 iPhone 一句、你問 Siri 一句說"幫我整理這封信的重點"，那真的負責看懂你的內容、理解內容最後產生答案的就是 AI 模型。

Apple 自己它有它的模型，但是沒有堅持說所有事情都一定要靠自己的模型完成。最新一代 Apple 的模型本身就有跟 Google 合作，等於是 Apple 它自己有一個大腦，但是其他人的大腦如果更聰明，它也願意拿來用。

這代表說 Apple 並沒有把勝負壓在說"全世界最強的 AI 模型一定要是我做的"這件事情上面，因為它真正的戰場不在這裡。

第三层：谁真正有权替你做事

The advantage of this is that no matter which brain you use, AI will always work for you in the system device of Apple.

This is the third point we want to see. Who really has the power to do things for you? For example, you and Siri said, "Hey, help me find my mom's flight information yesterday. Add it to the form."

AI may first understand what I'm talking about. This part can be used with Apple's model. It's easier. You can also use Google's AI. But next, it needs to know who my mom is. He even came to my message to find a flight and open my form. Finally, he really helped me put these things in.

These are all in the iPhone and all have to go through Apple's system.

类比：借来的大脑，Apple 的钥匙

If you want to imagine it better, you can think of it as Google can borrow an iPhone, a very smart brain. But can this brain enter your room? Can you open a drawer? What can I put in for you? This key is still in Apple's hands.

This may be Apple's thoughts on AI now. Their real battlefield is to control the key to everyone's exit, not to fight a very shallow pre-existing AI model.

Apple 并没有放弃 AI：新任 AI 主管登场

But there is a very important place here. Apple actually did not give up on finding this real AI expert.

At the end of 2025, he found Amar Subramania to be in charge of AI. This person has been at Google for 16 years before. He also worked as a Gemini Assistant. Later, he went to Microsoft to do AI. Now Apple's basic model AI research and AI security are all in charge of him.

新三巨头分工

Let's take a look at Apple's recent personnel arrangement:

  • AI expert is in charge of AI（Amar Subramanya）
  • Johnny Srouji, chip expert, is in charge of chip and hardware engineering
  • John Ternes sits on the CEO seat

This may mean that Apple thinks that the CEO may not be the best AI scientist in the company. He wanted to combine AI, chips, software, iPhone, Mac, Watch, AirPods, and all of these things into a product line that everyone would use. This is what John has been most familiar with and best at doing in the past 25 years.

结论：这个赌注也可能是错的

Now that we know all of this, let's look back at why they chose John Ternes, a hardware engineer, as CEO. This is a good way to put it. It's reasonable to hear this now.

But this bet may also be wrong. If the first thing you open your phone in the future, it's not an app, it's just a chat GPT directly open Gemini, everything starts with AI assistants, even if Apple can control the iPhone, may also slowly lose the most direct relationship with the user.

In fact, it may be simpler. We think too complicated. Maybe Apple's move is not because don't want to burn money to fight the "Predator", maybe it's just that it's lagging behind in the AI trend. So it can only be like this. I don't know which one it is.

So Apple in John Ternes' era, from the numbers, this company is making a lot of money. It's a good deal. It's just a super hard machine.

But the real answer we haven't got is: if the next 10 years of technology really starts from the phone to become an AI assistant, can Apple still control the first entry of iPhone as it did in the past?

互动与结尾

At the same time, I want to ask you: if you are ready to change your phone, you will choose this iPhone Duo folding phone—type 1 in the message area. I will choose iPhone 18 Pro—type 2.

I am currently choosing the 18 Pro, because I care more about whether the lens is good or not. What about you? Comment to discuss with everyone.

If you want to take free Apple US dollar and iPhone 18 Pro, remember to go to the information center to participate.

item.description:
## 一、真正令人意外的观察：Apple 选硬体 CEO，不是"保守"，而是一次极其精准的"战场识别"
大多数评论都在追问"为什么不是 AI 专家当 CEO？"——这个问法本身就掉进了硬件时代的旧框架。**真正的答案藏在 Apple 的组织重组里**：AI 交给 Amar Subramanya，芯片和硬件全交给 Johnny Srouji，John Ternus 只坐 CEO。这三个人的分工暴露了 Apple 对未来十年的赌注：
> **它不打算成为"最聪明的大脑"，而是要成为大脑与世界之间唯一的那把钥匙。**
这跟 Visa 的策略惊人相似——Visa 从不放贷、不发卡、不吸储，却在每一笔交易里抽成，因为它掌握的是"清算通道"。Apple 也一样：让 Google、OpenAI 去烧钱训练模型，让 Samsung 去做折叠屏——但 iPhone 里那个能"打开抽屉、翻你邮件、把航班加进日历"的执行层权限，只有 Apple 有钥匙。**AI 模型是租客，可以随时换；iOS 是房东，永远收租。** 一个硬件 CEO 恰好是这套哲学的最好代言人。

item.title: [Lex Clips] The ice pick lobotomy: The most horrifying experiment in psychiatry | Andrew Scull and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、诺贝尔奖作为"制度性错觉"的显微镜

最令人不安的不是冰锥本身，而是1949 年诺贝尔医学奖颁给了 Moniz。这意味着人类文明最高级别的科学奖励机制，与人类历史上最残酷的医学暴行之间，只隔了 14 年的"证据积累"。这不是个案，而是暴露了一个系统性盲点：诺贝尔委员会的决策周期（往往滞后数十年以"验证"疗效）恰好落在长期后果（人格解体、失禁、僵尸化）尚未浮出水面的窗口期。奖项本身成了一个信号放大器——它没有验证真相，反而把 Freeman 这样的边缘操作者变成了"合法先知"。这个模式在今天并未消失：从沙利度胺到阿片类药物到某些精神药物，奖励机制永远快于毒性显现的时间常数。

二、隐藏的跨领域连接：福特主义如何殖民了精神病学

真正令人毛骨悚然的一句话是他女儿的评价——Freeman 想成为"lobotomy 界的亨利·福特"。这暴露了一个几乎无人讨论的历史暗流：20 世纪早期的工业化逻辑（流水线、标准化、可复制性、缩短单位时间）正在从汽车厂溢出，殖民医学、教育、监狱、精神病院等一切"人的加工场"。"Lobotomobile"（叶切除车）就是流水线思维的极致——把手术室装进卡车，让治疗变成巡回演出。他一个下午做 20-30 例、双手同时操作、20 分钟培训任何人上手——这不是医学，这是工厂节拍（takt time）。当你意识到这一点，你会重新审视今天的"AI 辅助诊断"、10 分钟门诊、精神科药物的算法化处方——福特的幽灵从未离开，只是换了工具。凡是把"人"降解为"标准件"的技术，都携带着 lobotomobile 的基因。

三、出人意料的观察：沉默才是真正的手术刀

Scull 用了一个惊人的措辞——"shut up in a double sense"（双重意义上的闭口）：被关起来，且被剥夺了发声资格。这里藏着一个反直觉的因果链：lobotomy 之所以可能，不是因为它有科学，而是因为患者的话语已经被预先"手术"过了——他们的抗议被定义为"疯病的产物"，因此不构成证据。冰锥只是完成了话语系统早已完成的事：把主体转为客体。

这个模式的可怕之处在于它的普适性——任何一个把"当事人的反对"重新编码为"当事人症状"的系统（邪教、极权、某些企业文化、算法推荐"你不喜欢是因为你不懂"），都在执行一次话语层面的 lobotomy。One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest 的天才不在于展示了电击，而在于让一个"疯子"（Chief）成为最后的目击者和讲述者——叙事的复权，才是真正推翻这段历史的手术台。所以最深的问题不是"我们如何避免下一个 lobotomy"，而是：在你今天所处的系统里，谁的话被预先归类为"症状"而非"信息"？

📝 转录文本

被"双重封口"的人：20 世纪精神病学的实验对象

We can discuss a series of therapeutic experiments on people who were shut up in a double sense. They were locked away and their voices were not heated because it was the product of their madness.

And so what we see in the first five decades really of the 20th century is people with a variety of motivations — including the desire to improve the lot of the mentally ill — engaging in uncontrolled experiments that had terrible results. And the science behind it was shaky but nonetheless it existed. It wasn't just plucked out of the sky. And yes, it eventually those things break down.

最极端的例子：叶切除术（Lobotomy）

I mean, the clearest case of that — because it's the most extreme of these, at least in the public imagination — is lobotomy. The idea that you're going to solve psychotic breakdowns in people by excising part of their brain.

Um, initially by drilling holes in the skull and injecting alcohol, or using what looks like a butter knife to break connections between the brain. Uh, and then later, when that process seems to be too slow, the Henry Ford of lobotomy — that his daughter said Walter Freeman aspired to be the Henry Ford of lobotomy, the one who could mechanize the production of it and get it done fast — he invented the ice pick lobotomy, where he used an ice pick in the orbit of the eye, having rendered somebody unconscious after two or three electric shocks. And you banged it through the bone and wiggled it about and severed… I mean, it's just hard to even describe.

So this is from the 1930s to the 1970s.

Yes. Freeman starts his work in 1936, borrowing from the work of the preceding year of a Portuguese neurologist named Egas Moniz. And Moniz wins the Nobel Prize in medicine in 1949 for lobotomy. So, it's important to see that. That was 14 years of experience, and yet that won a Nobel Prize. I'm sure that's one they'd like to retract.

Walter Freeman 与"叶切除车"（Lobotomobile）

So, he popularized Walter Freeman — ice pick.

And his particular specialty after the war became this ice pick lobotomy, because there were over half a million patients in America's mental hospitals. Freeman was convinced this operation was a cure-all. And so, he traveled around in a camper truck which he called the lobotomobile, and he would descend in the summer on state hospitals, and he would teach them how to do this ice pick lobotomy.

This is, by the way, image of the tool.

Yes, those are the tools he used. Originally, he used an actual ice pick, and then he developed this.

This is what he developed. This is the state of the art technology.

State of the art — with a hammer or a mallet.

Oh, no.

Yes, I'm sorry. It's… it's very distressing. I… I don't know.

You having to write about this, by the way.

Really very, very, very, very difficult. I came across, for example, a picture of a woman — naked woman — being dragged away by attendants to be lobotomized, and she's resisting with all her might. And to no avail.

流水线上的手术

You have a picture there of Walter Freeman lobotomizing a patient in Washington state. Freeman was ambidextrous. And when he taught neurology, he would draw simultaneously with his left and right hand, and he could do it perfectly. When he was performing lobotomy, when his right hand got tired, he switched to his left hand. And he sometimes would do 20 or 30 lobotomies in an afternoon.

And he boasted, he said, "You know, I can teach any damn fool to perform a lobotomy in 20 minutes, even a psychiatrist." 'Cuz Freeman was a neurologist and he had a lot of contempt for psychiatrists.

So, um, so this was a very ugly episode.

如何终结：世代更替与抗精神病药物

How did it die away? It really took generational change. Uh, some of these lobotomists continued to operate into the '60s, even to the early '70s. But the younger generation who became acquainted with the really worst failures of that regime — the people on the back wards who were incontinent, who were, um, basically zombies, had lost all mental power — uh, they rebelled against this. And by then, they had a different treatment in the form of antipsychotic drugs, which looked much more like what regular medicine was doing, uh, and didn't have these horrible overtones.

文化记忆：《飞越疯人院》

And of course, in the popular mind, I think the — the probably the most famous, uh, instance of telling the public about some of these interventions was the film of Ken Kesey's novel One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, where you see Jack Nicholson — given, I think, the performance of a lifetime — who is given ECT, electroconvulsive therapy, uh, in a very dramatic rendition of what that was. Not, not really, um, what was going on by the 1970s with ECT, but nonetheless, certainly what had been going on back in the past.

And then finally, when ECT doesn't smash him to bits, they lobotomize him — and the film ends, obviously, with him being smothered to death, 'cuz Chief can't bear to see him in the state that he's in.

Um, so that fixed in the public mind some of the images of these things. It was one of the things that gave, uh, electroconvulsive therapy such a bad name.
